passages.title: The Ever-Living reveals the Book of truth
passages.tafsir:
# Āl ʿImrān 1–6: The Ever-Living reveals the Book of truth

These six ayat open the surah by naming Allah as the only One worthy of worship, and then proving it — first from what He *is* (the Ever-Living, the One Who sustains all that exists), then from what He has *sent down* (the Tawrāh, the Injīl, and now this Qur'an), and finally from what He *does* (shaping every child in the womb, with nothing in the heavens or the earth hidden from Him). What holds the passage together is a single claim argued from more than one direction: *lā ilāha illā Huwa* — there is no god but He. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the first five ayat as an explanation of **tawḥīd**, the Oneness of Allah, which it calls the basic point of difference between Islam and other religions; and it reads ayah 6 as drawing attention to the absolute power and wisdom of Allah.

## The setting: a delegation from Najran

Ibn Kathir notes that Sūrah Āl ʿImrān was revealed in Madinah, as is evident from the fact that the first eighty-three ayat of it relate to the delegation from Najran that arrived in Madinah in the ninth year of the Hijrah. He points forward to the ayah about the *Mubāhalah* (3:61), where he says he will elaborate on the subject. He also mentions that he covered the virtues of Sūrah Āl ʿImrān together with the virtues of Sūrat al-Baqarah at the beginning of his commentary on al-Baqarah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions that it is narrated in some aḥādīth that some Christians came to the Prophet ﷺ and engaged him in a conversation about religion, and that he ﷺ, by the will of Allah, presented these two ayat as arguments confirming the Oneness of Allah — and they had no answer to refute them. (The source reports this without naming a collection, so it is given here as it stands, and no collection is claimed for it.)

**Where the surah sits.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also traces the thread from earlier surahs: Al-Fātiḥah ends with a prayer for guidance to the straight path; Al-Baqarah opens by showing that the prayer has been accepted — *Alif Lām Mīm. This Book, in which there is no doubt* — and, after many injunctions of Islamic law and frequent mention of the hostility of the disbelievers, closes with the prayer *"Help us, then, against disbelieving people."* Āl ʿImrān, he says, takes up that closing prayer and elaborates it: how to deal with those who reject the message, and the need to strive against them verbally and physically.

## Ayah 1: Alif Lām Mīm

Ibn Kathir refers the reader to his explanation of *Alif Lām Mīm* at the opening of Sūrat al-Baqarah rather than repeating it here.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places these disconnected letters among the **mutashābihāt** — words of hidden meaning — and says plainly that their real meaning is a secret between Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. It is worth sitting with that: the surah that will go on to argue so carefully for tawḥīd begins with three letters whose meaning we are not given.

## Ayah 2: the argument from what Allah is

**"Allah! There is no god worthy of worship except Him — the Ever-Living (al-Ḥayy), the One Who sustains all that exists (al-Qayyūm)."**

Ibn Kathir points here to his treatment of the same words in Āyat al-Kursī (2:255), and mentions a hadith — cited there, and not named to any collection in this material — that **Allah's Greatest Name is contained in these two ayat**: the one in Āyat al-Kursī and the one before us here.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this a **rational proof** of tawḥīd — in the terminology of Islamic theology, a proof built on rational argument rather than on a report — and unpacks it beautifully. Worship, he explains, means presenting oneself before somebody in utter submission and humility. That act therefore requires that the one worshipped occupy the highest point of honour and power and be most perfect from every angle. So ask of any candidate for worship: can it hold *itself* in existence? Anything that cannot sustain its own being, and is instead dependent on something else for its very existence, could hardly claim any honour or power in its own right.

Run that test across the whole field. Idols carved in stone, or water, or trees — and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds pointedly, **even angels and apostles**: none of them has the power to come into being by itself, nor to sustain itself. "The only Being worthy of worship," he concludes, "is the One who has always been Alive and Present and shall always live and sustain." That Being is none but Allah.

Notice how *al-Ḥayy* and *al-Qayyūm* work as a pair. Ibn Kathir's rendering of *al-Qayyūm* is "the One Who sustains and protects all that exists" — the One who holds up everything that depends on Him. Life that is always alive and present, holding up all that cannot hold itself. That, and nothing less, is what deserves a forehead on the ground.

## Ayat 3–4: the argument from what Allah has sent down

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān labels ayah 3 the **reported proof** — in the same theological terminology, a proof grounded in a verse of a divine book, a declaration by an authority, or a report from a trustworthy narrator, as opposed to the rational proof just given.

**The Book, sent down with truth.** On *"He has sent down the Book to you with truth,"* Ibn Kathir says: He revealed the Qur'an to you, O Muhammad, in truth — meaning there is no doubt or suspicion that it is revealed from Allah. Allah revealed the Qur'an with His knowledge; the angels testify to this fact; and Allah is sufficient as a Witness.

**Confirming what came before.** On *"confirming what came before it,"* Ibn Kathir explains that this means the previously revealed Books sent to the servants and prophets of Allah. The confirmation runs both ways: those Books testify to the truth of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an testifies to the truth those Books contained — including their news and glad tidings of Muhammad's ﷺ prophethood and of the revelation of the Glorious Qur'an.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the argumentative force of this: the principle of tawḥīd as described in the Qur'an is not something peculiar to the Qur'an or to the Prophet of Islam ﷺ. Allah sent scriptures such as the Tawrāh and the Injīl, and sent His prophets, in earlier times, and this is what they all professed and all brought as the message. When the Qur'an came it simply confirmed their truth — it did not present some new claim that people would struggle to understand or accept.

He then makes the point at length as a kind of historical argument. The agreement of a large number of people on a certain principle from the very beginning of humanity may be taken as a natural proof of its reality, if they belong to different times and places and have no means of communicating with each other. So trace the chain: Ādam, the first prophet to present the message of tawḥīd to human beings; then, when the ways of his progeny had shifted away from the original message, Nūḥ calling people towards the same principle; then Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb (peace be upon them), born in Iraq and Syria, rising with the same call; then Mūsā, Hārūn and the prophets after them in order; then, after another long passage of time, ʿĪsā with the same call; and finally Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, who graced the world with the call common to all of them. Up to his time, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, some one hundred and twenty-four thousand blessed prophets had been born in different periods, speaking different languages, living in different countries — and all of them told and taught the same truth. Most never even had the chance to meet each other. They lived in an age when communication through writing was not in vogue, so no one could reach another prophet's books and pick up his call as his own. Each had no source of information about the others except the revelation he received from Allah. The consensus of such a large body of men would be enough to establish the principle even regardless of their intrinsic trustworthiness; and when one looks at their personal qualities, and the highest possible standards of truth and justice they set, one has to believe that their message is true and their call authentic.

**A necessary clarification.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a footnote worth keeping in mind: wherever the Qur'an speaks of the Tawrāh and the Injīl, it refers to the original books revealed to Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them) — this should not be confused with the present Old and New Testaments.

Ibn Kathir fills in the details of ayat 3–4: the Tawrāh was sent down to Mūsā son of ʿImrān, the Injīl to ʿĪsā son of Maryam; *"aforetime"* means before the Qur'an was revealed; and *"as a guidance to mankind"* means guidance for people **in their time**.

**The Criterion.** On *"and He sent down the Furqān"* — the Criterion, or Standard — Ibn Kathir explains it as the distinction between misguidance, falsehood and deviation on one hand, and guidance, truth and piety on the other. It is so because of the indications, signs, plain evidences and clear proofs it contains, and because of its explanations and clarifications. A criterion is not merely a set of assertions; it is what lets you *tell things apart*. That is what revelation puts in a believer's hands.

**The warning that closes ayah 4.** On *"those who disbelieve in the āyāt of Allah,"* Ibn Kathir says this means they denied them, refused them, and unjustly rejected them — and for them there is a severe torment on the Day of Resurrection. On *"and Allah is ʿAzīz"* he says: His grandeur is invincible and His sovereignty is infinite. And *Dhū-Intiqām*, All-Able of Retribution — retribution, Ibn Kathir specifies, from those who reject His signs and defy His honourable messengers and great prophets.

## Ayat 5–6: the argument from what Allah does

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the last two ayat further fortify the doctrine of tawḥīd on the ground that the attributes of **all-encompassing knowledge** and **unlimited power** are strong proofs that He is the One who possesses eternal, all-encompassing knowledge and whose power controls everything, and that He alone rightly deserves to be worshipped. Anyone having imperfect knowledge and limited power cannot be entrusted with this exalted station.

**Ayah 5** — *"Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah."* Ibn Kathir states simply that Allah has perfect knowledge in the heavens and the earth, and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch.

**Ayah 6** — *"He is the One Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills."* Ibn Kathir: He creates you in the wombs as He wills — whether male or female, handsome or otherwise, happy or miserable. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on the wonder of it: Allah shapes all men and women in the wombs of their mothers according to His supreme wisdom, which has created billions of men and women with clear, distinguishable features establishing the identity of each individual as distinct from all others. He is, therefore, the only One who should be worshipped.

Then the ayah closes as ayah 2 opened: *lā ilāha illā Huwa* — but now with two different names, **al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm**, the Almighty, the All-Wise. Ibn Kathir draws the inference: He is the Creator and thus is the only deity worthy of worship, without partners; His is the perfect might, wisdom and decision.

**Why the womb, and why here.** Ibn Kathir says this ayah refers to the fact that ʿĪsā son of Maryam is a created servant, just as Allah created the rest of mankind: Allah created him in the womb of his mother and shaped him as He willed. How, then, could ʿĪsā be divine, as the Christians claim? ʿĪsā was created in the womb and his creation changed from stage to stage — as Allah says elsewhere, *"He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three veils of darkness"* (39:6).

## Living it

**Test what you lean on.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's argument from *al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm* is a test you can actually run on your own heart. Whatever you turn to in hope or fear — money, status, a person, your own competence — ask whether it can hold itself in existence. On the reasoning he sets out, what cannot sustain its own being has no honour or power in its own right, and so cannot carry the weight you are placing on it. Only the One who is always Alive and Present is worth that weight of dependence.

**Read the Qur'an as a criterion, not only as a comfort.** Ibn Kathir defines the Furqān by what it enables: telling misguidance and falsehood apart from guidance and truth, by the evidences, proofs and clarifications it contains. That means engaging it with attention, so that it actually sharpens your judgement.

**Let ayah 5 sit with you.** Nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah — not the sin done where no one is watching, and not the good done where no one thanks you. Nothing escapes His watch.

**Ayah 6 speaks to why you are the way you are.** Your form and your circumstances — Ibn Kathir's list includes male or female, and appearance, and the outcome of happiness or misery — were shaped in a place you could not see, and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, according to a supreme wisdom that has given every single person features distinguishing them from everyone else. The names that close the ayah are *al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm*: His, says Ibn Kathir, is the perfect might, wisdom and decision — and He is therefore the only One deserving of your worship.

passages.title: Clear verses, ambiguous verses, and the firm-rooted
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat set out how the Qur'an is to be read — and what kind of heart is fit to read it. Ayah 7 divides the Book into verses of settled, plain meaning (*muḥkamāt*) and verses whose exact intent is not fully open to us (*mutashābihāt*), then divides people by how they handle that difference. Ayat 8 and 9 are the prayer that the second kind of person — the one who submits rather than schemes — is left saying. The unit holds together as a single movement: **a fact about revelation, a diagnosis of the heart, and a duʿāʾ.**

## The conversation that lies behind ayah 7

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān places these words in a specific scene. The sūrah has just established Allah's Oneness, and now answers doubts raised against it. A group of Christians came to the Prophet ﷺ and began talking about religion. He ﷺ refuted the doctrine of Trinity in detail and proved the Oneness of Allah with reference to His eternal existence, His perfect power, His all-encompassing knowledge and His utterly unique creativity — a One who had to be one and indivisible. The Christians had to accept these premises. Once *tawḥīd* was established, the converse — belief in Trinity — was left with nowhere to stand.

So they shifted ground. They raised doubts about some words of the Qur'an in which ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) is called *Rūḥullāh*, the Spirit of Allah, and *Kalimatullāh*, the Word of Allah — arguing that this language gave him a share in the divinity of Allah.

Ayah 7 is the answer. Maʿārif explains that expressions of this sort fall into the category of *mutashābihāt*: the outward meaning is not what is intended. They are, rather, a secret between Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, whose reality cannot become manifest to others — and for whom it is not even appropriate to go about determining possible meanings for such words. What is required is faith: that whatever Allah has elected to mean through them is the truth. It is not permissible to dig deeper and mount further research in that direction.

Notice what has happened. The argument was lost on the clear ground, so it was moved to the unclear ground. That is the exact manoeuvre ayah 7 goes on to name.

## Two kinds of verses

**Muḥkamāt.** Maʿārif (citing Mazhari) defines them as verses whose meaning is open and clear to one who knows the rules of Arabic grammar fairly well. Ibn Kathir describes them as entirely clear and plain, the foundations of the Book, "plain for everyone."

**Mutashābihāt** — verses whose definite meanings are unknown. Maʿārif's definition is relative to the first: when the meanings and explanations of particular verses are *not* clear to such a person, those verses are *mutashābihāt*. Ibn Kathir says the same: they are "not entirely clear for many, or some people," because they carry several meanings — some that agree with the *muḥkam*, and some that carry other literal indications, although those meanings might not be the ones desired.

Ibn Kathir also gives a working list. The *muḥkamāt* are the ayat that explain the abrogating rulings, the allowed, the prohibited, the laws, the limits, the obligations — rulings that should be believed in *and* implemented. The *mutashābihāt* include the abrogated ayat, parables, oaths, and what should be believed in but not implemented.

Muḥammad bin Isḥāq bin Yasār, quoted by Ibn Kathir, adds a striking description of the *muḥkamāt*: they contain "proof of the Lord, immunity for the servants and a refutation of opponents and of falsehood. They cannot be changed or altered from what they were meant for." And of the unclear ayat he said that they can — but must not — be altered and changed, and that this is a test from Allah to the servants, just as He tested them with the allowed and the prohibited. They must not be altered to imply a false meaning or be distorted from the truth.

That last point is worth pausing on. The presence of the unclear in the Book is not an oversight. It is part of the examination.

## "They are the mother of the Book"

Of the *muḥkamāt*, ayah 7 says **hunna umm al-kitāb** — rendered literally as "mother verses," and translated by Ibn Kathir as "the foundations of the Book." Ibn Kathir: they are the basis of the Qur'an, and should be referred to for clarification when warranted. Maʿārif: they are the very root and essence of all the teachings, their meanings and explanations free of doubt or ambiguity.

From this comes the governing rule of the whole passage. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: those who refer to the *muḥkam* ayat in order to understand the *mutashābih* will have acquired the correct guidance — and vice versa. Maʿārif puts it as a hard test: since the exact intention of the *mutashābihāt* remains uncertain, the correct method is to harmonize them with the *muḥkamāt*; **any interpretation of a *mutashābih* verse that goes against the *muḥkamāt* should be rejected absolutely**, and only what does not clash with them may be given credence.

Applied to the Christians' argument: the Qur'an says of ʿĪsā, "He was not more than a servant. We granted Our favor to him" (43:59), and, "Verily, the likeness of ʿĪsā before Allah is the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him: 'Be!' and he was" (3:59). These and several others like them show clearly that he is a chosen servant of Allah, created by Him. To close one's eyes to all of these and coil instead around *Kalimatullāh* and *Rūḥ minhu* — deducing from them meanings that are against the *muḥkamāt* — is, in Maʿārif's words, simply a case of going astray and being obstinate.

Maʿārif adds the principle underneath: the real meanings of the *mutashābihāt* are known to Allah alone. It is He who, in His mercy and favour, informs whomever He chooses of whatever part of the unknown He wills. It is therefore not correct to try to impose a meaning based on one's personal opinion.

## Three words that describe the crooked reader

Ayah 7 does not begin by saying these people are mistaken. It says something about their hearts first.

**Zaygh** — "those in whose hearts there is a deviation." Ibn Kathir glosses it as those who are misguided and deviate from truth to falsehood. The crookedness is in the heart *before* it appears in the argument. The reading follows the heart, not the other way round.

**Ibtighāʾ al-fitnah** — "seeking al-fitnah." Ibn Kathir: they seek to misguide their following by pretending to prove their innovation by relying on the Qur'an — on the *mutashābih* of it — though in reality this is proof against them and not for them. They go to the ambiguous precisely *because* its wordings encompass such a wide area of meanings that they can be altered to conform with a false interpretation. The *muḥkam* cannot be altered, because it is clear, and so it stands as unequivocal proof against them.

**Ibtighāʾ taʾwīlihi** — "seeking its taʾwīl," which Ibn Kathir explains here as altering the verses as they desire.

Maʿārif draws the contrast: people who are gentle in nature do not go about investigating much into the *mutashābihāt*. They accept these verses and simply believe in them as the true Word of Allah, realising that He, for some wise consideration of His, did not reveal their meaning to us. That approach, it says, is the safest and the most cautious. Quite contrary to this are those with crookedness in their hearts, who go on investigating and deliberating in order to justify meanings that suit their fancies and lead people astray. For such people, stern warnings have appeared in the Qur'an and Hadith.

## "But none knows its taʾwīl except Allah" — and where the reciter stops

This is the passage's most discussed point, and Ibn Kathir handles it with real care. The Arabic runs: *wa mā yaʿlamu taʾwīlahu illā Allāh — wa'r-rāsikhūna fi'l-ʿilmi yaqūlūna āmannā bih.* Everything depends on whether you pause after "except Allah" or read on through "and those who are firmly grounded in knowledge."

Ibn Kathir notes that the scholars of Qur'an recitation held different opinions about pausing at Allah's Name here. That stop was reported from ʿĀʾishah, ʿUrwah, Abū ash-Shaʿthāʾ and Abū Nahīk. Others pause after *"and those who are firmly grounded in knowledge,"* saying that the Qur'an does not address people with what they cannot understand — and Ibn Abī Najīḥ said that Mujāhid said that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "I am among those who are firmly grounded in its taʾwīl." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had supplicated for his benefit: *"O Allah! Bestow on him knowledge in the religion and teach him the taʾwīl."*

Ibn Kathir then shows that *taʾwīl* itself carries two meanings in the Qur'an:

1. **The true reality of things, and what they will turn out to be** — as in Yūsuf's words, "O my father! This is the taʾwīl of my dream aforetime" (12:100), and "Await they just for its taʾwīl? On the Day its taʾwīl is finally fulfilled" (7:53), referring to the true reality of the Resurrection they were told about. If *this* is the meaning intended in 3:7, then pausing at Allah's Name is warranted, because only Allah knows the true reality of things — and "those who are firmly grounded in knowledge" then connects to what follows: *they say, "We believe in it."*

2. **Explanation and description** — as in "Inform us of the taʾwīl of this" (12:36), meaning its explanation. If *this* is the meaning, then pausing after "and those who are firmly grounded in knowledge" is warranted, because the scholars do have general knowledge in, and understand, what they were addressed with, even though they do not have knowledge of the true reality of things. Ibn Kathir gives an example of that kind of explanation: "And your Lord comes, and the angels, in rows" (89:22) means your Lord will come, and the angels will come in rows.

Both readings are presented as warranted; Ibn Kathir does not force one. Related to this, he cites what has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that **tafsir is of four types**: tafsir that the Arabs know in their language; tafsir that no one is excused of being ignorant of; tafsir that the scholars know; and tafsir that only Allah knows. Some of the Book is simply not our portion — and knowing that is itself knowledge.

Whichever pause you take, the confession is the same: **"We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."** Ibn Kathir explains: they believe in the *mutashābih*, and both the *muḥkam* and the *mutashābih* are true and authentic, each testifying to the truth of the other — because both are from Allah, and nothing that comes from Allah is ever met by contradiction or discrepancy: "Had it been from other than Allah, they would surely have found therein many a contradiction" (4:82).

## From the Sunnah: a warning to take seriously

ʿĀʾishah related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this ayah — from "It is He Who has sent down to you the Book" through to "and none receive admonition except men of understanding" — and then said: **"When you see those who follow what is not so clear of the Qur'an, then they are those whom Allah described, so beware of them."** Ibn Kathir notes that this is the wording recorded by al-Bukhārī, who records it in the tafsir of this very ayah; Muslim recorded it in the book of *Qadar* in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and Abū Dāwūd in the *Sunnah* section of his *Sunan*. Imām Aḥmad recorded it from ʿĀʾishah with the wording, "When you see those who argue in it, then they are those whom Allah meant. Therefore, beware of them." Maʿārif cites the same report from ʿĀʾishah, attributing it to Bukhari.

Maʿārif also relays, from Ibn Kathir with reference to Ṭabarānī, a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ named three apprehensions he had about his ummah: that they become wealthy and start to envy one another, resulting in rifts and bloodshed; that the Book of Allah be trifled with — that even the uninitiated and ignorant claim its perfect understanding, and that what is not supposed to be understood becomes the very object of deliberation and investigation, although Allah alone knows its meaning; and that they allow their knowledge, once increased, to go to waste by forsaking the effort to increase it further.

## Who the firmly rooted actually are

What the passage praises in the *rāsikhūn* is not erudition. Ibn Kathir cites Nāfiʿ bin Yazīd, recorded by Ibn al-Mundhir in his Tafsir: *"Those firmly grounded in knowledge are those who are modest for Allah's sake, humbly seek His pleasure, and do not exaggerate regarding those above them, or belittle those below them."* And *"none receive admonition except men of understanding"* — *ulū'l-albāb* — means, says Ibn Kathir, those who have good minds and sound comprehension, who understand, contemplate and grasp the meaning in the correct manner.

Muslim scholars have offered different explanations of who the *rāsikhūn* are. Maʿārif holds that the weightier position identifies them with Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamāʿah, the main body of Muslims: those who give credence only to that interpretation of Qur'an and Sunnah which is authentically reported from the blessed Companions and the righteous generations after them and upon which there is the consensus of the Muslim community; who believe the *muḥkamāt* to be the axis and centre of the Book; and who, humbly confessing the limits of their own knowledge and insight, leave the real meanings of the *mutashābihāt* to Allah. They are never proud of their knowledge, however perfect it may be, nor of the strength of their faith. Instead they constantly pray to Allah, seeking steadfastness, grace and mercy from Him. They do not have mischief-prone temperaments that would instigate them to make the *mutashābihāt* alone the object of their intellectual pursuit. They take both kinds of verse to be the truth, because they firmly believe both have emanated from one single source.

Maʿārif adds a clean summary: the need to find out the meanings of the *muḥkamāt* was useful and essential for us, and Allah has not kept those meanings secret — they have been made very open and clear. Since Allah has elected, for some wise consideration of His, not to disclose the meanings of the *mutashābihāt*, it is simply not necessary for us to find them out. That we believe in them as they are is quite sufficient.

## Ayah 8: the prayer of a heart that knows it can slip

**"Our Lord! Let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us."** Ibn Kathir: do not deviate our hearts from the guidance after You allowed them to acquire it; do not make us like those who have wickedness in their hearts, who follow the *mutashābih* in the Qur'an; rather, make us remain firmly on Your straight path and true religion.

Look at the placement. The people just praised for depth of knowledge immediately ask not to be led astray. Their learning has not made them feel safe. As Maʿārif notes on the sequence: the previous verse mentioned those well-grounded in knowledge who, in spite of their excellent knowledge, were not proud of it but chose instead to have faith in what comes from their Lord — and this verse mentions a further excellence of theirs: that they pray for steadfastness on the right path, not for any worldly gain, but for salvation in the life to come.

**"And grant us mercy from Yourself" — *min ladunka*.** Ibn Kathir: from You — mercy with which You make our hearts firm and increase our faith and certainty. **"Truly, You are al-Wahhāb"** — the Bestower.

Maʿārif draws the doctrinal point: guidance and straying are from Allah alone. When He intends to guide someone, He makes his heart tilt towards what is good and right; and when He decides to let someone go astray, He turns his heart away from the straight path. It relates this to a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: there is no heart that is not between two of Allah's fingers — He makes it firm on the truth as long as He wills, and turns it away from the truth when He wills. He is Allah, absolute in power; He does what He wills. So those who are concerned about how to remain firm in their faith go to the source, requesting and praying to Allah for steadfastness.

And the Prophet ﷺ did exactly that. Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr recorded from Umm Salamah that he ﷺ used to supplicate: **"O You Who changes the hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion"** — and then he recited this very ayah. Maʿārif cites the same duʿāʾ in the plural: *O reverser of hearts, make our hearts firm on the faith chosen by You.*

## Ayah 9: why the prayer ends where it does

**"Our Lord! Verily, it is You Who will gather mankind together on the Day about which there is no doubt. Verily, Allah never breaks His Promise."**

The duʿāʾ does not end with a request. It ends with the horizon that gives the request its weight. Ibn Kathir explains their words: O our Lord, You will gather Your creation on the Day of Return, judge between them and decide over what they disputed about; thereafter You will reward or punish each according to the deeds they did in this life.

Read the passage backwards from here and it clicks into place. Ayah 7 opened with people *disputing* over the Book. Ayah 9 closes with the Day on which Allah Himself decides what they disputed about. That is the answer to argument-for-argument's-sake: a Day is coming when the matter is settled by the One who revealed the Book, and He never breaks His Promise.

## Living it

- **Read the unclear in the light of the clear, never the reverse.** This is the one rule both commentaries build everything on.
- **When a verse's reality is beyond you, say "we believe in it; all of it is from our Lord" — and stop.** Maʿārif calls that approach the safest and the most cautious. It is not intellectual laziness; ayah 7 makes it the mark of the firmly rooted.
- **Watch the motive, not just the argument.** Ayah 7 traces the twisting of verses back to *zaygh* in the heart. Before disputing, ask what you are actually seeking.
- **Be wary of those who live in the ambiguous.** The Prophet ﷺ said, in ʿĀʾishah's report recorded by al-Bukhārī, to beware of them.
- **Keep making the duʿāʾ of ayat 8 and 9.** Knowledge is no guarantee of steadfastness. The most learned in this passage are the ones praying.

passages.title: Wealth will not avail; the sign of Badr
passages.tafsir:
# Wealth will not avail; the sign of Badr (3:10–13)

These four ayat move from a warning to a proof. Ayat 10 and 11 tell those who reject faith that their wealth and their offspring will do nothing for them against Allah, and point to how such people ended before. Ayah 12 turns that into a direct announcement of defeat, and ayah 13 hands them the evidence: Badr. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the sequence exactly this way — the discourse shifts from verbal confrontation with the disbelievers to warning of a coming physical encounter, as pointed out in ayah 12, "You shall soon be overcome," with ayat 10 and 11 serving as the introduction to it.

## Ayah 10: the two things that always fail

**"Neither their properties nor their offspring will avail them whatsoever against Allah."** The ayah does not call wealth and children worthless; it says they will not *avail* — they will not shield or buy anything back against Allah.

Ibn Kathir explains "those who disbelieve" as those who disbelieved in Allah's signs, denied His Messengers, defied His Books and did not benefit from His revelation to His Prophets. And what they were granted in this life of wealth and offspring, he says, shall not avail them with Allah, nor save them from His punishment and severe torment.

He gathers other ayat that press the same point:

- **"The Day when their excuses will be of no profit to wrongdoers. Theirs will be the curse, and theirs will be the evil abode."** (40:52)
- **"So let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; in reality Allah's plan is to punish them with these things in the life of this world, and that their souls shall depart while they are disbelievers."** (9:55) — the very possessions that look like favour are the instrument of the punishment.
- **"Let not the free disposal and affluence of the disbelievers throughout the land deceive you. A brief enjoyment; then their ultimate abode is Hell; and worst indeed is that place for rest."** (3:196–197) — the affluence is brief; it is not the ending.

**"And it is they who will be fuel of the Fire."** Ibn Kathir says plainly what this means: they will be the wood with which the Fire is kindled and fed. In this world they owned things and consumed them; there they are what is consumed. Ibn Kathir places beside it: **"Certainly you and that which you are worshipping now besides Allah are but fuel for Hell!"** (21:98) — the objects of their devotion burn alongside them.

## Ayah 11: "like the daʾb of the people of Firʿawn"

The Arabic word is *daʾb*, and the classical commentators read it slightly differently. Ibn Kathir reports that Ad-Daḥḥāk said that Ibn ʿAbbās said the ayah means, "Like the **behaviour** of the people of Firʿawn," and that this is also the tafsir of ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, Ad-Daḥḥāk and others. Other scholars said it means, "Like the **practice, conduct, likeness** of the people of Firʿawn." Ibn Kathir's verdict is that these meanings are all plausible, for *daʾb* means practice, behaviour, tradition and habit — a settled way of going on, something done so persistently it becomes a person's signature.

So the word names their conduct — **"they belied Our signs"**, as Firʿawn's people did. And Ibn Kathir draws out the outcome that follows: the ayah indicates that the disbelievers will not benefit from their wealth or offspring; rather, they will perish and be punished. This is the same end the people of Firʿawn and the previous nations met — those who rejected the Messengers, the signs, and the proofs of Allah that they were sent with.

**"So Allah punished them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment."** Ibn Kathir comments: His punishment is severe and His torment is painful. None can escape Allah's grasp, nor does anything escape His knowledge. Allah does what He wills and prevails over all things; it is He to Whom everything is humbled, and there is no deity worthy of worship, nor any Lord except Him.

## Ayah 12: "Say to those who disbelieve: you will be defeated"

Now the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to *announce* it. Ibn Kathir splits the two verbs across two worlds: Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to proclaim to the disbelievers **"You will be defeated"** — in this life; **"and you will be gathered together"** — on the Day of Resurrection; **"to Hell, and worst indeed is that place of rest."**

**Who are "those who disbelieve" here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the natural question: some readers may doubt this, since not every disbeliever in the world has in fact been overcome. The answer given is that the doubt is unfounded, because those referred to here are the disbelievers and Jews of that particular time — among whom the pagans were overcome when killed or taken prisoner, and the Jews were overcome through killing or imprisonment as well as through jizyah and extradition. So this "overcoming" simply does not refer to disbelievers universally; it is a specific announcement to a specific audience.

**The setting.** Ibn Kathir records that Muhammad bin Isḥāq bin Yasār reported from ʿĀṣim bin ʿUmar bin Qatādah that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gained victory at the battle of Badr and went back to Al-Madinah, he gathered the Jews in the marketplace of Banū Qaynuqāʿ. (This is a historical report transmitted by Ibn Isḥāq; it is not a narration from any named hadith collection.) That is why ayah 13's "There has already been a sign **for you**" is addressed, as Ibn Kathir puts it, to those "who said what you said" — and the sign is an event they had just watched happen.

## Ayah 13: Badr as evidence

**"There has already been a sign for you."** The word is *āyah*, and Ibn Kathir glosses it here as **proof**: proof that Allah will make His religion prevail, award victory to His Messenger, make His Word apparent and His religion the highest. Badr is not being recalled as a war story. It is being submitted as evidence.

**"In the two armies that met."** Ibn Kathir: two camps, that met in combat, at Badr. **"One was fighting in the cause of Allah"** — the Muslims; **"and as for the other, in disbelief"** — the idolaters of Quraysh at Badr.

**The disparity.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the figures: the disbelievers had about a thousand men, seven hundred camels and a hundred horses, while the Muslim mujahidin were just over three hundred, with a total of seventy camels, two horses, six suits of armour and eight swords. Read those last numbers slowly. Six suits of armour and eight swords, against a thousand men.

**"They saw them with their own eyes twice their number."** Here Ibn Kathir offers two readings of who saw whom:

- First: the *idolaters* thought that the Muslims were twice as many as they were, for Allah made this illusion a factor in the victory that Islam had over them.
- Then he reports that it was said the meaning is that the *Muslims* saw twice as many idolaters as they were, yet Allah gave them victory over the disbelievers.

He then quotes ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd: "When we looked at the disbelievers' forces, we found that they were twice as many as we were. When we looked at them again, we thought they did not have one man more than we had" — and he connects this to **"And when you met, He showed them to you as few in your eyes and He made you appear as few in their eyes."** (8:44)

So the two readings are not rivals but two moments, and Ibn Kathir sets them out in order. When the two camps saw each other, the Muslims thought the idolaters were twice as many as they were, **so that they would trust in Allah and seek His help**; and the idolaters thought the believers were twice as many as they were, **so that they would feel fear, horror, fright and despair**. Then, when the two camps stood in lines and met in battle, Allah made each camp look smaller in the eyes of the other, so that they would be encouraged to fight each other — **"so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained"** (8:42), meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, so that truth and falsehood are distinguishable, the word of faith prevails over disbelief and deviation, the believers prevail and the disbelievers are humiliated.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the mercy hidden in the number. The disbelievers' actual number was **three** times that of the Muslims; had the believers realised it, they may have been overawed. Seeing "twice" made them turn to Allah more fervently — and they had hopes of Allah's help and of ultimate victory because they had placed their total trust in Allah, were steadfast, and sincerely believed the promise revealed to them: **"If there be among you a hundred patient ones, they shall overcome two hundred."** (8:66) That same source notes this seeing-as-twice belonged to a particular moment; at another time each group saw the other as few, as appears later in Sūrah al-Anfāl.

Two armies stood on the same ground, and each was shown something different — the same divine arrangement drawing one camp to rely on Allah and filling the other with dread.

**"And Allah supports with His victory whom He wills."** The believers had no material margin to explain the outcome. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel: **"And Allah has already made you victorious at Badr, when you were a weak little force."** (3:123)

**"Verily, in this is a lesson for those who understand."** The word for lesson is *ʿibrah*, and the ones addressed are *ulū al-abṣār*. Ibn Kathir explains: this should be an example for those who have intelligence and sound comprehension, who should contemplate Allah's wisdom, His decisions and His decree — that He gives victory to His believing servants in this life and on the Day the witnesses stand up to testify. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up: that a small group of people with very little should fight a much stronger group and score a victory, as prophesied in Makkah, is an unusual event full of lessons for the observant and the discerning.

## Living it

**Hold your provision loosely.** Ayah 10 is not a condemnation of having wealth or children; it is a correction of what you expect them to do for you against Allah. Ask honestly what you are actually leaning on when you feel secure.

**Do not be dazzled by what the heedless possess.** That is the explicit instruction in the ayat Ibn Kathir brings alongside this passage — do not let their wealth amaze you, do not let their free disposal in the land deceive you. What you are looking at is the brief enjoyment.

**Watch what you make into a habit.** *Daʾb*, as Ibn Kathir explains it, is practice, behaviour, tradition and habit — conduct that has hardened into a way of life. What the ayah records of the people of Firʿawn and those before them is exactly that: **"they belied Our signs."**

**Count differently.** Badr is submitted as proof that outcomes do not follow from resources. Six suits of armour and eight swords, against a thousand men — and the sources say the believers had hope because they had placed their total trust in Allah, were steadfast, and believed His promise. Their response to seeing themselves outnumbered was to turn to Allah, and that, Ibn Kathir says, is precisely why they were shown the number they were shown.

passages.title: Worldly desires weighed against the better reward
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat set two lists side by side and ask you to compare them. Ayah 14 lays out six things human beings are naturally drawn to in this world; ayah 15 answers with what Allah keeps for those who fear Him; ayat 16-17 tell you who those people are — not by their status, but by the words on their tongues and the shape of their nights.

## Why this passage comes here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the placement. The verses just before dealt with the hostility of the disbelievers and the duty to face it. Now the text explains *why* people set themselves against Islam and Muslims — and the reason for this, and for all evil deeds, is in fact the love of the worldly life. There are all sorts of people who line up against the truth: some driven by greed for wealth or power, some goaded by lust, some defending false ancestral customs. All of it is to grab a share in the temporal enjoyments of the present life that these verses go on to describe. Maʿārif quotes the saying of the Prophet ﷺ that the love of *dunyā* — the worldly life and its enjoyments — is the main source of all errors. So this is no digression into asceticism; it is a diagnosis of the enemy's motive, and a warning that the same motive works on you.

## Ayah 14: "It has been made beautiful"

The verse does not simply say people love these things. It says the love of them **has been made to look attractive** to them — *zuyyina*, a passive verb. And so, as Maʿārif puts it, people go after these things enticed by their glamour, brushing aside any concern for the life to come.

Maʿārif notes the ordering too: women come first, then children, because whatever a man goes about procuring is for the needs of his family, who share it with him. Other forms of wealth and possessions — gold, silver, cattle and tillage — attract people secondarily.

Then Maʿārif asks the obvious question — why has man been made in a way that he is temperamentally attracted to these things? — and answers that Allah has done so in His ultimate wisdom, giving three layers of it.

**First, the world would not function otherwise.** If man were not naturally inclined to and even enamoured with these things, all worldly business would have gone topsy-turvy. Why would anyone sweat on farms and fields, or a trader put his capital and labour into buying and selling? The worker goes out to earn; the well-to-do goes out to hire; the trader displays his best merchandise; the customer walks to the market for what he needs. It was love for what is desirable in this mortal world that brought them all out of their homes — and in this silent process, gave the world a strong and ongoing social system.

**Second, without a taste for pleasure here, we would have no appetite for Paradise.** If man had no liking for the blessings he finds in this mortal world, he would have no taste or desire for the blessings promised in the world to come — and then why would he ever take the trouble of doing good and thus deserving Paradise, or of avoiding evil and thus being safe from Hell?

**Third — and Maʿārif calls this the more significant consideration — it is a test.** Man, with love for these things in his heart, has been put to a test: who becomes engrossed in the enjoyments of the present life and forgets the life to come, and who comes to realize their real and temporal nature, shows concern for them only in proportion to his needs, and channels all his effort into deeds that will make his next life good and safe. Maʿārif cites the Qurʼān's own statement of purpose: *"We made whatever there is on the earth its adornment so that We can test as to who among them acts best"* (18:7).

A careful point follows. Elsewhere the Qurʼān attributes the making-attractive of things to Shayṭān — *"Shayṭān made their deeds look attractive to them"* (8:48; 16:63; 27:24; 29:38). Maʿārif resolves it: there, the reference is to things that are evil religiously and rationally, or to a false sense of adornment that is evil because it transgresses the limits Allah set. Otherwise it is not absolutely bad to adorn lawful things — in fact there may be benefits in it — which is why in our ayah the placing of attraction in things is attributed to Allah.

## The six things named

**Women first.** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah began with women *because the test with them is more tempting*, citing what the Ṣaḥīḥ recorded that the Messenger ﷺ said: "I did not leave behind me a test more tempting to men than women." But he immediately balances it: when one enjoys women for the purpose of having children and preserving his chastity, then he is *encouraged* to do so. Ibn Kathir cites several sayings of the Prophet ﷺ that encourage marriage — that this life is a delight, and the best of its delight is a righteous wife; and the Prophet's ﷺ own words, "I was made to like women and perfume, and the comfort of my eye is the prayer."

Notice the shape of the teaching: the same thing can be a snare or an act of obedience, and the difference is the intention.

**Children.** Ibn Kathir applies the same rule. The desire to have children is sometimes for the purpose of pride and boasting, and as such is a temptation; when the purpose is to reproduce and increase the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ with those who worship Allah alone without partners, it is encouraged and praised. He cites the ḥadīth: "Marry the loving and fertile woman, for I will compare your numbers to the rest of the nations on the Day of Resurrection."

**Heaped treasures of gold and silver — *al-qanāṭīr al-muqanṭarah*.** The scholars of tafsīr held conflicting opinions about the amount of a *qinṭār*, all of which indicate that it is a large amount of money, as ad-Ḍaḥḥāk and other scholars said. Abū Hurayrah said the *qinṭār* is twelve thousand *ūqiyah*, each *ūqiyah* better than what is between the heavens and the earth — recorded by Ibn Jarīr. Here too Ibn Kathir splits by intention: the desire for wealth that results from arrogance and the wish to dominate the weak and control the poor is prohibited; wanting more in order to spend it on acts of worship, on kindness to family and relatives, and on various acts of righteousness and obedience is praised and encouraged in the religion.

**Branded horses — *musawwamah*.** Ibn ʿAbbās said these are the branded, beautiful horses, and Ibn Kathir names Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin ʿAbdullāh bin Abzā, as-Suddī, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, Abū Sinān and others as giving the same explanation; Makḥūl said *musawwamah* refers to the horse with a white-spotted face and white feet. Ibn Kathir gives three kinds of owner: one who keeps horses to be used in the cause of Allah and to fight with when warranted, who is rewarded for this good action; one who collects them to boast and out of enmity to the people of Islam, who earns a burden for his behaviour; and one who keeps them to fulfil his needs while not forgetting Allah's right due on them — and for him these horses provide a shield of sufficiency.

**Cattle** — Ibn Kathir: camels, cows and sheep. **And fertile land** — the land that is used to farm and grow plants.

## The verdict that closes ayah 14

*"That is the enjoyment of the worldly life; and with Allah lies the beauty of the final resort."* Ibn Kathir reads *matāʿ* as the delights of this life and its short-lived joys, and *ḥusn al-maʼāb* as the best destination and reward. Maʿārif draws out the guideline: all these things are there simply to serve a purpose in man's mortal life, and certainly not so that he falls in love with them for their own sake — for the real beauty of the experience lies in one's ultimate resort with Allah in blissful eternity, enjoying what will never perish, diminish or weaken.

Maʿārif adds that these same things can become a sort of punishment right here, quoting: *"So, their wealth and children should not attract you. Allah wants to punish them with these in this lowly life"* (9:55).

**The image to carry away.** Maʿārif quotes the poet-sage Maulana Rumi: as long as the water stays beneath and around the boat it holds the boat up and serves its purpose; but if the water gets *into* the boat, it capsizes it and destroys all that was in it. Similarly, a man's wealth and possessions are means of convenience for his role in this world and the next — provided they do not enter into his heart, sit there, and kill it in the process.

## Ayah 15: the better offer

*"Say: Shall I not tell you what is far better than that?"* Ibn Kathir paraphrases: say, O Muhammad, to the people, "Should I tell you about what is better than the delights and joys of this life that will soon perish?" Maʿārif notes who is addressed — the Prophet ﷺ himself, asked to tell those who become obsessed with the imperfect and perishable blessings of the present life that he is in a position to lead them on to far better ones. These shall be the lot of those who fear Allah and are obedient to Him.

Then the answer: *for those who have taqwā, with their Lord, are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and wives purified, and approval from Allah.*

- **Gardens with flowing rivers** — Ibn Kathir: the rivers run throughout, carrying various types of drinks — honey, milk, wine and water — such that no eye has ever seen, no ear has ever heard, and no heart has ever imagined.
- **Abiding therein** — they shall remain in it forever and ever, and will not want to be removed from it.
- ***Azwāj muṭahharah*, purified spouses** — purified, Ibn Kathir says, from filth, dirt, harm, menstruation, post-birth bleeding, and other things that affect women in this world.
- **Riḍwān — pleasure from Allah** — Allah's pleasure will descend on them and He shall never be angry with them after that. This is why Allah says elsewhere, *"but the pleasure of Allah is greater"* (9:72) — greater, Ibn Kathir explains, than the eternal delight He has already granted them.

**A beautiful observation from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.** Ayah 14 counted *six* blessings that infatuate man; ayah 15 answers with only *three* — the gardens, the purified wives, and the approval of Allah. The rest are not absent from Paradise; Maʿārif walks through each.

*Children* go unmentioned because man loves children in this world as those who help and strengthen him in what he does, and through whom his name lives on. In the Hereafter he would need no such help, nor would he die and need an heir. Whoever has children will have them all with him in Paradise; whoever had none would, to begin with, simply not have the desire for them there — and should someone desire a child, Allah would bless him with one. Maʿārif cites a ḥadīth in Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī in which the Prophet ﷺ said that if a dweller of Paradise wishes to have children, the process of pregnancy, birth and growth would be completed in no time and he would have what he wished for.

*Gold and silver* go unmentioned because in this world they exist so that things may be bought and paid for; in the Hereafter there will be no buying, selling or paying at all — whatever the dweller of Paradise needs will be instantly provided. Incidentally, Maʿārif notes, Paradise itself is not without them: some sayings of the Prophet ﷺ mention that some places of Paradise will have bricks of gold and silver laid one after the other. But in view of the uniqueness of that life, they were not considered worth mentioning.

*Horses* help cover distances here; in the other world there is no travel and no riding — yet, Maʿārif says, sound ḥadīth reports do prove that fine horses will be presented before the dwellers of Paradise on Fridays, which they will ride to go and meet friends and relatives. The same is true of *cattle and tillage*: the services they provide have already been provided in Paradise by Allah directly, without their medium. And should someone there wish, for no necessity at all, to try farming, his wish will be granted — as appears in some reports in al-Ṭabarānī, everything needed will be assembled instantly, and the whole process of ploughing, seeding, ripening and cutting accomplished in no time.

Behind it all stands the Qurʼān's other promise for the people of Paradise, *"and for them there is what they wish for"* — and after such a comprehensive declaration, there remains no need to mention any particular blessing individually.

**And the greatest of the three is the last.** Maʿārif calls the approval of Allah — *riḍwān* — the ultimate thing man can and should aspire to, something one cannot easily conceptualize, after which there is no danger of displeasure from Allah. It reports a ḥadīth that when the people of Paradise have settled down there, happy and content with no desire remaining unfulfilled, Allah will speak to them, asking if they are happy and if they need anything. They will say: our Lord, You have given us everything — what else could we ever need? And Allah will say: now I give you the greatest of all blessings — you all have My approval, that I will never be displeased with you, and nearness forever. Since the danger of Allah's displeasure does not exist in Paradise, Maʿārif adds, there is also no danger that its blessings will ever be taken back or reduced.

Maʿārif closes with the ḥadīth it says summarises the very subject of these verses — reported by Ibn Mājah and al-Ṭabarānī on the authority of Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Worldly life is cursed and cursed is what is in there, except what is used to seek the pleasure of Allah" — and according to another narration, "except the remembrance of Allah and what Allah likes, and except a religious scholar and a student of religious knowledge."

## Ayat 16-17: who these people actually are

Having promised tremendous rewards to those who have taqwā, Allah now describes them — what Ibn Kathir titles the supplication and description of *al-muttaqīn*, His pious servants.

**Their words (ayah 16).** *"Our Lord, we have indeed believed"* — in You, Ibn Kathir explains, in Your Book and Your Messenger — *"so forgive us our sins"* — because of our faith in You and in what You legislated for us; therefore forgive us our errors and shortcomings, with Your bounty and mercy — *"and save us from the punishment of the Fire."* Notice what they do *not* do. They have just been promised Gardens, and their response is to ask for forgiveness and rescue. Faith is their only plea, and even that is offered as a ground for mercy rather than a claim on reward.

**Their character (ayah 17).** Five qualities, each explained by Ibn Kathir:

- **The patient (*al-ṣābirīn*)** — patient while performing acts of obedience and abandoning the prohibitions.
- **The truthful (*al-ṣādiqīn*)** — true concerning their proclamation of faith, by performing the difficult deeds.
- **The devoutly obedient (*al-qānitīn*)** — meaning, they submit and obey Allah.
- **Those who spend (*al-munfiqīn*)** — from their wealth on all the acts of obedience they were commanded: being kind to kith and kin, helping the needy, and comforting the destitute.
- **Those who seek forgiveness in the last hours of the night (*al-mustaghfirīn bil-asḥār*)**.

## The last part of the night

Ibn Kathir says this final phrase testifies to the virtue of seeking Allah's forgiveness in the latter part of the night. It was reported that when Yaʿqūb said to his children *"I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you"* (12:98), he waited until the latter part of the night to say his supplication.

Furthermore, the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Musnad and the Sunan collections recorded through several Companions that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every night, when the last third of it remains, our Lord, the Blessed, the Superior, descends to the lowest heaven, saying, 'Is there anyone to ask Me, so that I may grant him his request? Is there anyone to invoke Me, so that I may respond to his invocation? Is there anyone seeking My forgiveness, so that I may forgive him?'"

The Two Ṣaḥīḥs also recorded that ʿĀʼishah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed Witr during the first part of the night, the middle and the latter parts; then later in his life he would perform it only during the latter part. And ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUmar used to pray during the night and would ask, "O Nāfiʿ! Is it the latter part of the night yet?" — and if Nāfiʿ said yes, Ibn ʿUmar would start supplicating to Allah and seeking His forgiveness until dawn. This was collected by Ibn Abī Ḥātim.

## Living it

The passage closes with *"and Allah is All-Seer of the servants"* — and, says Ibn Kathir, He gives each provision according to what they deserve.

So these ayat do not ask you to despise the six things. Ibn Kathir treats each of them as capable of reward or of ruin depending on the intention behind it — wives, children, wealth and horses all appear in his commentary on both sides of the ledger. Maʿārif says plainly that we can seek the good things of life with moderation and even store them in accordance with our genuine needs, and that in this lies the ultimate good of this life and the life to come; using them in prohibited ways, or indulging so excessively that one forgets the reality after death, is nothing but self-destruction. What the passage asks is that you keep the water outside the boat.

passages.title: Allah's own testimony that Islam is His way
passages.tafsir:
**In brief:** These three ayat put the whole argument of the sūrah on its firmest footing. Allah Himself testifies that He alone is worthy of worship (ayah 18); therefore the only way of life He accepts is submission to Him — Islam (ayah 19); and therefore, when people argue, the Prophet ﷺ is told simply to state where he stands and to invite them, leaving their hearts to Allah (ayah 20). What holds the passage together is a single movement: **testimony → the religion that follows from it → the invitation extended to everyone.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Sūrah Āl ʿImrān began with the confirmation of Allah's Oneness and the refutation of Trinity, and that the subject of *tawḥīd* (Allah's Oneness) reappears here "in a very special manner."

## Ayah 18: the greatest witness in the Book of Allah

**"Allah bears witness that there is no god but He."** Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah bears witness, and Allah is sufficient as a Witness. He is the Most Truthful and Just Witness there is, and His statement is the absolute truth. Before any human being is asked to accept *lā ilāha illā Huwa*, Allah has already declared it about Himself.

Ibn Kathir explains the content of that testimony: **"He Alone is the Lord and God of all creation."** Everyone and everything is His servant, His creation, and in need of Him — while **Allah is the Most Rich, free from needing anyone or anything.** He cites a parallel: "But Allah bears witness to that which He has sent down unto you" (4:166).

**How does Allah "bear witness"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that of the three witnesses named here, Allah's own evidence is given in a figurative sense — meaning that **His Being, His attributes, and the manifestations of His power and creativity throughout the universe are themselves open signs of His Oneness**, and that the Messengers and Books He sent all confirm that same truth.

## Three witnesses, in order

**Allah first, then the angels, then the people of knowledge.**

*The angels* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes them as those who are close to Allah, who carry out His instructions and bear testimony **knowing and seeing** that Allah alone is worthy of worship.

*Ulū al-ʿilm, the people of knowledge* — Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion out: that Allah mentioned their testimony after His own and that of the angels "emphasizes the great virtue of those who have knowledge." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that **Imām al-Ghazālī and Ibn Kathir** both find this a matter of great honour for the ʿulamāʾ, since Allah has mentioned their witness along with His own and that of the angels.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the expression two possible ranges. In the first, *ulū al-ʿilm* means **the blessed prophets and men who have the knowledge of Islam** — knowledge acquired under a formal discipline from Islam's own original sources. In the second, taken in an absolute sense, it may refer to **anyone who, by inquiry based on sound intellectual principles or by deliberating over this universe, arrives at the knowledge of Allah's unity**, even if he is not an ʿālim in the traditional sense. Both readings are offered; neither is presented as the only one.

## "Maintaining justice" — and the two names at the close

**Qāʾiman bil-qisṭ** — Ibn Kathir glosses it briefly and comprehensively: He maintains His creation in justice **in all that He does.**

Then the declaration is repeated — *lā ilāha illā Huwa* — which Ibn Kathir says is to emphasize this fact. And the ayah closes with two of Allah's names, as Ibn Kathir explains them:

- **al-ʿAzīz**, the Almighty — "the Mighty that does not submit to weakness due to His might and greatness."
- **al-Ḥakīm**, the All-Wise — "the Wise in all His statements, actions, legislation and decrees."

## Two scholars from Syria: how this ayah was answered

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, on the authority of **Imām al-Baghawī**, the renowned exegete, that two leading Jewish scholars came to Madinah from Syria. With the township before them, they began talking to each other about how the look of the place matched the prophecy in the Torah that the last of the prophets would live there. Later they came to know that someone very pious lived there whom people referred to as the prophet.

They went to see him ﷺ. The sight of him reminded them of all the attributes the Torah had predicted he would have. They presented themselves before him and said, "You are Muhammad?" He said, "Yes." Again they said, "You are Aḥmad?" He said, "Yes, I am Muhammad and Aḥmad." Then they said: "We are going to ask you a question. If you answer it correctly, we shall embrace Islam." He ﷺ said, "Go ahead and ask." They asked: **"Which is the greatest witness in the Book of Allah?"**

This ayah of *shahādah* was revealed as the answer to their question. He recited it for them, and both embraced Islam immediately.

Sit with the question they chose. Of everything two learned men could have asked to test a prophet, they asked what the greatest testimony in Allah's Book is — and the answer that came down was Allah's testimony to His own Oneness.

## "And to that, O my Lord, I too am a witness"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, citing a hadith in the **Musnad of Aḥmad**, that when the Prophet ﷺ recited this ayah at ʿArafāt, he said right after it:

> *wa anā ʿalā dhālika min ash-shāhidīn, yā Rabb* — "And to that, O my Lord, I too am a witness."

Here is the passage's quiet invitation: after hearing Allah's testimony, you add your own.

A narration from **Imām al-Aʿmash** (cited via Ibn Kathir) says that whoever recites this ayah and then says these words, Allah will say to the angels on the Last Day: "My servant has made a promise while I am the Foremost to keep a promise when I make it, so let my servant be admitted into Paradise."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites a narration from **Sayyidnā Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu)** that the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever recites Āyat al-Kursī (2:255), this ayah *Shahidallāhu* (3:18), and *Qul-illāhumma Mālik al-mulk* up to *bi-ghayri ḥisāb* (3:26–27), Allah will forgive all his sins, admit him to Paradise, and take care of seventy — that is, plenty — of his needs, the simplest of these being his forgiveness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives its source as **Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, with reference to Dailamī**.

## Ayah 19: "the religion with Allah is Islam"

Ibn Kathir states it plainly: **Allah accepts no religion from any person except Islam.** And he defines Islam broadly — it includes obeying all of the Messengers, up to Muhammad ﷺ, who finalized their commission, thus closing all paths to Allah except through him ﷺ. So whoever now meets Allah following a path other than the Prophet's ﷺ, it will not be accepted of him — as Allah says elsewhere, "And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted of him" (3:85).

**Two words worth understanding properly.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes real attention to them.

*Dīn* has more than one meaning in Arabic, one of them being "the way." In the Qur'an's own terminology it stands for **the principles and injunctions common to all the prophets** from Sayyidnā Ādam to Sayyidnā Muhammad ﷺ. Subsidiary injunctions — which have differed during different ages and communities — are covered by other terms: *sharīʿah*, *al-minhāj*, or the later term *madhhab*. Hence: "Allah made you follow the same religion with which He bound Nūḥ" (42:13).

That shared *dīn* is spelled out: belief in the most perfect Being and attributes of Allah and in His being free of all shortcomings; that He alone is worthy of worship, believed from the depth of the heart and confirmed verbally; belief in the Day of Judgment, the final reckoning of deeds, reward and punishment, Paradise and Hell; and belief in every prophet and messenger Allah sent and in all the commandments they brought — again, held in the heart and affirmed aloud.

*Islām*, in its real meaning, is **to submit oneself to Allah and be obedient to His commands.** Given that meaning, those who believed in the prophets of their own time and obeyed the commands of Allah those prophets brought were all entitled to be called Muslims, and their religion was Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the Qur'an's own usage: Nūḥ says, "I have been commanded that I be from among the Muslims" (10:72); Ibrāhīm prays, "Our Lord, make us Muslims, the submitting ones to You, and from our progeny a community of Muslims submitting to You" (2:128); the disciples of ʿĪsā say, "And bear witness that we are Muslims" (3:52).

Sometimes the word is applied in a narrower sense: **the dīn and sharīʿah brought finally by Muhammad ﷺ**, which abrogated all previous ways in religion and shall sustain right through the Day of Judgment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it is in this manner that the Prophet ﷺ explained Islam in the well-known hadith of Jibrāʼīl.

**Which meaning applies here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the word *al-Islām* in this ayah carries the likelihood of both — and that the end-result is the same either way. During the age of every prophet, the religion acceptable in the sight of Allah was that particular Islam which conformed to the revelation and teachings credited to that prophet: the Islam of Mūsā's period was what came in the form of the Torah and his teachings; the Islam of ʿĪsā's period was what came as the Injīl and his teachings. Once laws of an earlier code were abrogated by a later prophet, they no longer remained Islam. So after the coming of the Last of the prophets ﷺ, **the only religion deserving the name Islam is the one that conforms to the Qur'an and his teachings** — and that alone is acceptable in the sight of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion out: since no other religion is acceptable to Allah, it cannot become a source of salvation either. It explicitly rejects the claim — advanced, it says, in the name of the tolerance preached by Islam — that every faith of the world, Judaism, Christianity, even paganism, could each become a source of salvation on condition that its followers perform good deeds and observe good morals. It answers that light and darkness cannot be the same, and that it is impossible that Allah would like disobedience and rebellion against Him just as He likes obedience and submission. Salvation in the Hereafter depends first of all on obedience to Allah and His Messenger; of one deprived of that, the Qur'an says: "We shall not assign weight to their deeds on the Day of Judgment" (18:105).

## Why the People of the Book split apart

The ayah is precise about the cause: they differed **only after knowledge had come to them**, and out of *baghy* — rivalry between them.

Ibn Kathir: some of them wronged others. They differed over the truth out of envy, hatred and enmity for each other, and this hatred made some of them defy those whom they hated **even if they were correct.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies this directly to their disputing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and challenging Islam as false: they did this not because they had any doubts — they knew the truth of the matter through their own scriptures — but because **they were scared of losing their ground against the Muslims.** It names three motives: their malice towards the Muslims, their love for power and influence, and their arrogant self-image as traditional leaders.

Note where the sources locate the fault. Not in a lack of knowledge — knowledge had already come to them — but in *baghy*, and in the motives Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists.

**"Allah is Swift in reckoning."** Ibn Kathir explains *whoever disbelieves in the āyāt of Allah* as whoever rejects what Allah sent down in His Book — Allah will punish him for his rejection, reckon him for his denial, and torment him for defying His Book. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a sobering note on the swiftness: the reckoning starts initially soon after death, when a person passes into the state known as *barzakh* (the interval between death and resurrection), while the detailed accounting for one's deeds, down to the minutest detail, takes place on the Day of Judgment — when the penchant for disputing truth will be exposed.

## Ayah 20: what to say when the arguing will not stop

**"So if they dispute with you"** — Ibn Kathir: so if they argue with you about *tawḥīd*.

**"Say: I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have those who follow me."** Ibn Kathir's gloss: *I have made my worship sincere for Allah Alone without partners, rivals, offspring or companion* — and "those who follow me" means those who followed his religion and embraced his creed. He compares it with "Say: This is my way; I invite unto Allah with sure knowledge, I and whosoever follows me" (12:108).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the counsel here: where the deniers among the People of the Book persist in argument even after the truth of Islam has been proved conclusively, their acceptance or rejection should be of no consequence to the believer, who simply has to declare **that he and those with him have entered the fold of Islam, being in no doubt about its truth.**

**"And say to those given the Scripture and to the unlettered: Do you submit?"** Ibn Kathir sees in this a command from Allah to His servant and Messenger ﷺ to call **both** the People of the Two Scriptures **and** the unlettered idolaters to his religion, way, Law and all that Allah sent him with — and he treats this and similar ayat as clear proofs that the message of Muhammad ﷺ is universal to all creation, as is well established in the religion according to the various texts of the Book and Sunnah. He cites: "Say: O mankind, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah" (7:158), and "Blessed be He Who sent down the criterion to His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds" (25:1).

He adds that **the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and other collections of hadith** record that the Prophet ﷺ sent letters to the kings of the earth during his time and to different peoples — Arabs and non-Arabs, People of the Book and the unlettered — just as Allah had commanded him. And he cites a hadith of Abū Hurayrah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu), which **Muslim** recorded, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! No member of this Ummah, no Jew or Christian, hears of me but dies without believing in what I was sent with, but will be among the people of the Fire."

Ibn Kathir also relates that the Prophet ﷺ said, "I was sent to the red and black," and, "A Prophet used to be sent to his people, but I was sent to all mankind."

**"If they submit, they are rightly guided; if they turn away, your duty is only to convey."** Ibn Kathir: their reckoning is with Allah, their return and final destination is to Him; **it is He Who guides whom He wills and allows whom He wills to stray**, and He has the perfect wisdom and the unequivocal proof for all of this. Hence the closing words, *"and Allah sees the servants"* — for He has perfect knowledge of who deserves to be guided and who does not. He then quotes: "He cannot be questioned for what He does, while they will be questioned" (21:23), because of His perfect wisdom and mercy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ending as comfort. The Prophet ﷺ is being told that his duty is limited to conveying the message of Allah and His commandments. That the message does not seem to get across — that they elect to reject rather than accept — **should really not be a matter of concern for him.** This is something Allah will take care of in His own way, for He is in full sight of what His servants are doing.

## Living it

- **Take your place in the testimony.** The passage does not merely inform you of *lā ilāha illā Huwa*; it names witnesses. Recite ayah 18 and, following what the Prophet ﷺ said at ʿArafāt as reported in the Musnad of Aḥmad, say: *wa anā ʿalā dhālika min ash-shāhidīn, yā Rabb.*
- **Guard knowledge from rivalry.** Ayah 18 places the people of knowledge among the witnesses to Allah's Oneness; ayah 19 describes a community to whom knowledge had already come and who still differed — out of *baghy*, and, as Ibn Kathir says, out of envy, hatred and enmity. Ask Allah for the first and protection from the second.
- **Say your piece; do not force the outcome.** Ayah 20 gives a complete instruction for disagreement: declare your submission plainly, extend the invitation, and then leave it. In Ibn Kathir's words, it is Allah Who guides whom He wills — *"and Allah sees the servants."*

passages.title: Killing prophets and turning from the Book
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:21–25

**What this passage is about.** These five ayat expose a single, terrible pattern: people who were given revelation from Allah, and who used it as a shield rather than a guide. They rejected His signs, killed the prophets sent to them and the righteous men who called for justice, refused to be judged by their own Book when invited to it, and comforted themselves with the idea that the Fire would barely touch them. The passage begins with their crimes (21), states the verdict on their deeds (22), traces the behaviour that flows from it (23), diagnoses the false belief underneath it (24), and ends by placing them before the Day when the accounting will be exact (25).

What holds the unit together is cause and effect. Ayah 24 opens with **"This is because they say…"** — the Qur'an itself links the turning away in ayah 23 back to a lie they told themselves about the Hereafter. And ayah 25 answers that lie by naming the Day they were pretending not to fear.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the shift. The earlier part of Āl ʿImrān is aimed mostly at the Christians. Then in ayah 20, the phrase "those who have been given the Book" widens to include both Christians and Jews. Now, in ayat 21–22, the address narrows again: these verses speak of particular conduct of the Jews.

Ibn Kathir frames the same verses as a chastisement of the People of the Book for their denials of Allah's signs and His Messengers "in the past and more recent times." Whatever specific episodes he has in view, the phrase itself makes one thing clear: the censure is not sealed off in a single distant generation. Ibn Kathir adds why it happened — "due to their defiance and rejection of the Messengers, denial of the truth and refusal to follow it."

Notice too that the Qur'an's own wording in ayah 23 says **"a party of them turned away."** The censure falls on a described conduct and the attitude behind it, not indiscriminately.

## Ayah 21: three crimes named together

**1. Disbelief in the signs of Allah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "those who disbelieve in the verses of Allah" here refers to those who did not believe in the Injīl — the Gospel — and the Qur'an.

**2. Killing the prophets "without right."** Ibn Kathir is careful about the nature of this crime: they killed prophets who came to them "when they conveyed to them what Allah legislated for them, without cause or criminal behaviour committed by these Prophets, for they only called them to the truth." There was no charge that could be brought. The men were killed for the message alone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the force of "unjustly": it means **they knew** they were doing it without justice. This was not confusion or a mistaken verdict. It was killing with the conscience awake.

**3. Killing "those men who order just dealings."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that these were people who taught moderation in deeds and morals. They are named in the same breath as the prophets, though no prophetic office is claimed for them. There is only a man saying: *be just.* And he is killed for it.
