Of this third item Ibn Kathir says it demonstrates "the worst type of arrogance," and he cites the Prophet ﷺ as saying that **arrogance (kibr) is refusing the truth and degrading people.** (The bundle records this teaching from the Prophet ﷺ without naming a collection, so it is conveyed here as Ibn Kathir reports it.) That teaching maps onto the ayah: refusing the truth is what they did to the prophets; degrading people is what they did to those who called for justice. Ibn Kathir adds that this is precisely why "when they rejected the truth and acted arrogantly towards the creation, Allah punished them with humiliation and disgrace in this life, and humiliating torment in the Hereafter." The punishment matches the crime: those who thought themselves above the truth are brought low.

**A report on the scale of it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, relates a narration from the Prophet ﷺ as narrated by Ibn Abī Ḥātim in which, explaining this verse, he said that Banī Isrāʾīl slew forty-three prophets at one and the same time; one hundred and seventy pious elders then stood up asking them to uphold justice, and they were slain as well, on the same day. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this via Bayān al-Qurʼān.) Whatever else one takes from the report, it shows why the ayah pairs the two killings: the prophets and the men who bid justice fell together, in one act of defiance.

**"Then announce to them a painful torment."** Ibn Kathir glosses the punishment as "painful and humiliating" — pain and disgrace together, answering the arrogance described above.

## Ayah 22: the bill for a life's work

*"They are those whose works will be lost in this world and in the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up plainly: because of this whole set of their terrible deeds, all their good deeds have gone to waste both here and there, and when they are punished, they will find no one to assist them.

Two things are worth sitting with here.

**First, "in this world and the Hereafter."** The loss is not deferred entirely. Ibn Kathir has already noted that humiliation and disgrace came upon them in this life as well. Deeds that were meant to build something left nothing standing on either side of death.

**Second, "no helpers."** These were people who held scripture and standing. The ayah strips all of it away in four words. In the moment of the punishment, nothing in that inventory reaches out a hand.

## Ayah 23: invited to their own Book — and refusing

*"Have you not seen those who have been given a portion of the Scripture? They are being invited to the Book of Allah to settle their dispute, then a party of them turned away, and they are averse."*

Ibn Kathir explains the situation with precision: Allah criticizes the Jews and Christians who claim to follow their Books, the Tawrāh (the Torah) and the Injīl (the Gospel), "because when they are called to refer to these Books where Allah commanded them to follow Muhammad ﷺ, they turn away with aversion."

Read that carefully. They are not being asked to abandon their scripture for a rival one. They are being asked to *open their own scripture* and let it decide. And that is what they will not do. Ibn Kathir says this censure and criticism from Allah "was all because of their defiance and rejection."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point from the other side: the address in this ayah is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the reference is to the Torah given to the Jews, "who would have found it enough for them if they were really looking forward to guidance." The Book they already possessed was sufficient for anyone genuinely seeking. The problem was never a shortage of evidence — it was, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, that they elected to be indifferent.

And the ayah's own phrasing carries a quiet judgement: they were given **a portion** of the Scripture. People who hold a part of something can be tempted to behave as though they hold all of it. The turning away in this ayah is what that looks like in practice.

## Ayah 24: the lie that made it possible

*"This is because they say: 'The Fire shall not touch us but for a number of days.' And that which they used to invent in their religion has deceived them."*

Here the Qur'an names the root. Ibn Kathir: "what made them dare to challenge and defy the truth is their false claim that Allah will only punish them for seven days in the Fire" — a day for every one thousand years in this life. He notes that he has mentioned this subject in his tafsir of Sūrat al-Baqarah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the reasoning behind it from another angle: they contended that they had worshipped the calf for forty days, so any punishment they incurred would last only that long. And it adds a second strand of the same self-deception — their belief that they were the progeny of prophets and would therefore escape punishment in the Fire.

Either way, the mechanism is identical. **A person who has capped his own worst-case outcome will risk almost anything.** If the Fire is only a short stay, then defying a prophet is a manageable expense. Turning away from your own scripture becomes affordable. The behaviour in ayah 23 is not a separate failing from the belief in ayah 24; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān joins them directly — they elect to be indifferent *because* they say and believe the Fire will not touch them except for a few days.

**"What they used to invent."** Ibn Kathir presses on this: what caused them to remain on their false creed "is that they deceived themselves, believing that the Fire will only touch them for a few days for their errors. However, it is they who have invented this notion, and Allah did not grant them authority to support this claim." The comfort had no revelation behind it. They wrote the reassurance themselves, then believed it — and the ayah says it deceived them **in their religion**. This is a dangerous kind of self-deception, because it wears the clothing of faith.

## Ayah 25: the Day that answers all of it

*"How will it be when We gather them together on the Day about which there is no doubt, and each person will be paid in full what he has earned, and they will not be dealt with unjustly?"*

Ibn Kathir reads the opening **"how will it be…"** as Allah threatening and warning them — and he fills in what the question is really asking: what will their condition be like "after they have uttered this lie about Allah, rejected His Messengers and killed His Prophets and their scholars who enjoined righteousness and forbade evil? Allah will ask them about all this and punish them for what they have done." The ayah does not describe their state on that Day. It leaves the question hanging, which is more frightening than any description.

Three phrases finish the passage, and each one answers a piece of the fantasy in ayah 24:

- **"a Day about which there is no doubt"** — Ibn Kathir: "there is no doubt that this Day will come." They had made the Hereafter negotiable; here it is fixed.
- **"each person will be paid in full what he has earned"** — paid *in full*, and for what he **earned**. Their claim rested partly on ancestry and partly on a discount they had invented; the standard on that Day is one's own earning, measured completely.
- **"and they will not be dealt with unjustly"** — the very justice they killed men for calling to is the justice that will now be applied to them, exactly.

## Living it

The passage is history, but the pattern it exposes is worth carrying. A few things it asks of us:

**Watch what you do with an inconvenient truth.** The chain in these ayat begins not with killing but with refusing the truth and looking down on the one who brings it — which is exactly how the Prophet ﷺ defined arrogance in the narration Ibn Kathir cites. That refusal is available to anyone, in any argument, on any ordinary day. Where it leads, in the extreme, is ayah 21.

**Honour the one who calls for justice, even when he holds no office.** The ayah puts the killing of ordinary men who "order just dealings" alongside the killing of prophets. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes them as those who teach moderation in deeds and morals — people with only a right word to offer. Their standing with Allah is high enough to be named beside prophets.

**Be willing to be judged by the Book you claim.** Ayah 23 describes people invited to their own scripture who turn away from it. It is a searching question for anyone who honours a revelation in principle while quietly declining to let it settle the matter at hand.

**Audit your comforts.** Ayah 24 is a warning about consoling beliefs that no revelation actually taught — assumed lineage, an assumed short punishment, a private certainty that the accounting will go easy. Ibn Kathir's phrase is unsparing: Allah "did not grant them authority to support this claim." Any hope we carry about the Hereafter should be one Allah Himself has given us, not one we have written for ourselves.

**Let ayah 25 be the corrective.** "Paid in full what he has earned" is severe and merciful at once: nothing real is lost, and nothing false is credited. Against the emptiness of ayah 22 — works lost, no helpers — stands the assurance that on that Day no one will be dealt with unjustly. That is where a believer's hope belongs.

passages.title: Prayer to the Owner of all sovereignty
passages.tafsir:
# Āl ʿImrān 26–27: The Prayer of the One Who Owns All Sovereignty

These two ayat are a single supplication that the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say — a prayer that hands over to Allah every throne, every honour, every humiliation, every sunrise and every provision. Ayah 26 speaks of power among people; ayah 27 speaks of power in the heavens and in the soil. Read together, they name one power, not two.

In Ibn Kathir's rendering the passage reads:

> Say: "O Allah! Possessor of the power, You give power to whom You will, and You take power from whom You will, and You endue with honor whom You will, and You humiliate whom You will. In Your Hand is the good. Verily, You are able to do all things. **(26)** You make the night to enter into the day, and You make the day to enter into the night, You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living. And You give wealth and sustenance to whom You will, without limit. **(27)**"

---

## The moment this prayer was revealed: the trench

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives an occasion of revelation that unlocks the whole passage. It reports — citing Rūh al-Maʿānī, from al-Wāhidī, from Ibn ʿAbbās and Anas (may Allah be pleased with them) — that when the Prophet ﷺ promised that Byzantium and Persia would be taken, the hypocrites and the Jews laughed at the idea. It was then that this ayah was revealed.

The setting is the battle the Qur'an calls *al-Ahzāb* — called *Khandaq* ("the Trench") in history, because the Prophet ﷺ decided, after consulting his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), that a trench be dug around parts of Madinah to block the enemy's unhindered attack.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The disbelievers of Makkah had been defeated at Badr and Uhud, had failed to register any gains in their hostility against the Muslims, and were watching the growing strength of the Muslims and the rise of Islam. It made them very nervous, almost reckless. The whole thing ended in a conspiracy: the disbelievers of Arabia, the Jews and the Christians joined in a united front, resolved to attack Madinah and fight a conclusive battle, determined to erase Islam and the Muslims from the face of the earth.

The digging was brutal. According to narrations in al-Baihaqi, Abu Nuʿaim and Ibn Khuzaimah, the plan allotted a forty hand-span stretch of trench to each group of ten men. The trench ran several miles, deep and wide enough that the enemy would find it impossible to cross. It had to be finished in the shortest possible time, so the Companions put in whatever time and energy they had — so much so that they found it difficult to leave the job even for the most pressing of their needs. They were working non-stop on hungry stomachs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that a modern army engineering service with its latest equipment would not have found this kind of job any easier. What made it possible here was the power of faith.

The Prophet ﷺ took part in the digging as an individual like everybody else.

Then the diggers came upon a huge rock. Those assigned to that stretch tried their best to break it apart, became helpless, and gave up. They asked Sayyidnā Salmān al-Fārisī to go to the Prophet ﷺ, tell him the problem and seek his instructions. He came at once to the spot, took the pick-axe in his blessed hands and struck. The rock shattered, and out of it rose a streak of light that illuminated the area far and wide. He ﷺ said: *In this light, I see the palaces and buildings of Hirah in the country of Persia.* He struck again; a second beam of light rose, and he said: *In this light, I was shown the red palaces and buildings of the Byzantinians.* He struck a third time, the flame beamed its light around, and he said: *In this I was shown the great palaces of Sanʿā in Yemen.* Then he said: *I share the good news given by Jibrāʾīl (peace be upon him) with you, that my community of Muslims will prevail over all these countries.*

When the hypocrites of Madinah heard about it, they found an occasion to ridicule the Muslims: *just look at these people — all scared of the enemy, digging trenches without eating and resting, not knowing for sure if their own lives will be safe, yet they are dreaming of running over Persia, Byzantium and Yemen.*

**Ayah 26 is the answer to that mockery.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that it was in answer to a people so unfair and unjust that Allah revealed this verse — not as a rebuttal in the form of an argument, but as a prayer put on the believers' tongues.

---

## Why the answer came as a prayer

This is the passage's most striking feature, and it is worth pausing on. Allah did not tell the Prophet ﷺ to argue with the hypocrites about troop numbers or empires. He told him to *say* — to turn to Allah and name Him by what He is.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verse, appearing in the form of a prayer, so eloquently brings into focus the most perfect power of Allah as it manifests itself **in the rise and fall of nations and in the revolutions that rock countries**. At the same time it gives a hint that the prophecy made by the Prophet ﷺ will come to pass, and Persia and Byzantium will fall to the Muslims. The enemies of Islam are warned that they have not learnt their lesson from the rise and fall of past wielders of power, because they judge events and personalities **from the material angle** — when the truth is that all the powers and governments of the world are in the hands of the most pristine power of Allah, the One in whose hands lies all honour and disgrace. There is no doubt that He is capable of making the poor and the meek sit on thrones and wresting power from kings and monarchs. Why then, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks pointedly, should it be difficult for Him to choose *these ragged believers digging trenches* to rule over Persia, Syria, Iraq and Yemen?

Ibn Kathir approaches the same word from a different angle. He notes that *Say* means: O Muhammad ﷺ — **while praising your Lord, thanking Him, relying in all matters upon Him and trusting in Him.** So the prayer is simultaneously praise, gratitude, and reliance on Allah (*tawakkul*). It asks for nothing at all; it is a recognition, and the recognition is itself the answer.

---

## "O Allah! Possessor of all power"

Ibn Kathir glosses *Allāhumma Mālik al-Mulk* simply: **all sovereignty is Yours.** Then, on "You give power to whom You will, and You take power from whom You will, and You endue with honor whom You will, and You humiliate whom You will," he says: *You are the Giver, You are the Taker; it is Your will that occurs, and whatever You do not will, does not occur.*

Notice the shape of the ayah: giving is paired with taking, honour with humiliation. Four verbs, all with the same subject, all ending in *whom You will* — and Ibn Kathir's gloss on *Mālik al-Mulk* leaves no room for a second party: **You decide what You will concerning Your creation and You do what You will.**

Ibn Kathir then turns this into a reason for **gratitude**. This ayah, he says, encourages thanking Allah for the favours He granted His Messenger ﷺ and his Ummah. Allah transferred the prophethood from the Children of Israel to the Arab, Qurashi, Makkan, unlettered Prophet — the Final and Last of all Prophets, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to all mankind and jinn. Allah endowed him with the best of qualities from the prophets before him, and granted him extra qualities that no other Prophet or Messenger before him was given: more knowledge of Allah and His Law, and knowledge of more of the matters of the past and the future, such as what will occur in the Hereafter. Allah allowed his Ummah to reach the eastern and western parts of the world and gave dominance to his religion and Law over all other religions and laws. *May Allah's peace and blessings be on the Prophet ﷺ until the Day of Judgment, and as long as the day and night succeed each other.*

That transfer of prophethood is exactly why Ibn Kathir cites the objection of those who thought they could decide for Allah: *"Why is not this Qur'an sent down to some great man of the two towns?"* (43:31) — Makkah and Ṭāʾif. Allah refutes them: *"Is it they who would portion out the Mercy of your Lord?"* (43:32) — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, *We decide for Our creation what We will, without resistance or hindrance by anyone. We have the perfect wisdom and the unequivocal proof in all of this, and We give the prophethood to whom We will.* He adds two further ayat on the same point: *Allah knows best with whom to place His Message* (6:124), and *See how We prefer one above another (in this world)* (17:21).

So *Mālik al-Mulk* is not an abstract slogan. On Ibn Kathir's reading it is the reason the Qur'an came to an unlettered man of Makkah rather than to the notables others would have chosen.

---

## "In Your Hand is the good" — the word that is missing

Here is the subtlest point in the passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out beautifully.

The first half of ayah 26 works in pairs: the giving and taking of power, the bestowing of honour and the bringing of disgrace, mentioned side by side. So when the ayah reaches *bi-yadika-l-khayr*, "In Your hand lies the good," the ear expects the matching pair. It would have seemed in keeping with the occasion, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, for **sharr** (evil) to be coupled with **khayr** (good). But the text elects to use *khayr* alone.

That choice, the commentary says, points out something real and significant in human affairs. A person or a people may regard something as unwelcome — and it may even be so *for that particular person or people* — but looked at from the wider angle of the whole community of nations, it may not be really evil. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the Arab poet al-Mutanabbī:

> مصایب قوم عند قوم فوائد
> *The calamities of one group are the gains of another.*

In short: **the evil of things we regard as evil is partial.** Looked at from its relationship to the Creator of the Universe and the Lord of all there is, and viewed in the perspective of the totality of the world of our experience, nothing is really evil or bad as such. Given the wisdom, the power, and the consideration of the created universe as a whole, everything is *khayr* — which is why the verse saw it sufficient to say only that.

Sit with that alongside the trench. The men working non-stop on hungry stomachs were living through hardship; the confederates had marched to end them. The commentary's point is about where a person has to stand before he can judge what he is looking at.

The ayah then closes: *Verily, You are able to do all things.* Nothing named above is beyond Him.

---

## Ayah 27: from the cosmos to the soul

Ayah 27 widens the frame. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it demonstrates that Allah controls all spaces and heavenly bodies, and employs the sun and the moon to make the days longer than the nights and the nights longer than the days, at His will and command.

Ibn Kathir explains *You make the night enter into the day, and You make the day enter into the night* concretely: **You take from the length of one of them and add it to the shortness of the other, so that they become equal; and take from the length of one of them and add it to the other so that they are not equal.** This occurs throughout the seasons of the year — spring, summer, fall and winter. It is a quiet, continuous rebalancing of the world.

Then: *You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living.* Ibn Kathir lists the everyday miracles — the seed from the plant and the plant from the seed; the date from its seed and the date's seed from the date; the chicken from the egg and the egg from the chicken — **and, in the same breath, the faithful from the disbeliever and the disbeliever from the faithful.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the chick from an egg, the human infant from the sperm, the tree from a seed; and in the other direction, eggs from birds and beasts, sperm from humans, fruit from trees, dried grain from plants.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then takes the wider reading. If we were to take "the living" and "the dead" in a broad and general sense, this becomes inclusive of the learned and the ignorant, the perfect and the imperfect, the believer and the disbeliever. It goes to show that Allah's perfect power exercises absolute control over all phenomena, **both physical and spiritual**: He can make a Muslim out of a disbeliever, a perfect believer out of a staunch disbeliever, a scholar out of an ignorant person — if He so wills. And if He so wills, He can let a believer turn into a disbeliever, or a rustic into a scholar. He brought Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) out of an idol-worshipper. He let the son of the Prophet Nūh (peace be upon him) remain an infidel. Strange but true, the commentary adds, that the son of an *ʿālim* (scholar) can remain illiterate, and the son of someone illiterate can become an *ʿālim*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the arrangement itself: a discerning reader will not fail to notice the eloquent order in which Allah's most perfect power, which reigns and runs the universe **from the cosmos to the soul of man**, has been demonstrated so effectively.

The passage ends where a struggling believer most needs it: *And You give wealth and sustenance to whom You will, without limit.* Ibn Kathir: **You give whomever You will innumerable amounts of wealth while depriving others from it, out of wisdom, and justice.** Not randomness. Not neglect. Wisdom and justice.

---

## The special merit of this passage

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, under "The special merit of this verse," that **Imām al-Baghawī** reports a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ in which he said: it is Allah's promise that anyone who recites, after every Sūrah, Sūrah al-Fātihah, Āyat al-Kursī, and two verses of Āl ʿImrān — *Shahida-llāhu annahu lā ilāha illā huw* (3:18) and the present verses from *Quli-llāhumma Mālika-l-Mulk* (26–27) — Allah will make his abode in Paradise, have him placed in the Sacred Enclosure, bless him with His mercy seventy times every day, fulfil seventy of his needs, and protect him against every envier and enemy and make him prevail over them.

---

## Living it

**Say it when the numbers are against you.** This prayer was given to men digging a trench while a united front closed in and their neighbours laughed. It is the du'ā for the moment when the material calculation says you lose.

**Read the world the way the ayah reads it, not the way the hypocrites did.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān locates their error precisely: they judged events and personalities *from the material angle*, when all the powers and governments of the world are in the hands of Allah, in whose hands lies all honour and disgrace.

**Let it turn into gratitude.** Ibn Kathir's whole framing is that this ayah "encourages thanking Allah" — you are not simply reciting a doctrine of divine power, you are thanking the One who chose to give what He gave.

**And let it kill despair over another person, or over yourself.** The One who brings the plant from the seed and the living from the dead brings, as Ibn Kathir says in the same breath, the faithful out of the disbeliever. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names it outright: He brought Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) out of an idol-worshipper. That door is never closed — and by the same token, the commentary is equally clear that the movement runs the other way too, so no one should feel secure about himself. Both directions belong to Him.

passages.title: Alliance with disbelievers and the hidden heart
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from a command about the outside of life to a warning about its inside. Ayah 28 forbids the believers to take the disbelievers as their friends and allies instead of the believers; ayah 29 declares that Allah knows what the breast conceals as surely as what it reveals; ayah 30 sets the whole matter on the Day when every deed is brought out and laid before its owner. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the three together explicitly: because close friendship (muwālāt) "relates to the heart and the affairs of the heart are known to none but Allah," a person might be inwardly bound in love to the disbelievers "but may deny it verbally." So, it says, ayah 29 "has already covered it" — "No denial or false claim is tenable before Him."

## The command in ayah 28

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah: *"Let not the believers take the disbelievers as friends instead of the believers, and whoever does that, will never be helped by Allah in any way, unless you indeed fear a danger from them. And Allah warns you against Himself, and to Allah is the final return."*

He states what is prohibited: Allah "prohibited His believing servants from becoming supporters of the disbelievers, or to take them as comrades with whom they develop friendships, rather than the believers." Two things are named there — giving them one's support, and taking them as intimate comrades — and both are set against the believers, who are the ones such loyalty properly belongs to.

**"Will never be helped by Allah in any way."** Ibn Kathir's comment on this clause is stark: "whoever commits this act that Allah has prohibited, then Allah will discard him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in relational terms — those who take them as friends "will find that their bond of love and friendship with Allah has been cut off."

## The Qur'an says this in many places

Both commentaries gather the parallel verses, and reading them together shows how consistently the Qur'an returns to this theme:

- *"O you who believe! Take not My enemies and your enemies as friends, showing affection towards them … And whosoever of you does that, then indeed he has gone astray from the straight path."* (60:1)
- *"O you who believe! Take not for friends disbelievers instead of believers. Do you wish to offer Allah a manifest proof against yourselves?"* (4:144)
- *"O you who believe! Take not the Jews and the Christians as friends, they are but friends of each other. And whoever befriends them, then surely, he is one of them."* (5:51)
- *"And those who disbelieve are allies of one another, (and) if you do not behave the same, there will be Fitnah and oppression on the earth, and a great mischief and corruption."* (8:73) — a verse Ibn Kathir notes comes after Allah mentions that the faithful believers gave their support to the faithful believers among the Muhājirīn, the Anṣār and the bedouins.
- *"You shall not find those who believe in Allah and in the Hereafter having friendship with those who have enmity with Allah and His messenger, even though they may be their fathers or sons or brothers or members of their tribe."* (58:22) — the ayah itself names fathers, sons, brothers and tribe.

## The four degrees: what is actually forbidden

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the passage its most useful service. It observes that non-Muslims "who are not aware of the true intention and application of this rule start thinking that the religion of Muslims does not seem to have any place for toleration or bilateral relations or even common courtesy" — while a great many other verses, together with the words and acts of the Prophet ﷺ and the practice of the rightly-guided Khulafāʾ and the revered Companions, bring to light dealings with non-Muslims "by way of favour, compassion, generosity, sympathy and concern, which has little or no parallel in world history." The sense of contradiction, Maʿārif says, "is a result of only a cursory study of the true teachings of the Qur'an." The resolution is that relations between people come in degrees, and only the first of them is closed.

**1. Muwālāt — the relation that comes from the heart.** Maʿārif describes the first degree as one "of affection and love involving intense emotional commitment. This is called Muwalat or close friendship. This sort of friendship is restricted to true Muslims. A Muslim is not permitted to have this kind of relationship with a non-Muslim." In its opening comment on these verses it puts the ruling plainly: "Any emotionally involved friendship that comes from the heart is absolutely forbidden (Ḥarām)." And when it later gathers the four degrees together, it restates the same point as its summary: "friendship which binds a Muslim in very close ties with non-Muslims is not permissible under any condition."

**2. Muwāsāt — sympathy, kindness and concern.** A relationship "based on sympathy, kindness and concern. It includes charitable help and support, condolence and consolation and any well-meaning attitude of wishing well." This is **permitted** with all non-Muslims except those at war with the Muslims. Maʿārif grounds it in 60:8: *"Allah does not forbid you from treating those who do not fight you on your faith, nor have they driven you out of your homes, with benevolence and equity."*

**3. Mudārāt — cordiality and good manners.** Relations "based on customary cordiality, adequacy in courtesy, pleasant and friendly behaviour, and mannerly politeness." This too is **permitted** with all non-Muslims — "especially so," Maʿārif says, when the objective is to present them with some beneficial aspect of the Faith, or when they are guests, or when the purpose is to stay safe from possible harm coming through them.

**4. Muʿāmalāt — dealings.** "Dealings and transactions in business or employment or wages or industry or technology." **Permitted**, and Maʿārif says the continued practice of the Prophet ﷺ, the rightly-guided Khulafāʾ and the Companions proves it so — except where such dealings harm the general body of Muslims. On this basis, it notes, Muslim jurists prohibited the sale of arms to disbelievers who are at war with the Muslims, while trade and activities allied to it are permitted, as is having them as employees or being employed in their institutions. Maʿārif adds one note of restraint: a formal friendship at the level of mutual dealings is "no doubt, permissible; but, that too is not favoured if unnecessary."

So the heart is reserved, and benevolence, courtesy and honest dealing remain open.

## The exception in ayah 28: *illā an tattaqū minhum tuqāh*

The ayah itself carves out an exception — *"unless you indeed fear a danger from them."* Ibn Kathir explains it as applying to "those believers who in some areas or times fear for their safety from the disbelievers. In this case, such believers are allowed to show friendship to the disbelievers outwardly, but never inwardly."

He cites two reports here from Al-Bukhari. Al-Bukhari recorded that **Abu Ad-Dardāʾ** said: *"We smile in the face of some people although our hearts curse them."* And Al-Bukhari said that **Al-Hasan** said: *"The Tuqyah is allowed until the Day of Resurrection."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the emphasis slightly differently, citing Bayān al-Qurʼān: these words denote the degree of **mudārāt** — meaning that muwālāt, friendship with disbelievers, "is not permissible except when you are in a situation where you want to defend yourself against them." And since mudārāt "somewhat resemble[s] Muwalat or friendship, it was exempted from the category of Muwalat." Either way the principle holds: the outward face may soften under threat; the inward loyalty may not move.

## What the Prophet ﷺ actually did

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds all of this in the conduct of the Prophet ﷺ, "who graced this world as the universal mercy," and whose compassion, generosity and politeness towards non-Muslims "it would be difficult to find its example in the world history":

- When Makkah was in the grip of famine, **he personally went out to help his enemies** — the very people who had made him leave his home town.
- At the conquest of Makkah, when those same enemies fell under his power and control, **he set all of them free**, saying: *lā tathrība ʿalaykum al-yawm* — "Not only that you are being given amnesty this day, we are not censuring you at all for your past tyranny against us either."
- Non-Muslim prisoners of war were treated by him with a tenderness "which many cannot claim to have done even in respect of their children."
- Despite every sort of injury and pain inflicted on him, "he never raised his hand in revenge. He did not even wish ill of them."
- A delegation from the tribe of **Banū Thaqīf**, who had not embraced Islam up to that time, came to visit — and were given the honour of staying **in the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ**, "a place regarded by Muslims as most honourable."

And after him, **Sayyidnā ʿUmar** raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu gave stipends and allowances to needy non-Muslim dhimmīs — "an elegant conduct the examples of which are spread all over in the accounts of dealings credited to the rightly-guided Khulafāʾ and the noble Companions."

Maʿārif then makes the crucial observation: **all of these were in one or another form of muwāsāt, mudārāt or muʿāmalāt.** "It had nothing to do with Muwalat or close and intimate friendship which had been forbidden." Two things follow, it says: that Islam teaches its adherents "all possible tolerance, decency and benevolence while dealing with non-Muslims," and that the apparent contradiction "stands removed."

## Why is this one door shut so firmly?

Maʿārif raises the remaining question directly: why has the Qur'an "so strongly block[ed] close friendship with disbelievers, so much so that it has not allowed it in favour of any disbeliever under any condition"?

One reason it gives goes to the meaning of a human life. Islam does not see a person existing in this world "like common animals or jungle trees and blades of grass which sprout, grow, flourish and die and that is the end of it." A human life here is **purposeful**: eating, drinking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, even living and dying, "all revolve around a central purpose." What conforms to that purpose is correct and sound; what is against it is wrong. Maʿārif quotes the poet-sage Rumi:

> The purpose of life is to remember the Creator and serve Him well
> Life without that devotion is nothing but shame

And when a person abandons that purpose, Maʿārif says, "he does not remain the human being he was created to be" — "They are not men, they are just the shell of men."

The Qur'an has human beings declare this purpose as their solemn creed: *"My prayer and my sacrifice and my life and my death are all for Allah, the Lord of the Worlds."* (6:162)

Once that is established, Maʿārif argues, everything else — "business, government, politics, personal and social relations" — must follow from it. It follows that those set against that purpose "are the worst enemies of man." Satan is foremost in this enmity, and so the Qur'an says: *"Surely, Satan is your enemy, so take him as enemy."* (35:6) Those who follow Satan's alluring dictates and oppose what Allah revealed through the prophets, Maʿārif concludes, "can hardly be the kind of people to deserve deep love and friendship based on close ties and any degree of intimacy."

It closes the argument with a hadith it attributes to **Bukhari and Muslim**, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever loves for the sake of Allah and hates for the sake of Allah alone, has perfected his faith."* From this we know, Maʿārif says, that **īmān — faith — remains incomplete unless a person subordinates his love and friendship and his hatred and enmity to Allah.** Deep emotional commitment, therefore, belongs to the one "who is with him all the way in the pursuit of this noble purpose." This, it says, is why the Qur'an declares of the one who maintains relations of deep love and friendship with disbelievers that he "is one of them."

## Ayah 29: the chest has no lock

*"Say: 'Whether you hide what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it, and He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth. And Allah is able to do all things.'"*

Ibn Kathir: Allah tells His servants that He knows "the secrets and apparent matters and that nothing concerning them escapes His observation. Rather, His knowledge encompasses them in all conditions, time frames, days and instances." His knowledge takes in all that is in heaven and earth — "nothing not even the weight of an atom, or what is smaller than that in the earth, seas and mountains, escapes His observation."

Then the ayah adds power to knowledge: *"And Allah is able to do all things"* — "and His ability encompasses everything." Ibn Kathir draws the practical conclusion, joining the two: this ayah "alerts Allah's servants that they should fear Him enough to not commit what He prohibits and dislikes, for He has perfect knowledge in all they do and is able to punish them promptly." If some are given respite, that respite is not oversight — "He gives respite to some of them, then He punishes them, and He is Swift and Mighty in taking account."

Maʿārif shows exactly how this answers ayah 28. Since muwālāt "relates to the heart and the affairs of the heart are known to none but Allah," a person may be intensely attached to the disbelievers "but may deny it verbally." Ayah 29 has already covered that: whether you conceal what is in your hearts or disclose it, Allah shall know it. "No denial or false claim is tenable before Him."

## Ayah 30: the Day the deeds are brought out

*"On the Day when every person will be confronted with the good he has done, and all the evil he has done, he will wish that there were a great distance between him and his evil."*

Ibn Kathir explains that this means the Day of Resurrection, when "Allah brings the good and evil deeds before the servant" — as He said elsewhere, *"On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward, and what he left behind"* (75:13).

Then he describes the scene with unusual human feeling. When the servant sees his good deeds, "he becomes happy and delighted." When he sees the evil deeds he committed, "he becomes sad and angry. Then he will wish that he could disown his evil work and that a long distance separated it from him." Ibn Kathir connects this to the words the person will say to the devil "who used to accompany him in this life, and who used to encourage him to do evil": *"Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts — a horrible companion (indeed)!"* (43:38)

Maʿārif ties ayah 30 back to the opening theme: Allah warns you of Himself "lest you should indulge in friendship with disbelievers for the sake of fleeting interests and objectives and thus invite the anger of Allah." That phrase — *fleeting interests and objectives* — names the motive the passage is guarding against.

## The warning that is itself a mercy

Both ayah 28 and ayah 30 contain the same clause: *"And Allah warns you against Himself."* Ibn Kathir explains it in ayah 28 as a warning against "His anger and the severe torment He prepared for those who give their support to His enemies, and those who have enmity with His friends"; in ayah 30, as a warning against "His punishment." And ayah 28 ends: *"And to Allah is the final return"* — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, that "the return is to Him and He will reward or punish each person according to their deeds."

But ayah 30 does not end on the warning. It ends: *"And Allah is full of kindness with the servants."* Ibn Kathir says Allah said this "while bringing hope to His servants, so that they do not despair from His mercy or feel hopeless of His kindness."

And then he preserves a remark of **Al-Hasan Al-Basri** that turns the whole passage over: *"Allah is so kind with them that He warns them against Himself."*

Read that slowly. On this reading the warning is not the opposite of the kindness — the warning **is** the kindness: to be told in advance, plainly, while there is still time. Others, Ibn Kathir adds, commented that "He is merciful with His creation and likes for them to remain on His straight path and chosen religion, and to follow His honorable Messenger."

## Living it

Taken together, the passage asks for something more precise than either coldness or naivety.

**Be generous, courteous and fair without hesitation.** Charitable help, condolence, kindness, good manners, hospitality, honest business, employment — Maʿārif establishes all of these as permitted, and the life of the Prophet ﷺ sets the standard: famine relief for his persecutors, amnesty at Makkah, tenderness to captives, a delegation of non-Muslims housed in his mosque. Nothing in ayah 28 licenses meanness.

**Reserve the heart's deepest attachment.** The one thing withheld is the close, emotionally committed bond that Maʿārif calls muwālāt — that your loves and your dislikes follow Allah. That is what the hadith of Bukhari and Muslim calls the perfection of faith.

**Watch for the small motive.** Maʿārif names the danger as "fleeting interests and objectives."

**And do not read the warning as a rejection.** Ayah 29 tells you that Allah knows what no one else can, and ayah 30 tells you that a Day is coming when the deeds will be set before you — but the sentence that closes it is that He is full of kindness with His servants. Al-Hasan Al-Basri's reading is the mercy hidden in plain sight: it is out of kindness that He warns them against Himself.

passages.title: Love of Allah proven by following the Messenger
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 31–32: Love of Allah, Proven by Following the Messenger ﷺ

These two ayat take a claim that is easy to make — *I love Allah* — and give it a test it cannot escape. Ayah 31 sets the condition (if you love Allah, follow the Messenger ﷺ, and Allah will love you and forgive you); ayah 32 states the same truth as a command and names what turning away really amounts to. They hold together as a single unit: the first shows love proved by following, the second shows refusal exposed as disbelief.

## Where these ayat sit

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the sequence. The verses just before this affirmed the Oneness of Allah and condemned disbelief in it. Now comes the affirmation of belief in prophethood, together with the necessity of following the Messenger ﷺ. The placement is deliberate — it teaches, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, that rejecting prophethood or refusing to obey the Prophet ﷺ is an act of disbelief (*kufr*) just as the rejection of the Oneness of Allah is. The two are affirmed side by side, and turning from either one is given the same name.

## Love is hidden — so Allah gave it a visible measure

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens with an observation anyone can verify from their own life. **Love is something secret.** Whether a person loves another, and whether they love a little or a great deal, are questions that cannot be answered precisely. There is no measure or yardstick for it. All one can do is make an educated guess from visible conditions and dealings — because love leaves traces and signs by which it can be recognised.

That is the problem this ayah solves. People were claiming that they loved Allah and hoping to be loved by Him, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that here Allah tells them the real criterion of His love. A person who claims to love his Creator and Master must test that claim **on the touch-stone of his obedience to the Messenger ﷺ** — matching it against the frequency and quality of where and how he has actually been following him. Once this is done, as the commentary says, the genuine and the fake of it will be exposed right there.

And the test measures degrees, not just pass and fail. How true a person turns out to be in his claim will be visible from how much he makes it a point to follow the noble Prophet ﷺ, using the guidance he brought as the guiding force of his life. The same test shows the reverse: the weaker a person is in his claim, the weaker he will be found in his obedience to the Prophet ﷺ. Love and following rise and fall together.

## "Some people claimed that they love Allah — so Allah tested them with this ayah"

Ibn Kathir preserves a comment from **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and several scholars among the Salaf** (the earliest generations of Muslims): *Some people claimed that they love Allah. So Allah tested them with this ayah:* "Say: If you really love Allah, then follow me, Allah will love you."

Notice what the ayah does not do. It does not argue with the claimants, and it does not call them liars. It hands them a single sentence and lets their own lives answer. Ibn Kathir says this honourable ayah **judges against** those who claim to love Allah yet do not follow the way of Muhammad ﷺ: such people are not true in their claim until they follow the Sharīʿah (Law) of Muhammad ﷺ and his religion.

## The exchange in ayah 31: you receive more than you asked for

Read ayah 31 as a chain of three links: *if you love Allah* → *then follow me* → *Allah will love you*. The love you claim is the starting point; the following is what you must do; and what comes back is not merely acceptance of your claim, but Allah's love for you.

Ibn Kathir makes exactly this point: **what you will earn is much more than what you sought in loving Him, for Allah will love you.** You came asking to be one who loves; you are answered by becoming one who is loved. The return is incomparably greater than the offering.

## What "follow me" actually covers

The command in ayah 31 is not a vague warmth toward the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir defines its scope precisely: following his Sharīʿah and his religion **in all his statements, actions and conditions** — what he said, what he did, and the states and circumstances in which he lived. Following is a whole-life imitation, not a selection of the parts that suit us.

And there is a converse side to it. Ibn Kathir notes that it is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"Whoever commits an act that does not conform with our matter (religion), then it will be rejected of him."**

This is the other blade of the same principle. If following him is the way Allah's love is earned, then an act invented outside of what he brought — however sincere the feeling behind it, however impressive the effort — does not qualify. It is returned to the doer. Devotion that bypasses the Messenger's ﷺ way is not a shortcut to Allah's love.

## Forgiveness folded into the same promise

Ayah 31 does not stop at love. It continues: *"and He will forgive you your sins. And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

Ibn Kathir explains: by your following the Messenger ﷺ, **you will earn all this with the blessing of his mission.** The love and the forgiveness both come through the same channel. This matters for anyone who hesitates at this ayah thinking their record disqualifies them from claiming love of Allah. The verse does not demand a clean past as the entry price. It names a direction of travel — follow him — and attaches both the love and the pardon to it, sealing the promise with Allah's own description of Himself: Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

## Ayah 32: the same truth as a command

Ayah 31 addressed those making a claim of love. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah **next commands everyone**: *"Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger."*

Two things are worth noticing in the wording. First, obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger ﷺ are placed together in a single command. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes, from Tafsir Mazhari, the Prophet's ﷺ own statement of this: **"He who obeyed Muhammad ﷺ obeyed Allah, and he who disobeyed Muhammad ﷺ disobeyed Allah."** Second, both ayat are opened with *Qul* — "Say." The Prophet ﷺ is not asserting his own authority; he is told to convey it. The demand for obedience to him comes from Allah.

**"But if they turn away…"** Ibn Kathir glosses the turning away as **defying the Prophet ﷺ**, and reads the closing clause — *then Allah does not like the disbelievers* — as testifying that defiance of the Messenger's way constitutes *kufr*. The ayah does not say "then Allah does not like those who turn away." It says *disbelievers*, and in that word the verdict is delivered.

The closing clause also answers ayah 31. Ayah 31 promised *Allah will love you*; ayah 32 ends with *Allah does not like the disbelievers*. What is held out in the first is withheld in the second, and what decides between them is one thing: following the Messenger ﷺ, or turning from him.

## No independent route to Allah

Ibn Kathir presses the point as far as it goes. Allah does not like whoever defies the Messenger's ﷺ way — **even if he claims that he loves Allah and seeks a means of approach to Him** — unless, and until, he follows the unlettered Prophet, the Final Messenger ﷺ, sent from Allah to the two creations: mankind and the jinn.

Then Ibn Kathir raises the point to its highest pitch. This is the Prophet ﷺ who, if the previous Prophets and mighty Messengers had been alive during his time, would have had no choice but to follow him, obey him, and abide by his Law — and Ibn Kathir refers the reader forward to the ayah on the Covenant Allah took from the Prophets (3:81), where he says he will explain this. If even the mighty Messengers, had they lived to see him, would owe him allegiance, then no one has a private path to the love of Allah that runs around him.

## Living it

The passage is unusually practical, and it asks for something quite specific.

**Stop treating the claim as the proof.** Saying "I love Allah" is where the matter begins, not where it is settled. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point stands: love is secret and can only be read from its traces and signs, so ask what traces yours has left this week.

**Test yourself where Allah told you to test.** Not against how moved you feel in worship, but against your obedience to the Messenger ﷺ — measured, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, by the frequency and quality of your actual following of him, and covering, per Ibn Kathir, the full range of it: his statements, his actions, and his conditions.

**Check that your devotion has his authorisation.** Given the words recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that an act not conforming to his religion is rejected of the doer, the question about any act of worship is not only "is my intention good?" but "did he bring this?"

**Treat obedience to him as obedience to Allah.** Ayah 32 joins them in one command, and the report cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Tafsir Mazhari makes the equation explicit. There is no version of loyalty to Allah that goes quiet when the Messenger ﷺ speaks.

**Do not let past sins silence the claim.** The same ayah that demands following promises forgiveness alongside the love, and names Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful. Begin following, and both are promised together.

The deepest consolation of this passage is the trade it offers. You bring a claim you cannot prove and a record you cannot defend. Follow the Messenger ﷺ, and Allah answers with His love and His forgiveness — which is, as Ibn Kathir said, far more than you were asking for.

passages.title: Allah's chosen families and Mary's dedication
passages.tafsir:
These ayat announce that Allah chose certain households above the nations — and then move straight into one of those households at its most intimate moment: a woman who could not have children promising her unborn child to Allah. Ayah 33 names four chosen ones; ayah 34 says they are offspring, one of the other; and ayat 35–37 show what happened in one of those households — a mother's vow, a mother's disappointment, and Allah's acceptance.

## Why these names, and why here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the setting. The disbelievers were refusing to obey the Prophet ﷺ because they doubted his prophethood, so the names of some past prophets are cited — both to comfort the Prophet ﷺ and for the guidance of the doubters, to help remove such doubts. But notice how brief the mention is: four names in one ayah, no stories told. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why. These prophets are referred to very briefly because the main purpose is to mention Sayyidnā ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), which follows immediately — because he will come again to this world and will work with the followers of the Prophet ﷺ, so it is necessary for Muslims to know his identification.

## What "chose" means, household by household

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as Allah stating that He has chosen these households over the people of the earth, and he then shows what the choosing looked like in each case:

**Adam.** Allah chose him, created him with His Hand and blew life into him. He commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, taught him the names of everything and allowed him to dwell in Paradise — but then sent him down from it out of His wisdom. Being chosen did not mean being spared the descent; and the descent itself, Ibn Kathir says, was out of His wisdom.

**Nūḥ.** Allah chose him and made him the first Messenger to the people of the earth, when the people worshipped idols and associated others with Allah in worship. Ibn Kathir dwells on the cost: Nūḥ kept calling his people day and night, in public and in secret, for a very long time, and his calling them only made them shun him more. This is when Nūḥ supplicated against them. So Allah caused them to drown, and none among them was saved except those who followed the religion that Allah sent to Nūḥ — and in this Allah avenged the way Nūḥ had been treated. A messenger long refused by his people: exactly the comfort Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says these mentions were sent down to give.

**The family of Ibrāhīm.** Ibn Kathir points out that this household includes the master of all mankind and the Final Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ. So the households named here reach as far as the very Messenger whose prophethood his people were doubting.

**The family of ʿImrān.** ʿImrān is the father of Maryam bint ʿImrān, the mother of ʿĪsā, peace be upon them. And Ibn Kathir closes the circle: ʿĪsā is from the offspring of Ibrāhīm.

## Ayah 34: "descendants of one another"

Ibn Kathir's rendering is: *offspring, one of the other.* The households named are not unconnected — they stand in one descent.

Then the ayah closes: **"And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing."** Hold on to those two names, because they are the very words Maryam's mother uses at the end of her supplication in the next ayah — *"Verily, You are the All-Hearer, the All-Knowing."* Ibn Kathir spells out what she meant by them: *You hear my supplication and You know my intention.* Hearing is for the words she says; knowing is for the heart she says them from.

## Ayah 35: the vow of Maryam's mother

Ibn Kathir identifies "the wife of ʿImrān" as the mother of Maryam, and names her Ḥannah bint Fāqūdh. He then relates from Muhammad bin Isḥāq that Ḥannah could not have children, and that one day she saw a bird feeding its chick. She wished she could have children and supplicated to Allah to grant her offspring. Allah accepted her supplication, and she became pregnant.

When she became aware that she was pregnant, she made her vow: that her child would concentrate on worship and on serving Bayt al-Maqdis, the Masjid in Jerusalem.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the institution behind that vow. In the religious code of the earlier prophets there was a method of worship by which a child, out of one's children, could be freed from all worldly services and devoted exclusively for Allah. Following this practice, Maryam's mother vowed during her pregnancy that she would let the newborn serve Bayt al-Maqdis in the way of Allah, and that she would not put the child on worldly chores.

Then: *"so accept this from me. Verily, You are the All-Hearer, the All-Knowing."* She does not assume acceptance. She asks for it. And Ibn Kathir adds a detail easy to skim past: **she did not know then what she would give birth to, a male or a female.** She made the pledge before she could know what she was pledging.

## Ayah 36: "I have given birth to a female"

She had expected a son. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that Maryam's mother thought she would deliver a male child, but when she delivered a girl she was full of remorse, thinking that a girl would not be able to do this duty. Ibn Kathir glosses her words *"and the male is not like the female"* in exactly that direction: not alike in strength and in the commitment to worship Allah and serve the Masjid in Jerusalem. She is not disparaging her daughter. She is a woman looking at a newborn girl and thinking she cannot keep her own promise.

And set apart from her words comes another phrase: **"and Allah knew better what she bore."** She thinks she knows what she has been given. She does not. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: Allah Almighty, out of His consideration for the sincerity of Maryam's mother, accepted that very girl, and thereby made her status distinct from any other girl of the world.

**"And I have named her Maryam."** Ibn Kathir treats this as evidence in law: it testifies to the fact that it is allowed to give a name to the newly born on the day it is born, as is apparent from the ayah, and this was also part of the law of those who were before us. He supports it further from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said:

> "This night, a son was born for me and I called him by my father's name, Ibrāhīm."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim collected this hadith. They also recorded that Anas bin Mālik brought his newborn brother to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who chewed a piece of date and put it in the child's mouth and called him ʿAbdullāh. Other newborn infants were also given names on the day they were born.

Ibn Kathir further cites Qatādah, narrating from Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī, from Samurah bin Jundub, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Every newborn boy is held in security by his ʿaqīqah, until his seventh day a sacrifice is offered on his behalf, he is given a name, and the hair on his head is shaved."

(The ʿaqīqah is the sacrifice the hadith itself describes as offered on the child's behalf.) This hadith, Ibn Kathir notes, was collected by Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan, and was graded Ṣaḥīḥ by At-Tirmidhi — and, being careful, he adds that another narration of it contained the wording "and blood is offered on his behalf," which is more famous and established than the former narration, and Allah knows best.

**"And I seek refuge with You for her and for her offspring from Shayṭān, the outcast."** Having handed the child over, she does the one thing still in her power: she asks Allah to guard her. Ibn Kathir explains that she sought refuge with Allah from the evil of Shayṭān, for her and for her offspring — that is, ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. And Allah accepted her supplication. ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Every newly born baby is touched by Shayṭān when it is born, and the baby starts crying because of this touch, except Maryam and her son."

Abū Hurayrah then said: "Read if you will: *And I seek refuge with You for her and for her offspring from Shayṭān, the outcast.*" Ibn Kathir states that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded this hadith.

Follow the sequence as Ibn Kathir lays it out. A woman who could not have children prays for a child, and Allah accepts her supplication. She dedicates that child, and Allah accepts the child. She asks protection for that child and her offspring, and Allah accepts that supplication too.

## Two rulings the scholars drew from a mother's words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Jaṣṣāṣ, takes two points from this episode:

- **A mother holds a certain measure of guardianship over her child** in respect of the child's education and training — for Maryam's mother would never have vowed if she had no right of guardianship over her child.
- **A mother also has the right to give her child a name**, as she did in ayah 36.

## Ayah 37: the acceptance

**"So her Lord accepted her with goodly acceptance."** Ibn Kathir says Allah accepted Maryam as a result of her mother's vow. The vow was not voided because the child was a girl.

**"He made her grow in a good manner."** Ibn Kathir unpacks it: Allah made her conduct becoming, her mannerism delightful, and made her well liked among people. He also made her accompany the righteous people, so that she learned righteousness, knowledge and religion. Even a soul Allah has accepted is formed through means: righteous company, and learning.

**"and put her under the care of Zakariyyā."** Ibn Kathir: Allah made Zakariyyā her sponsor and guardian for her benefit, so that she would learn from his tremendous knowledge and righteous conduct. On the exact relationship there is more than one statement. Ibn Isḥāq and Ibn Jarīr said Zakariyyā was the husband of Maryam's maternal aunt; or he was her brother-in-law, as mentioned in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in the report worded: *"I saw Yaḥyā (John) and ʿĪsā, who are maternal cousins."* Ibn Kathir judges that in general terms what Ibn Isḥāq said is plausible, and in that case Maryam was under the care of her maternal aunt. And that fits a ruling of the Prophet ﷺ himself: the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ decided that ʿAmārah, the daughter of Ḥamzah, be raised by her maternal aunt, the wife of Jaʿfar bin Abī Ṭālib, saying, **"The maternal aunt is just like the mother."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in how the guardianship was settled. To fulfil her vow, Maryam's mother took her to the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis and spoke to the caretakers and worshippers there — Sayyidnā Zakariyyā (peace be upon him) among them — telling them that she had vowed to dedicate the child to the service of Allah and therefore could not keep her with her, and asking them to take her and keep her. Sayyidnā ʿImrān (peace be upon him) had been the Imam of that Mosque; he had died during the pregnancy of Maryam's mother, otherwise he would have been the most deserving person to take charge of the child, being both her father and the Imam of the Mosque. So every keeper and worshipper of the Mosque wished to take her into his custody. Sayyidnā Zakariyyā pleaded his bid for custody on the grounds that his wife was Maryam's aunt and, being next to her mother, certainly deserved to keep her — but people did not agree to prefer him over the others. Finally everybody agreed to draw lots, and it was Zakariyyā who turned out to be the winner.

So he got custody of her. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions that according to some reports he employed a wet-nurse to have her suckled, while other reports say she simply did not need to be suckled. She grew up able to sit and walk, and Zakariyyā put her in a good house adjacent to the Mosque; when he went out he locked the house, and opened it on his return. All of this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is stated briefly in this one ayah.

**"Every time he entered the Miḥrāb to visit her, he found her supplied with sustenance."** Ibn Kathir presents this as Allah emphasising Maryam's honour and virtue at the place of worship she attended. And he lists an unusually long line of early authorities on what that sustenance was: Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Abū Ash-Shaʿthā, Ibrāhīm An-Nakhaʿī, Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, ʿAṭiyyah Al-ʿAwfī and As-Suddī all said: **"He would find with her the fruits of the summer during winter, and the fruits of the winter during summer."**

When Zakariyyā would see this he asked: *"O Maryam! From where have you gotten this?"* — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, where did you get these fruits from? And the girl who was once grieved over at birth answers with a lesson about Allah alone: **"This is from Allah. Verily, Allah provides sustenance to whom He wills, without limit."**

## Living it

**Pledge before you can see the outcome.** She dedicated a child she had not met, whose sex she did not know — Ibn Kathir is explicit that she did not know then whether she would give birth to a male or a female. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that Allah accepted that very girl out of consideration for her mother's sincerity.

**Do not grade Allah's gifts.** She received what she took to be the lesser gift and was full of remorse. "And Allah knew better what she bore." When a supplication is answered in a shape you did not expect, you are standing where she stood — with the advantage of knowing how her story ended.

**Ask for your children's children.** Her seeking of refuge covered Maryam *and her offspring*, and Ibn Kathir says that offspring means ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. A supplication can reach further than the one who makes it.

**Put the young near the righteous.** Allah's own means of raising Maryam well, as Ibn Kathir describes it, was righteous company and a guardian of tremendous knowledge and righteous conduct. If that was the method for her, it is not beneath us.

**And remember the miḥrāb.** Zakariyyā locked the house behind him, and still found her supplied. Her answer is the whole lesson: Allah provides sustenance to whom He wills, without limit.

passages.title: Zachariah's prayer and the promise of John
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the prayer of an old man who had long held back from asking for a child, and the answer that came to him mid-prayer. Ayat 38–41 form a single scene: a supplication (38), the angels' announcement of Yahya and a portrait of who he would be (39), Zakariyya's astonished question and the answer that settles it (40), and finally the sign he asked for and the three days of silence and remembrance it imposed (41). What holds the unit together is a single movement — from a servant's hidden asking to Allah's overwhelming giving, and then back again to remembrance and gratitude.

## The moment that unlocked the prayer

Ayah 38 opens with a word of place and time: **هُنَالِكَ** — *hunālika*, "then and there." It ties this prayer directly to what Zakariyya (peace be upon him) had just witnessed.

Ibn Kathir explains: when Zakariyya saw that Allah provided sustenance for Maryam by giving her the fruits of winter in summer and the fruits of summer in winter, he became eager to have a child of his own.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the psychology of that moment with unusual care. Zakariyya had no offspring up to that time. He had grown old, and one does not usually have children at that age — yet he firmly believed that Allah, in His ultimate power, could change the usual course of things and bless him with a child even in his advanced age. So the obstacle was never doctrine. The obstacle was **courage**. He had not personally witnessed such unusual divine acts, and so, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, he did not have the courage to extend his hand of prayer for an offspring. Now he had seen the miracle with his own eyes. The reasoning that persuaded him was simple and beautiful: the One who can provide a servant with out-of-season fruit can also bless him with an offspring even in this late age. And so he prayed.

This is worth sitting with. Zakariyya's faith was not created by the miracle; it was *emboldened* by it. Seeing Allah's generosity to someone else enlarged what he was willing to ask for himself.

## How he asked

Ibn Kathir sketches the state he was in: by then Zakariyya had become an old man, his bones feeble and his head full of gray hair; his wife was an old woman who was barren. And yet, Ibn Kathir says, he still supplicated to Allah and **called Him in secret**.

The request in ayah 38 is short, and Ibn Kathir walks through it phrase by phrase:

- **رَبِّ هَبْ لِي مِن لَّدُنكَ** — "My Lord! Grant me from *ladunka*." Ibn Kathir glosses *min ladunka* plainly: **"from You."**
- **ذُرِّيَّةً طَيِّبَةً** — *dhurriyyatan ṭayyibah*, "a good offspring." Ibn Kathir explains this as **a righteous offspring**. He did not simply ask for a child; he asked for a *good* one.
- **إِنَّكَ سَمِيعُ الدُّعَاءِ** — "You are indeed the All-Hearer of invocation." He seals the request by naming the very quality of Allah on which the request depends: that Allah hears the one who calls on Him.

## Praying for children is prophetic practice

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this second sentence of ayah 38 as evidence that **making prayers to have children is a blessed practice of the prophets and the righteous**. It supports this with Allah's words, "And We sent messengers before you and provided them with wives and children" (13:38) — meaning children are among the blessings of Allah, bestowed on the Prophet ﷺ as they were on the prophets before him. So, it adds, whoever tries to stop the birth of children deprives himself of acting in harmony with the agreed practice of the prophets (peace be upon them).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how much importance the Prophet ﷺ gave to marriage and children — so much that he did not allow anyone capable of it to avoid married life and children. It cites his words: that marriage is his sunnah (his way); that whoever turns away from his sunnah is not from him; and "therefore, marry a woman who is loving and fertile, for I shall compete with other communities on the basis of your numbers." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes these without naming a collection, so the teaching stands as reported there rather than being traced to a specific book here.)

And it points to another Qur'anic prayer of the same family, in which Allah praises those who ask Him for a spouse and children who grow up good and righteous: "O our Lord, bless us with such among our wives and our children as be the delight of our eyes" (25:74). **Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him)** explained *qurrata aʿyun* — literally the coolness or lustre of the eyes, meaning someone dearly loved and cherished — as the one praying **seeing his children and wife devoted in obedience to Allah**. That is precisely the shape of Zakariyya's request: not offspring, but *good* offspring.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a report that Umm Sulaym (may Allah be pleased with her) asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for his attendant Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), and he prayed: "O Allah, increase his wealth and his children and make him prosper in what You have bestowed on him." It was the outcome of that very prayer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that Anas had about a hundred children and was blessed with an ample measure of wealth. (Here too the bundle names no collection.)

## The answer arrives mid-prayer (ayah 39)

**فَنَادَتْهُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَهُوَ قَائِمٌ يُصَلِّي فِي الْمِحْرَابِ** — "the angels called him while he was standing in prayer in the *miḥrāb*." Ibn Kathir explains: the angels spoke to him **directly**, while he was secluded, standing in prayer at his place of worship. He asked in secret; the answer came in that same secret place, before he had even risen.

**"Allah gives you glad tidings of Yahya."** Ibn Kathir notes that this is a child from his own offspring, whose name is Yahya. **Qatadah and other scholars** said he was called Yahya — the word literally means *he lives* — **because Allah filled his life with faith**.

Then comes the portrait, four qualities in a row.

**مُصَدِّقًا بِكَلِمَةٍ مِّنَ اللَّهِ — "believing in a Word from Allah."** Ibn Kathir reports that Al-ʿAwfi related from **Ibn ʿAbbas**, and likewise **Al-Hasan, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, Abu Ash-Shaʿtha, As-Suddi, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas, Ad-Dahhak** and several others, that this means: believing in ʿIsa, son of Maryam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *why* ʿIsa is called "a word of Allah": because he was created in an unusual manner, simply by the will and command of Allah, without a paternal linkage. Note how the passage is already reaching forward — Zakariyya's son will be the one who confirms Maryam's son.

**وَسَيِّدًا — "and a *sayyid*."** The commentators offer a rich spread of meanings, and Ibn Kathir preserves the differences rather than flattening them:
- **Abu Al-ʿAliyah, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas, Qatadah and Saʿid bin Jubayr**: a wise man.
- **Ibn ʿAbbas, Ath-Thawri and Ad-Dahhak**: the noble, wise and pious man.
- **Saʿid bin Al-Musayyib**: the scholar and *faqīh* (one with deep understanding of the religion).
- **ʿAtiyah**: the man noble in behaviour and piety.
- **ʿIkrimah**: one who is not overcome by anger.
- **Ibn Zayd**: the noble man.
- **Mujahid**: one honoured by Allah.

Taken together, these readings describe a person whose standing rests on wisdom, nobility of character, self-command in the face of anger, and honour given by Allah.

**وَحَصُورًا — "and *ḥaṣūr*."** Here the two commentaries genuinely differ, and both deserve to be heard.

*Ibn Kathir* is firm that it does **not** mean he refrained from relations with women, but that **he was immune from unlawful relations**. It does not mean he would not marry and have lawful relations — and his evidence is the wording of the father's own prayer: "Grant me from You, a good offspring," meaning, Ibn Kathir says, grant me a son who will himself have offspring. He closes with "and Allah knows best."

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* reads *ḥaṣūr* as abstinence in a broader sense — that Yahya was very particular about keeping himself shielded from temptations, from the things one habitually enjoys, including permissible enjoyments such as good food, good dress and marital life. Since the quality is mentioned here in a positive frame, that seems to suggest it is the better way; yet, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the ahadith prove the higher merit of living in the bond of marriage. Its considered opinion: for someone whose condition resembles Yahya's — so absorbed in the thought of his life to come that he feels no need of a wife and has neither the time nor the frame of mind to fulfil the rights of a wife and children — this abstention is the better choice for *him*. This is why, it observes, the ahadith describing the merit of marriage carry a restrictive clause: the one **who is able** to marry and capable of fulfilling the due rights of his wife should marry; otherwise he is not advised to.

So the disagreement is real, and a reader should hold it as such: one reading makes *ḥaṣūr* a shield against sin, the other a voluntary abstention suited to a particular kind of life.

**وَنَبِيًّا مِّنَ الصَّالِحِينَ — "a Prophet, from among the righteous."** Ibn Kathir points out that this is good news layered on good news: after being told the child will be born, Zakariyya is told what the child will *become* — and **this news was even better than the news of the birth itself**. He compares it to Allah's word to the mother of Musa: "Verily, We shall bring him back to you, and shall make him one of the Messengers" (28:7).

## "How can I have a son?" (ayah 40)

Ibn Kathir says that when Zakariyya heard the good news he started contemplating having children at his age, and said: "My Lord! How can I have a son when I am very old, and my wife is barren?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the obvious difficulty head on: he already believed in the absolute power of Allah, had seen its manifestation repeatedly, had made the prayer himself and knew of its acceptance — so what could the question mean? Its answer: the question **was not because of any doubt** in Allah's absolute power. Quite the contrary — its purpose was to find out **the state in which** this was to happen: whether the present extreme old age of both of them would remain just as it was, or whether that state would be changed.

And the reply, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is eloquent precisely because it settles that: **كَذَٰلِكَ اللَّهُ يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ** — "That is how Allah does what He wills." They were to remain at the same age, and would have an offspring in that very state. Ibn Kathir's gloss carries the same weight: this is Allah's matter; He is so Mighty that nothing escapes His power, nor is anything beyond His ability.

## The sign, and what it forced him to do (ayah 41)

Zakariyya then asks: "My Lord! Make a sign for me." Ibn Kathir explains he wanted a sign that would alert him that the child would come.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the motive behind the request: he wanted the sign of pregnancy so as to be happy at the prospect and **thus be enabled to show gratitude all along, even prior to the actual birth of the child**.

And this is where the passage turns quietly stunning. The sign given was, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, remarkably suitable to its purpose: since his request for a sign was prompted by his wish to show his gratefulness, the sign set for him **leaves him incapable of doing anything but this**. Even a hundred signs would not have done what this one sign did.

**آيَتُكَ أَلَّا تُكَلِّمَ النَّاسَ ثَلَاثَةَ أَيَّامٍ إِلَّا رَمْزًا** — "Your sign is that you shall not speak to the people for three days except by *ramz*," that is, by signals or gestures. Ibn Kathir is careful: this means he *would not be able* to speak except with signals — **although he was not mute**. He cites the parallel elsewhere in the Qur'an, "For three nights, though having no bodily defect" (19:10).

Then the command that completes the sign: **وَاذْكُر رَّبَّكَ كَثِيرًا وَسَبِّحْ بِالْعَشِيِّ وَالْإِبْكَارِ** — "And remember your Lord much, and glorify Him in the afternoon and in the morning." Ibn Kathir: Allah then commanded him to supplicate, thank and praise Him often **in that condition**. His tongue was closed to people and opened to Allah. That is the sign and the gratitude in one stroke.

## A ruling drawn from the last phrase

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a practical principle in "except through gestures": in a situation where speech is not possible because of a valid reason, **a gesture is deemed its substitute**. It supports this with the report — cited from al-Qurtubi — that the Prophet ﷺ asked a maidservant, "Where is Allah?" and she pointed towards the sky, and he said: "This maidservant is a Muslim."

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, and no more than the sources support:

**Let what you see of Allah's generosity enlarge what you ask for.** Zakariyya's turning point was witnessing provision given to someone else. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is that his belief was already sound — what he gained was the courage to extend his hand in prayer. Most of us are not short on doctrine; we are short on daring in our duʿāʾ.

**Ask for good, not just for gifts.** He said *dhurriyyatan ṭayyibah* — which Ibn Kathir explains as righteous offspring — and Hasan al-Basri's (may Allah have mercy on him) reading of *qurrata aʿyun* points the same way: what delights the eye is seeing one's wife and children devoted in obedience to Allah. And Ibn Kathir's remark on ayah 39 reframes everything: being told the child would be a prophet among the righteous was better news than the birth itself.

**Turn the gift back into remembrance.** The moment the answer came, Zakariyya was commanded to remember his Lord much and glorify Him in the afternoon and in the morning.
