Two things are worth pausing over. First, look at what made the garden precious — it was not only fertile and valuable, it was the place the Prophet ﷺ himself came to drink from. Abū Ṭalḥah did not hunt for something he could spare; he went straight for the thing his heart was most attached to. Second, the Prophet's ﷺ answer teaches something many people miss: **charity is not confined to the poor and the needy.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out explicitly — giving to one's own family and relatives is equally charitable and meritorious.

### ʿUmar and his share of Khaybar

Ibn Kathir adds that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs also recorded that ʿUmar said: "O Messenger of Allah! I never gained possession of a piece of property more precious to me than my share in Khaybar. Therefore, what do you command me to do with it?" The Prophet ﷺ said: **"Retain the land to give its fruits in Allah's cause."**

The beloved asset was not liquidated and scattered; it was locked into permanent benefit, its produce flowing out in Allah's path.

### Zayd ibn Ḥārithah's horse

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates (from Tafsīr Maẓharī, citing Ibn Jarīr and others) that Sayyidunā Zayd ibn Ḥārithah came with a horse, saying he loved it more than anything else he owned and wished to spend it in the way of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ accepted it — and then gave it to Zayd's own son, Sayyidunā Usāmah (may Allah be pleased with them both). Zayd felt some disappointment at that, thinking his charity had found its way back into his own home. The Prophet ﷺ comforted him: **"Allah Almighty has accepted this charity of yours."**

This is a tender lesson. Once the gift leaves your hand for Allah's sake, it is *done* — accepted. Where Allah then directs it is His affair, not a measure of your sincerity.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions two more: Sayyidunā ʿUmar had a bond-maid he liked most, and he freed her for the sake of Allah; and Sayyidunā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar likewise had a bond-maid he loved, and freed her in the name of Allah.

## Six things this ayah teaches

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out several rulings that protect the ayah from being misread.

**1. It covers both obligatory and voluntary giving.** Some commentators took the spending here to mean obligatory charity such as zakah; others took it to mean voluntary (*nafl*) charity. But according to a consensus of respected researchers in the field, its sense is general and includes both. And the recorded actions of the Companions cited above bear witness that their charitable initiatives were voluntary. So: give your zakah, give your voluntary charity — but that perfect excellence and merit will blossom only when what you spend is something you actually like and love. Not that you pick out the spare, the useless or the worthless, as though you were shedding the burden of charity, as if it were some sort of punitive tax on you. The same theme is taken up more clearly elsewhere: "O those who believe, spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have brought forth for you from the earth, and do not opt for a bad thing spending only from there, while you are not going to accept it at all unless you close your eyes to it…" (2:267).

**2. "From what" — moderation is built into the wording.** This is the second ruling, drawn from the hint in the word **مِمَّا (mimmā)**, "from what." The purpose is not to spend away everything one likes and loves, wholesale, in the way of Allah. The purpose is that whatever has to be spent should be spent **from among** the good things. Spending in this way will bring the full reward of charity.

**3. What counts is sincerity, not price tags.** Spending the cherished is not tied to spending something of high value. However small it may be in quantity or cost, if it is something you genuinely like and hold dear, you become deserving of this *birr*. Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: whoever spends sincerely for the good pleasure of Allah, **even if it be a single date**, that too is good enough to make him deserving of the great merit and perfect righteousness promised in this ayah.

**4. The poor are not shut out.** On the surface it might seem that someone with little or nothing to give must remain deprived of this great good. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: the ayah does not mean this great good is unobtainable by any route other than spending cherished possessions. It can be attained by other means as well — worship (ʿibādah), remembrance of Allah (dhikr), recitation of the Qur'an (tilāwah), and abundance of voluntary prayers (nawāfil) — as has been clearly explained in the hadith narrations.

**5. What does "what you love" actually mean?** Another ayah of the Qur'an tells us that something liked and loved means a thing that is still working for you, that you yourself need — not something spare and useless. "And they give food, in spite of love for it, to the needy" (76:8): the favoured servants of Allah feed the poor although they need the food themselves. And, clarifying the same theme: "they prefer others over their own selves even though they themselves are in need" (59:9). The test is whether giving it away costs you something real.

**6. Giving your surplus is still rewarded.** Entry into the fold of perfect good and the ranks of the righteous depends on spending one's cherished possessions in the way of Allah — but it does not follow that there is no merit at all for one who spends what is extra to his needs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds this in the closing clause: **"And whatever of good you spend, Allah knows it well."** No charity is devoid of merit, whether one spends the cherished or the extra. A person who spends good things he likes *and also* gives away what is surplus to his needs — left-over food, used clothing, defective utensils or articles in use — commits no sin by including these among his acts of charity; he will definitely be rewarded for those too. What *is* certainly undesirable and prohibited is getting into the habit of always picking out the extra and the bad to spend in the way of Allah.

## "Allah knows it well"

The ayah ends where charity is really weighed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments that this closing clause tells us Allah is fully aware of the real quality of what a person spends: whether or not it was dear to him, and whether he is spending it for the good pleasure of Allah or for pretence and publicity. A mere verbal claim by somebody that he is spending what he cherishes settles nothing. **Keeping vigil over him is the One, the all-Knowing, the all-Aware, who is cognizant of the secrets of the heart** — He is watching, and He knows the true worth of the spending in His way.

## Living it

The ayah does not ask for a grand gesture on demand. It asks a quiet question: *what, of what I have, do I love most?* Then it asks whether Allah has any share in that.

Abū Ṭalḥah's answer was a garden. ʿUmar's was land at Khaybar. Zayd's was a horse. Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's threshold was a single date given sincerely. The scale differs; the movement of the heart is identical — reaching past the pile of things you were going to discard anyway, and choosing something that will actually be missed.

And the Prophet's ﷺ guidance to Abū Ṭalḥah keeps this from becoming abstract: the first place to look for someone to give it to may well be your own relatives.

passages.title: Food made unlawful to Israel and Abraham's way
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat settle a single dispute: the Jews objected that the Prophet ﷺ could not be following the way of Ibrāhīm while eating camel meat and drinking camel milk, since — they claimed — these had been forbidden all the way back to Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm. Allah answers by correcting the history: **all** food was lawful to the Children of Israel; the only exception was what Isrāʾīl (Yaʿqūb) imposed **on himself**, and that was before the Tawrāh was even revealed. The passage then turns the correction into a challenge (bring the Tawrāh and read it), a verdict (whoever lies about Allah after this is a wrongdoer), and a call (follow the way of Ibrāhīm).

What holds the three ayat together is one thread: a false claim about Allah's law is exposed by Allah's own record, and the exposure ends in an invitation.

## The objection that provoked the revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports — citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī on the authority of al-Wāḥidī and al-Kalbī — that the Prophet ﷺ stated his adherence to the community of Ibrāhīm ﷺ in all the fundamentals of the religious code and most of its branches. The Jews objected: *"You eat camel meat and partake of its milk, although these were unlawful for Abraham."* The Prophet ﷺ replied: *"No, this was lawful for him."* They insisted: *"All that we consider unlawful has continued to be unlawful since the days of Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm, to the point that this unlawfulness reached us."*

Their argument was not really about camels. It was about **permanence** — the claim that a sacred law, once given, never changes. Allah's reply in ayah 93 goes straight to the historical fact they had misremembered.

## The four questions

Ibn Kathīr brings a longer scene here. Imam Ahmad records that Ibn ʿAbbās said: a group of Jews came to Allah's Prophet ﷺ and said, "Talk to us about some things we will ask you and which only a Prophet would know." He said: "Ask me about whatever you wish. However, give your pledge to Allah, similar to the pledge that Yaʿqūb took from his children, that if I tell you something and you recognise its truth, you will follow me in Islam." They said, "Agreed."

They asked about four matters: what kinds of food Isrāʾīl prohibited for himself; the discharge of the man and the woman and what role each plays in producing male or female offspring; the condition of the unlettered Prophet during sleep; and who his *walī* (supporter) among the angels is. He ﷺ took their covenant that they would follow him if he answered, and they agreed.

To the first he ﷺ said: *"I ask you by He Who sent down the Tawrāh to Mūsā, do you not know that Isrāʾīl once became very ill? When his illness was prolonged, he vowed to Allah that if He cures his illness, he would prohibit the best types of drink and food for himself. Was not the best food to him camel meat and the best drink camel milk?"* They said, "Yes, by Allah." The Messenger ﷺ said: *"O Allah, be Witness against them."*

For the second he ﷺ swore a fuller oath — *"I ask you by Allah, other than Whom there is no deity (worthy of worship), Who sent down the Tawrāh to Mūsā"* — and put to them what they knew about the two discharges and how the offspring takes its sex by Allah's leave. They said simply, "Yes." He said, *"O Allah, be Witness against them."* For the third he returned to the first formula — *"I ask you by He Who sent down the Tawrāh to Mūsā, do you not know that the eyes of this unlettered Prophet sleep, but his heart does not sleep?"* They said, "Yes, by Allah!" He said, *"O Allah, be Witness."*

Then came the fourth: "Tell us now about your *walī* among the angels, for this is when we either follow or shun you." He said: *"My walī — who brings down the revelation from Allah — is Jibrīl, and Allah never sent a Prophet but Jibrīl is his walī."* They said, "We then shun you. Had you a walī other than Jibrīl, we would have followed you." The report ends by noting that concerning this Allah revealed *"Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl…"* (2:97).

Notice what this scene establishes. **They knew the answer.** Their own scripture confirmed it, and they confirmed it aloud, three times over — twice swearing by Allah as they did — while the Prophet ﷺ called Allah to witness after each admission. And then, at the fourth of the very questions they had come to ask, they turned away. That is the backdrop against which ayah 94 speaks of inventing a lie against Allah "after that."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the medical detail from Ibn ʿAbbās in an authentic report: Yaʿqūb suffered from sciatica and had taken a vow that he would abandon what he liked most in what he ate if Allah cured him of the disease. He was cured; camel meat was what he liked most; so he abandoned it. (Maʿārif cites al-Ḥākim and al-Tirmidhī as quoted in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī.)

## The exact words of ayah 93

Two phrases carry the whole argument.

**"…except what Isrāʾīl made unlawful *upon himself* (ʿalā nafsihi)."** The Arabic does not say Allah forbade it. It says Isrāʾīl forbade it, and forbade it *on himself* — a personal undertaking, born of a personal vow in a personal illness. His children then imitated the practice after him, as Ibn Kathīr puts it, and Maʿārif notes that it remained unlawful for his progeny as well.

**"…before the Tawrāh was sent down."** Ibn Kathīr says there are two objectives behind revealing this segment of the ayah.

*First*, it praises Yaʿqūb: he forbade himself the most delightful things for Allah's sake, and this practice was allowed during his period of Law. Placed right after ayah 92 — *"By no means shall you attain al-Birr (righteousness) unless you spend of that which you love"* — the sequence is suitable. But Ibn Kathīr is careful to mark the difference: what we are allowed in our Law is to spend in Allah's obedience from what we like and covet — not to prohibit what Allah has allowed. He cites *"and gives his wealth, in spite of love for it"* (2:177) and *"and they give food, in spite of their love for it"* (76:8).

*Second*, it dismantles their denial that abrogation (*naskh* — Allah replacing one ruling with another) ever occurs, by showing that it already occurred in their own Law. Ibn Kathīr lists cases:

- When Nūḥ departed from the ark, Allah allowed him to eat the meat of all types of animals. Afterwards Isrāʾīl forbade camel meat and milk to himself, his children imitated him, and the Tawrāh later prohibited that food and added several more prohibitions.
- Allah allowed Ādam to marry his daughters to his sons; this was later forbidden.
- The Law of Ibrāhīm allowed a man to take female servants as companions along with his wife — as Ibrāhīm did when he took Hājar while married to Sārah; the Tawrāh later prohibited this.
- It was previously allowed to take two sisters as wives at the same time — as Yaʿqūb did; the Tawrāh later prohibited this.

All these examples, Ibn Kathīr says, are in the Tawrāh and constitute *naskh*. So let them consider what Allah legislated for ʿĪsā and whether that falls under abrogation or not — and why they did not then follow him. Rather, they defied and rebelled against ʿĪsā, and against the correct religion Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with. (Note also where this sits in the sūrah: Ibn Kathīr observes that after Allah refuted the false Christian beliefs about ʿĪsā and his mother, He began here to answer the Jews.)

**"Bring here the Tawrāh and recite it, if you are truthful."** This is the most confident kind of argument there is: *your own book is my witness.* Ibn Kathīr comments simply — "for the Tawrāh affirms what we are stating here."

## Ayah 94 — inventing a lie against Allah

*"Then after that, whosoever shall invent a lie against Allah — then it is these that are the wrongdoers."*

The words "after that" are the hinge. This is not aimed at honest ignorance; it is aimed at people who have been shown the evidence and shown where to verify it, and who go on asserting the falsehood anyway. Ibn Kathīr specifies who is meant: those who lie about Allah and claim that He made the Sabbath and the Tawrāh eternal, and who claim that Allah did not send another Prophet calling to Allah with proofs and evidences — although the evidence indicates that abrogation had already occurred within the Tawrāh itself.

The verdict is *al-ẓālimūn*, the wrongdoers. To attribute to Allah a law He never gave is to put something in its wrong place at the highest possible level: it misrepresents the Lawgiver Himself.

## Ayah 95 — "Allah has spoken the truth"

*"Say: Allah has spoken the truth; follow the religion of Ibrāhīm the Ḥanīf, and he was not of the Mushrikīn (idolaters)."*

Ibn Kathīr reads *"Allah has spoken the truth"* as: say, O Muhammad, that Allah has said the truth in what He conveyed and legislated in the Qur'an. The dispute is closed not by out-arguing them but by declaring where truth actually rests.

Then comes the invitation. *Millat Ibrāhīm* — rendered "the religion of Ibrāhīm" by Ibn Kathīr and "the community of Abraham" in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — is the religion Allah has legislated in the Qur'an. Ibn Kathīr's translation renders *ḥanīf* here in a single word: "monotheist." That is why the ayah immediately adds "and he was not of the *mushrikīn*" — the idolaters, those who associate partners with Allah. The two halves define each other: to be ḥanīf is precisely *not* to be an idolater.

Ibn Kathīr's comment is worth hearing in full force: indeed, this is the truth, there is no doubt in it, and the perfect way; no Prophet has brought a more complete, clear, plain and perfect way than he did. He brings two parallels — *"Say: Truly, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a right religion, the religion of Ibrāhīm, the Ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters"* (6:161), and *"Then We have sent the revelation to you: Follow the religion of Ibrāhīm, the Ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters"* (16:123).

There is a quiet symmetry in the passage: the objectors invoked Ibrāhīm to accuse the Prophet ﷺ, and the ayah ends by handing Ibrāhīm's way back to them as the invitation they should have accepted.

## Living it: the vow that forbids the lawful

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the legal lesson. Among the Banī Isrāʾīl, a prohibition that began because of a vow went on to continue as a divine injunction; it seems their code recognised a vow as a cause of unlawfulness of something lawful.

Our Sharīʿah is not the same. A vow may make a permissible act obligatory on a person — that much Maʿārif affirms. But a vow or pledge that renders something **unlawful** is, in reality, an oath, and such a prohibition is not permissible in our Sharīʿah. In that case, Maʿārif states, it is obligatory to break the oath and make amends by *kaffārah* (the prescribed expiation). This accords with Allah's own address in the Qur'an: *"Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?"* (66:1).

So the practical shape of the passage is this. Renouncing something you love, for Allah's sake, is a real and honoured impulse — that is why ayah 93 sits where it does, after the call to spend from what you love in ayah 92. But in this Ummah the outlet for that impulse is **giving**, not **banning**. Spend the food you love; do not declare it forbidden. No one — however sincere, however grateful for a healing — holds the authority to move a thing from the lawful column to the unlawful one. That authority belongs to Allah alone, and ayah 94 names the penalty for anyone who claims it: to be counted among the wrongdoers.

## In sum

Ayah 93 corrects a false history with a fact their own scripture could confirm. Ayah 94 warns those who persist in the falsehood after the correction. Ayah 95 closes the case and opens a door — *Allah has spoken the truth; so follow the religion of Ibrāhīm the Ḥanīf, who was not of the idolaters.* An argument that begins over camel meat ends as a call to pure, undivided worship of the One who alone decides what is lawful and what is not.

passages.title: The first House at Bakkah and the duty of pilgrimage
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat answer a claim with a building. Ibn Kathir frames it plainly: the House at Bakkah is the Ka'bah built by Ibrahim al-Khalil — and it is *his* religion that the Jews and Christians claim they follow. Yet they do not perform Hajj to the very House he built by Allah's command and to which he invited people to come. Ayah 96 says what the House **is** (first, blessed, a guidance for all the worlds); ayah 97 sets out, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists them, three distinctions: the signs of Allah's power standing in it, the security given to whoever enters it, and the obligation of Hajj upon everyone who has the means and ability to reach it.

## "The first House set up for the people" (ayah 96)

Ibn Kathir reads *wudiʿa lin-nas* — appointed for mankind — as **for all people, for their acts of worship and religious rituals**: they go around the House in tawaf, pray in its vicinity, and remain in its area in iʿtikaf. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws something further from "set up for the people": the honour in which this House is held was never to be limited to one nation or group. Allah has placed a built-in aura of dignity and awe in its presence, which draws in the hearts of people of itself.

**In what sense "first"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings:

- **The first house of any kind in the world.** Adam (peace be upon him) was a prophet of Allah; given his stature and his position as Allah's vicegerent, it is likely that soon after his appearance on the earth he chose to build the House of Allah before building his own residence. This is the opinion reported from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, Mujahid, Qatadah and others among the Companions and their successors.
- **The first house made exclusively for worship**, houses where people lived having possibly existed before it — a view reported from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him).

Al-Bayhaqi, in his book *Dala'il al-Nubuwwah*, reports on the authority of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs that the Prophet ﷺ said that after Adam and Hawwa' came into this mortal world, Allah commanded them through the angel Jibril to build the House of Allah; when they had done so they were told to go round it in tawaf, and they were told that they were the first among people and that this was the first House appointed for people.

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Dharr said: "I said, 'O Allah's Messenger! Which Masjid was the first to be built on the surface of the earth?' He said, 'Al-Masjid al-Haram.' I said, 'Which was built next?' He replied, 'Al-Masjid al-Aqsa.' I said, 'What was the period of time between building the two?' He said, 'Forty years.'" He ﷺ added that wherever the prayer becomes due, one should pray there, for the whole earth was made a masjid. Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhari and Muslim also collected this hadith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same exchange from the Sahihayn, and explains that the forty years relates the House of Allah to the *initial* construction of Bayt al-Maqdis: there are reports that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) undertook that initial construction forty years after the Ka'bah, and that Sulayman's (peace be upon him) later building at Bayt al-Maqdis was likewise a rebuilding on the original Abrahamic foundations, not a fresh one — so the reports do not contradict one another.

**Why "Bakkah"?** Ibn Kathir explains that Bakkah is one of the names of Makkah, and gives two senses: it brings *buka'* — crying, weeping — upon the tyrants and the arrogant, meaning they weep and become humble in its vicinity; or that people do *buka'* next to it, in the sense that they gather around it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that in common Arab usage *mim* is substituted for *ba'*, so it makes no difference whether one says Bakkah is Makkah by that substitution or simply an alternate name for it. Ibn Kathir lists other names the city carries, among them al-Bayt al-ʿAtiq (the Ancient House), al-Bayt al-Haram (the Sacred House), al-Balad al-Amin (the City of Safety), Umm al-Qura (Mother of the Towns) and Umm Rahm (Mother of Mercy).

## The House rebuilt again and again

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the history, and it explains the Ka'bah you see today. The structure built by Adam (peace be upon him) stood until the time of Nuh (peace be upon him), when it collapsed in the Flood and its traces were obliterated; Ibrahim (peace be upon him) then rebuilt it on the same foundations. When it collapsed again, a group from the tribe of Jurhum raised it; at a further collapse the Amalekites rebuilt it; and when it collapsed close to the early period of the Prophet ﷺ, the Quraysh built it all over again — a construction he ﷺ himself took part in, helping place the Black Stone with his blessed hands.

Note that Ibrahim did not lay this House out from nothing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to Allah's own words, "and when Ibrahim was raising up the *foundations* of the House along with Isma'il" (2:127), as an indication that the foundations were already there, and to "and when We settled for Ibrahim the site of the House" (22:26) as suggesting that the site had been pre-determined since earlier times. Some reports say an angel led him to the site and to the foundations lying hidden under sand dunes.

The Quraysh's structure departed from Ibrahim's foundation in three ways: they left out a section of the House now known as the **Hatim**; the original had two doors, one for entry and another at the back for exit, and they retained just the one door in the east; and they raised the level of the entry door far above the ground so that not everybody could go in easily — restricting entry to those they permitted. The Prophet ﷺ said to ʿA'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that he wished he could demolish the present structure and raise it exactly on the Abrahamic foundation, correcting the Quraysh's deviation, but that doing so was likely to create a misunderstanding among Muslims who were new and whose knowledge was not yet perfect — so he would leave it as it was for the time being. He ﷺ did not live long enough to act on that wish.

ʿAbdullah ibn az-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him), ʿA'ishah's nephew, had heard this. When he came to rule Makkah, he had the House rebuilt in accordance with it and with Ibrahim's original foundation. His rule was brief: Hajjaj ibn Yusuf invaded Makkah, ʿAbdullah was martyred, and Hajjaj — unwilling to leave that deed as a source of fame for him — demolished the structure and rebuilt it as the Quraysh had it. Later Muslim rulers intended, on the strength of that hadith, to restore the Abrahamic form; but the master-jurist of the age, Imam Malik ibn Anas (may Allah have mercy on him), gave a fatwa that re-demolishing and re-building at this stage would render the House of Allah a plaything in the hands of the rulers to come, each doing the same to earn fame for himself — so it was appropriate to leave it as it is. The whole ummah accepted this, and Hajjaj's structure is what stands to this day, with repairs continuing ever since.

## "Blessed" — what *mubarakan* says

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the word to its root: *mubarak* is derived from *barakah*, which means **to grow** and **to sustain**. That growth can be looked at from two angles. Something may grow by visibly increasing in quantity — or it may add nothing noteworthy to its quantity yet prove so useful in so many situations that far more would ordinarily have been needed to do the same job. That too counts as growth.

**Outwardly:** in spite of Makkah and its environs being dry and barren desert, all sorts of fruits and vegetables and items of need are available there in all seasons — not merely enough for the people of Makkah, but for visitors from everywhere in the world, who in the Hajj season outnumber the residents by at least four or five times and stay not for days but for months together. It has never happened that articles of use ran out of the market and became unavailable, nor that the sacrificial animals failed, and this without special arrangements to import them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the Qur'an's words "brought toward it are fruits of everything" (28:57) as a clear indication of this.

**Inwardly:** the spiritual blessings are so numerous it is impossible to count them. Some acts of worship belong to this House alone — Hajj and ʿUmrah. Others increase in merit several degrees when done there: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that the Prophet ﷺ said that a man offering salah at his home receives the reward of one salah; in the masjid of his locality, twenty-five; in a great congregational mosque, five hundred; in al-Masjid al-Aqsa, one thousand; in his ﷺ own masjid, fifty thousand; and in al-Masjid al-Haram, one hundred thousand. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this narration has been reported by Ibn Majah and at-Tahawi and others. All of this, it says, is what the closing word of ayah 96 gathers up: *hudan lil-ʿalamin*, **a guidance for all the worlds**.

## "In it are clear signs" (ayah 97)

Ibn Kathir explains *ayatun bayyinat* as clear signs that Ibrahim built the Ka'bah and that Allah has honoured and blessed it. Al-ʿAwfi reported that Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned among them the Maqam and al-Mashʿar al-Haram.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers several such signs. Since the foundations of the House were laid, Allah has, because of its enormous blessings, protected the people of Makkah against enemy attack — when Abrahah invaded with his army of elephants, Allah in His most perfect power destroyed them through birds. Those who enter the sacred precincts stand protected: men, women, even animals. It also observes that when rain falls on a certain side of the House, countries lying on that side have been found to receive substantial rainfall; and it points to the Jamarat, the pillars at which every pilgrim throws seven pebbles a day for three days. Millions come each year; had the pebbles remained, the Jamarat would lie under a mountain of them, yet after the three days no such deposit is to be seen. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that the Prophet ﷺ stated that angels pick up these pebbles in a manner invisible to mankind, and that the few left behind belong to those whose Hajj was not accepted — which is why it is forbidden to take up pebbles lying near the Jamarat and throw them as part of the rites. Shaykh Jalal ad-Din as-Suyuti said in *al-Khasa'is al-Kubra* that some of the miracles of the Prophet ﷺ still stand and will continue to the Day of Judgment for everyone to see: chief among them the Qur'an itself, which the whole world cannot match — "then produce a Surah like it" (10:38) — and among them this sign at the Jamarat.

**The Maqam of Ibrahim.** Ibn Kathir: when the building was raised, Ibrahim stood on the Maqam so that he could raise the walls higher, while his son Isma'il handed him the stones. Mujahid said, "The impression of Ibrahim's feet remains on the Maqam as a clear sign" — and it was reported that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbdul-ʿAziz, al-Hasan, Qatadah, as-Suddi, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and others said similarly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds narrations that the stone raised itself along with the rising level of the construction and came down again when required, and comments that an inert, unconscious stone being given such response to need — or the plasticity of wax, so that a perfect footprint appears on its surface — is a sign of the most perfect power of Allah.

Ibn Kathir notes that the Maqam used to be situated right next to the House; later, during his reign, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab moved it farther east so that those performing tawaf could do so easily without disturbing those praying at the Maqam afterwards — for Allah commanded, "And take the Maqam of Ibrahim as a place of prayer" (2:125). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the same move and its later housing, and rules that offering the two rakʿah of tawaf behind or close to it is more merit-worthy; but since the name "Maqam Ibrahim" taken in a literal sense covers the entire Sacred Mosque, the Muslim jurists have ruled that offering those two rakʿah anywhere within al-Masjid al-Haram satisfies the obligation.

## "Whoever enters it is secure"

Ibn Kathir: the Haram of Makkah is a safe refuge for those in a state of fear — in its vicinity they will be safe, just as was the case in the time of Jahiliyyah. Al-Hasan al-Basri described it: a man would commit murder, then wear a piece of wool around his neck and enter the Haram; and even when the son of the murdered person met him there, he would not make a move against him until he left the sanctuary. Ibn Kathir joins this to Allah's words about a secure sanctuary "while men are being snatched away from all around them" (29:67), and to "So let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear" (106:3–4).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes two layers of this security. **Legally**: Allah has ordained that one who enters is not to be molested or killed; even one who has killed someone or committed some other crime and taken refuge there is not punished inside — he is compelled to come out of the Haram, and the punishment due is carried out then. **Factually**: in the very design of His creation, Allah has caused awe and reverence for this House to take root in human hearts. The Arab tribes of Jahiliyyah, wild and warring as they were, were ready to give their lives to uphold its honour — a son whose father had been killed would say nothing to the killer and quietly move away from him, in spite of his burning rage for revenge.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the one time fighting was allowed within the Haram was for a few hours, by revelation, restricted to the Prophet ﷺ at the conquest of Makkah so that he might cleanse the House and serve an important objective of faith; and that soon after the conquest he ﷺ announced expressly that the original unlawfulness of fighting there remains valid for ever. As for Hajjaj ibn Yusuf's armed action against ʿAbdullah ibn az-Zubayr, it says that this was a grave sin and a flagrant violation of the Ka'bah's sanctity in the sight of the whole community, and does not affect the divine declaration of that sanctity.

**In the Prophet's ﷺ own words.** Ibn Kathir states that it is not allowed for anyone to hunt in the Haram, to drive game out of its den to be hunted, to cut the trees in its vicinity, or to pick its grass, as the hadiths of the Prophet ﷺ and the statements of the Companions testify. The Two Sahihs recorded — this being the wording of Muslim — that Ibn ʿAbbas said that on the day of the conquest of Makkah the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Beware! Allah made this town a sanctuary when He created the heavens and earth, and it is sacred by Allah's decree until the Day of Resurrection. Fighting in Makkah was not permitted for anyone before me, and it was made legal for me for only a few hours or so on that day… It is not allowed to uproot its thorny shrubs, hunt its game, pick up its lost objects, except by announcing it, or to uproot its trees." Al-ʿAbbas said, "Except the lemongrass, O Allah's Messenger, as they use it in their houses and graves." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Except lemongrass."

The Two Sahihs also recorded that Abu Shurayh al-ʿAdawi related what he had heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say on the day following the conquest — his ears heard it and his heart memorised it, and he saw the Prophet ﷺ with his own eyes: **Allah, not the people, made Makkah a sanctuary.** Therefore anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should neither shed blood in it nor cut down its trees; and if anybody argues that fighting there is permissible on the basis that Allah's Messenger fought in Makkah, say to him, "Allah allowed His Messenger and did not allow you." He ﷺ was allowed only a few hours on that day, and today its sanctity is as valid as it was before — so let those present inform those who are absent.

Muslim also recorded that Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, "None of you is allowed to carry a weapon in Makkah." And ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAdi ibn al-Hamra' az-Zuhri said that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, while standing at al-Hazwarah in the marketplace of Makkah, "By Allah! You are the best of Allah's land and the most beloved land to Allah. Had it not been for the fact that I was driven out of you, I would not have left you." Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad collected this hadith and that the wording given is his; at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah also collected it, and at-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan sahih."

## "Hajj to the House is a duty people owe to Allah"

Ibn Kathir: this ayah established the obligation of performing Hajj. There are many hadiths that mention it as one of the pillars and fundamentals of Islam, and this is agreed upon by the Muslims. According to the texts and the consensus of the scholars, it is obligatory for the adult Muslim to perform it **once during his lifetime**.

Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once gave a speech in which he said, "O people! Hajj has been enjoined on you, therefore perform Hajj." A man asked, "Is it every year, O Allah's Messenger?" The Prophet ﷺ remained silent until the man had repeated the question three times, and then said, "Had I said yes, it would have become an obligation and you would not have been able to fulfil it." He said next: "Leave me as I leave you. Those before you were destroyed because of their many questions and their disputing with their Prophets. If I command you with something, perform it as much as you can; and if I forbid you something, then refrain from it." Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim recorded similarly.

Read the ayah's own wording again: Hajj is *a duty that mankind owes to Allah* — a right upon people, not a favour offered. And read the mercy in that silence: the Prophet ﷺ himself explained it — an answer given would have bound the ummah to what it could not have fulfilled.

**What "able to undertake the journey" means.** Ibn Kathir says there are several categories of ability: the physical ability of the person himself, and the ability related to other things as set out in the books of jurisprudence. He then relates from Ibn ʿUmar a session of questions put to the Prophet ﷺ. His text introduces it as recorded by Abu ʿIsa at-Tirmidhi and closes the quotation with the words, "This is the narration that Ibn Majah collected" — so both collections are named for it, and we pass on both rather than choose between them. A man stood up and asked, "O Messenger of Allah! Who is the pilgrim?" He ﷺ said, "He who has untidy hair and clothes." Another asked, "Which Hajj is better?" He ﷺ said, "The noisy — with supplication to Allah — and bloody, with sacrifice." Another asked, "What is the ability to undertake the journey?" He ﷺ said, "Having provision and a means of transportation."

Al-Hakim narrated that Anas said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about this very phrase, "for those who are able to undertake the journey," and answered, "Having sufficient provision and a means of transportation." Al-Hakim stated that this hadith's chain of narration is authentic following the guidelines of Muslim in his *Sahih*, though the Two Sahihs did not collect it. And Ahmad recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever intends to perform Hajj, let him rush to perform it" — Abu Dawud also collected this hadith.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out what "means" comes to: resources **surplus to one's basic needs**, sufficient for the cost of travel there and back and the expenses of the stay — and good enough to cover the expenses of one's family until one's return, since that is a standing obligation. Physical capacity is likewise required: one who cannot see, or use hands and feet, would not have the ability to go that far and complete the many requirements of Hajj. Since a woman is not legally permitted to travel without a *mahram* (a relative marriage with whom is prohibited), she is counted "able" when travelling with a mahram who is himself making Hajj, whether he bears his own expenses or she pays for them as well. And the route must be secure: where peaceful conditions do not exist and there is acute danger to life and property, the ability is absent.

Note the root: *hajj* literally means **to intend**. What it means as a prescribed observance is stated in the Qur'an itself — the tawaf of the Ka'bah, the stay at ʿArafat, and Muzdalifah — with the remaining details made clear by the Prophet ﷺ through his words and deeds. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls the hadith Muslims generally know, that one who performs his Hajj obligations correctly is so cleansed of his past sins as if he were born on that day, pure and pristine.

## "And whoever disbelieves — Allah is beyond need of the worlds"

Ibn Kathir reports Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and several others as commenting on this ayah: **"Whoever denies the necessity of Hajj becomes a disbeliever, and Allah is far Richer than to need him."** Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr al-Ismaʿili recorded that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said, "Whoever can afford Hajj but did not perform it, there is no difference in his case if he dies while Jew or Christian." Ibn Kathir notes that this has an authentic chain of narration leading to ʿUmar.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān separates two cases, and the distinction matters:

1. **One who intentionally rejects the belief that Hajj is obligatory.** Such a person cannot be considered a Muslim; the words "and whoever disbelieves" fit him clearly and comprehensively.
2. **One who believes it obligatory yet, having the means and the ability, does not perform it.** He too is, in a way, no less a denier of the divine command; and the words fall upon him **in the form of admonition and warning**, since he is acting like those who do not perform Hajj at all. This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is why the Muslim jurists (may Allah have mercy on them) have called the ayah a severe warning to those who stay home in spite of having the means. "Let us seek refuge with Allah from such a fate."

The closing clause guards the heart: Allah is independent of all the worlds. He is far richer than to need the one who turns away.

## Living it

**If you have the means, do not wait.** Ahmad and Abu Dawud recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to hasten — "Whoever intends to perform Hajj, let him rush to perform it" — and ʿUmar's words are not decoration. "Ability" cuts both ways: it is a real condition, and once it is crossed, a real threshold.

**Let the sanctuary teach restraint.** A place where a killer walked unharmed, where a weapon may not be carried, where even a thorny shrub may not be uprooted, shows what restraint looks like when Allah has set the boundary — and Abu Shurayh's report is exact on why: it was **Allah**, not people, who made Makkah a sanctuary.

passages.title: Barring others from the path; a warning to believers
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a single, carefully ordered confrontation. Two of them (98–99) are addressed to the People of the Book and put two questions to them — *why do you reject Allah's signs?* and *why do you turn away from Allah's path those who have believed?* The other two (100–101) turn and face the believers with a warning and a question of their own: if you obey such people they would render you disbelievers after you have believed — and how could you disbelieve, when the verses of Allah are being recited to you and His Messenger ﷺ is among you?

What holds the four together is one incident, and one idea. The incident is an attempt to break Muslim unity from the outside. The idea is that the danger is real but the protection is nearer than the danger.

## The event behind the revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that these verses relate to a particular event. Several verses earlier the text had been dealing with the People of the Book, their false beliefs and their doubts; then came the mention of the Bayt Allah — the Sacred House — and Hajj; and now the People of the Book are once again the ones addressed.

There was a Jew named Shammas ibn Qays who harboured a chronic malice against the Muslims. Once he saw two Ansar tribes, Aws and Khazraj, gathered together amiably at one place, and his malevolence got the better of him. He went about looking for ways to sow seeds of discord between them.

He found one. He set up a man to make a suggestion: these two tribes had fought a long, drawn-out war in the days before Islam, and both parties had recited poetical compositions highlighting their tribal pride. So why not recite those self-congratulating poems now, while both sit together?

The poems were recited. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes what followed in a few devastating lines: emotions rose high, there were charges and counter-charges, to the limit that the place and time of a fresh war was all set.

When the Prophet ﷺ heard about this he came to them and said: *"What is all this? Here I am present amidst you and you are doing this after having become Muslims and after having become united and friendly with each other. This is sheer ignorance. Do you want, in this state of yours, to revert to kufr?"*

They took the warning to their hearts. They knew this was a slip caused by Shaytan. They embraced each other, wept and repented. These verses were revealed in the background of that event.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the transmission of the incident honestly: it appears in *Ruh al-Maʿani* as narrated by Ibn Ishaq, while there are others who narrate it from Zaid ibn Aslam. It adds that the subject continues through several verses after this one.

**Notice how much of the passage this story unlocks.** The Prophet's ﷺ own words to the Ansar — *"Here I am present amidst you"* — stand very close to the argument Allah makes in ayah 101: *how would you disbelieve, while unto you are recited the verses of Allah, and among you is His Messenger?* And the man who engineered the trouble never argued a single point of theology. He simply had old tribal poems recited among people whom Allah had made friends with one another.

## Ayah 98: the charge is put back on the accuser

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the eloquence of the ordering here. Before the People of the Book are taken to task for what they *did* — the scheming — they are first taken to task for their disbelief as well. The implication is pointed: it would have made better sense if they themselves had taken to the right path and become Muslims, rather than devoting themselves to distracting others to the wrong track.

Ibn Kathir explains that in this ayah Allah criticises the disbelieving People of the Book for refusing the truth and rejecting Allah's Ayat, *although they know* that what the Messenger ﷺ was sent with is the truth from Allah. They learned this from the previous Prophets and honourable Messengers, may Allah's peace and blessings be on them all. They all brought the glad tidings of the coming of the unlettered, Arab, Hashimi Prophet ﷺ from Makkah — the master of the Children of Adam, the Final Prophet, the Messenger of the Lord of the heavens and the earth. Ibn Kathir puts the tragedy in a single sentence: they rejected, denied and refused the very Messenger whom they were ordered to convey the glad tidings about.

**"While Allah is Witness to what you do."** This is not a closing formality. Ibn Kathir reads it as Allah warning them against this behaviour by stating that He is Witness over what they do — which indicates their defiance of the knowledge conveyed to them by the Prophets. It is one thing to be wrong. It is another to be wrong while a Witness who knows exactly what you know is watching you be wrong.

## Ayah 99: barring the path

The second question is heavier than the first. Ayah 98 asks about their own rejection of Allah's signs; ayah 99 asks why they stop *those who have believed* from the path of Allah, "seeking to make it seem crooked, while you yourselves are witnesses."

Ibn Kathir's heading over these two ayat is exactly this: *Chastising the People of the Book for Their Disbelief and Blocking the Path of Allah.* He describes them as hindering those who seek to believe from His path, although they know that what the Messenger ﷺ was sent with is the truth from Allah.

That is the thread running through his whole comment on these two ayat: knowledge. They learned of this Prophet ﷺ from the previous Prophets. They were the ones ordered to announce his coming. The obstruction described here is not the confusion of people who were never told; it comes from people who were told, and told first.

The charge closes with **"And Allah is not unaware of what you do."** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah states He is never unaware of what they do, and that He will hold them responsible for their actions — and he brings, as the setting for that accounting, Allah's words about *the Day whereon neither wealth nor sons will avail* (26:88). Wealth and sons: the two things a person leans on hardest in this life, named and set aside in a single phrase.

## Ayah 100: the warning turns to the believers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks the turn: after the admonition to the People of the Book who had engineered this affair, the Muslims themselves are addressed and served with a word of caution.

Ibn Kathir titles this section *Warning Muslims Against Imitating People of the Scriptures*, and names the motive driving the whole business: envy. Allah warns His believing servants against obeying the People of the Book, who envy the believers for the favour that Allah gave them by sending His Messenger ﷺ. He supports this with Allah's words in Surah al-Baqarah: *Many of the People of the Scripture wish that they could turn you away as disbelievers after you have believed, out of their own envy* (2:109) — a verse that names both the wish and its root.

Two things in ayah 100 are worth pausing on.

**"A group of those who were given the Scripture."** The ayah says *a group* — not everyone who was given a scripture. Ibn Kathir preserves that restriction in his own wording of the verse, and it should be preserved in ours.

**"If you obey them."** The verb is obedience — following their lead, taking their suggestion, letting them set the agenda. It is not "if you speak with them" or "if you live beside them." The Aws and the Khazraj were never asked to abandon Islam. They were asked to recite some old poetry. They went along with the suggestion, and before long the place and time of a fresh war was set. The ayah's warning — *they would render you disbelievers after you have believed* — sits alongside the warning the Prophet ﷺ gave them face to face: *"Do you want, in this state of yours, to revert to kufr?"*

## Ayah 101: how could you, of all people, disbelieve?

Having stated the danger, Allah immediately shrinks it. *And how would you disbelieve, while unto you are recited the verses of Allah, and among you is His Messenger?*

Ibn Kathir draws out the sense: **disbelief is far from touching you**, since the Ayat of Allah are being sent down on His Messenger ﷺ day and night, and he recites them and conveys them to you. The question is not an accusation — it is an argument from their situation. Revelation arriving day and night, and the Messenger ﷺ himself among them: these are the last people with an excuse to slip.

He places alongside it Allah's words: *And what is the matter with you that you believe not in Allah! While the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord; and He has indeed taken your covenant, if you are real believers* (57:8).

### From the Sunnah: the most amazing faith

Ibn Kathir cites a hadith here in which one day the Prophet ﷺ said to his Companions: *"Who among the faithful believers do you consider has the most amazing faith?"*

They said, "The angels." He said, *"Why would they not believe, since they are with their Lord?"*

They mentioned the Prophets. He said, *"Why would they not believe while the revelation is sent down to them?"*

They said, "Then, we are." He said, *"Why would not you believe when I am among you?"*

They asked, "Who has the most amazing faith?" He said: *"A people who will come after you and who will find only books that they will believe in."*

(Ibn Kathir introduces this simply as "a Hadith," without naming the collection, so it is passed on here exactly as he gives it.)

Notice why it belongs at this exact point. The Prophet ﷺ is reasoning as ayah 101 reasons — *why would not you believe when I am among you?* — and then he carries that reasoning forward in time. The Companions had every support, and in this hadith that is precisely why their faith, astonishing as it was, was not named the most astonishing of all. The greater wonder, he ﷺ said, belongs to a people coming afterwards who find only written pages and believe what is in them. The argument of ayah 101 does not weaken with distance; in this hadith it turns into a compliment.

## Holding fast: what *iʿtiṣām* means

The passage ends with its remedy: *And whoever holds on to Allah is surely guided to a straight path.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the key word. *Iʿtiṣām* — the act of holding on to Allah firmly — means one who stays firm in, and is totally committed to, his *iman*, his faith. It denotes three things:

- that one should **affirm His Being and His Attributes**;
- that one should be **staunchly faithful to what He has ordained**; and
- that in the process one should be **sure not to be lured into supporting the position of any adversary, whoever that may be**.

Read alongside the incident Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, the third of these is striking. The Ansar were not asked to deny Allah. They were drawn into taking up an old quarrel — and the quarrel was somebody else's project. Holding fast, on this description, includes noticing whose position you have quietly ended up advancing.

The one who acts in this manner, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "is surely guided to the straight path" — meaning that such a person *is* on the straight path, and being on the straight path is the key to all that is good and beneficial which the Word of Allah promises him.

Ibn Kathir's comment runs in the same direction: trusting and relying on Allah are the basis of achieving right guidance and staying away from the path of wickedness; they are also the tool for acquiring guidance and truth and achieving righteous aims.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the caution given to the Muslims in a line worth carrying away: they have by their side **the Book and the Messenger of Allah — two powerful, never-failing sources** — which would help them stay firm in their belief. The passage does not leave a believer frightened; it leaves him located.

A few things follow plainly from these four ayat:

**Old wounds are a weapon.** The scheme worked by reviving poems from the days before Islam. Nothing new was invented. When something reopens a settled grievance among believers and the heat rises fast, this passage prompts a simple question: who arranged for this to be recited, and who benefits?

**"This is sheer ignorance."** That was the Prophet's ﷺ own word for what the Aws and Khazraj had begun to do — after having become Muslims, and after having become united and friendly with each other. That is why he ﷺ asked whether they wanted, in that state of theirs, to revert to kufr.

**Repentance closed it.** The Ansar did not defend themselves or apportion blame. They took the warning to their hearts, knew the slip for Shaytan's doing, embraced each other, wept and repented. That is the model response, and it took no longer than the quarrel had.

**And the protection is already at hand.** Ayah 101 does not say *try harder*; it points to what is already there. The verses of Allah are recited, and what the Messenger ﷺ conveyed is with us. Whoever holds on to Allah — affirming His Being and His Attributes, staying faithful to what He has ordained, and refusing to be lured into supporting an adversary's position — has, in the words of the ayah, been guided to a straight path.

passages.title: Hold to the rope of Allah and do not divide
passages.tafsir:
# Hold to the rope of Allah

**What this passage is.** These four ayat give a community its charter. Ayah 102 works on the individual — taqwa, held to the end of life. Ayah 103 turns that inward soundness outward: hold together to Allah's rope, and remember what He did for hearts that once wanted each other's blood. Ayah 104 gives the community a standing mission — calling to good. Ayah 105 shows the ruin that comes when a people abandons that mission and splinters. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads them as one architecture: two principles that secure collective well-being (taqwa and unity), then the work that sustains them (daʿwah), then the warning.

**The moment behind them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the preceding verses warned the Muslims that the People of the Book and others wanted them to slip from the straight path, so they must stay alert to such moves. The specific mischief in view was an attempt to set the Anṣār tribes of Aws and Khazraj against each other by stirring up the memory of their old feuds. Read against that, ayah 103 is not an abstract sermon on brotherhood — it is a direct counter-move. It reminds the very people being provoked exactly Who ended that war. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: once inside Islam, division is unthinkable.

## Ayah 102: taqwa "as is His due"

*Taqwa* in Arabic carries the sense of avoidance and abstinence. It is usually rendered "fear" because what one is told to keep away from is precisely what should frighten a person — the danger of divine retribution. So taqwa is really a way of organising your whole life with a live sense of accountability before Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out three degrees of it. The lowest is avoiding *kufr* (disbelief) and *shirk* (associating partners with Allah); in this sense every Muslim counts as *muttaqī*, even one with sins, and the Qur'an sometimes uses the word that way. The second degree — avoiding whatever Allah and His Messenger ﷺ dislike — is what is really wanted, and it is on this level that the Qur'an's and the Sunnah's promised blessings of taqwa rest. The third is a high station destined for the prophets, their devoted deputies and the men of Allah: guarding the heart against the onslaught of everything unrelated to Allah, and keeping it filled with His remembrance and the desire for His pleasure.

**What "as is His due" means.** Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Abī Ḥātim that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd explained *ḥaqqa tuqātihi* as: "That He is obeyed and not defied, remembered and not forgotten, and appreciated and not unappreciated." Ibn Kathir notes the chain to Ibn Masʿūd is authentic, and that al-Ḥākim collected it in his *Mustadrak* as a report going back to the Prophet ﷺ, calling it authentic by the criteria of al-Bukhārī and Muslim — but Ibn Kathir himself judges that it appears to be a statement of Ibn Masʿūd, "and Allah knows best." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same wording from Ibn Masʿūd, Rabīʿ, Qatādah and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (citing *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*), and adds that the explanation has also been reported with a chain ascending to the Prophet ﷺ himself.

Commentators have unfolded it differently. Some say due taqwa means standing firm on justice in obedience to Allah and dismissing every derogatory criticism, wherever it comes from, even when being just costs you — against your own self, your children, your parents. Others say no one attains it until he guards his tongue; Ibn Kathir relates from Anas that a servant will not have taqwa as is His due until he keeps his tongue idle.

**Does it demand the impossible?** No. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Ṭāwūs, the verse "Fear Allah as much as you can" (64:16) is simply an explanation of *ḥaqqa tuqātihi*. If you are genuinely spending your attention and energy guarding against evil, the obligation stands fulfilled; if someone who has already done all he could still slips into something impermissible, that is not counted against "taqwa as is His due."

**"And die not except as Muslims."** Death is not in our hands, so how can it be commanded? Ibn Kathir answers: preserve your Islam while you are well and safe, so that you die upon it — for Allah has decreed that whatever state a person lives in is the state he dies in and is raised in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the same principle in the well-known form: *as you live, so shall you die; and as you die, so shall you be raised.* The command, then, is on the living: whoever is resolved to live his whole life by Islam and acts on that resolve to the best of his ability will, by Allah's will, die upon it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a caution about narrations describing people whose lifetime of good deeds is wasted by something terrible at the end — that fate, it says, befalls those who were never sincere and steadfast from the outset; and Allah knows best.

And because the last state matters so much, Ibn Kathir places two hadiths here. Imām Aḥmad records from Jābir that three nights before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, he heard him say: "None of you should die except while having sincere trust in Allah, the Exalted and Most Honorable." Muslim also recorded it. And the Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah says, "I am as My servant thinks of Me." The command to die as a Muslim is therefore not meant to terrify you into despair. It is meant to make you live carefully while thinking well of your Lord.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the two halves of the ayah together: taqwa *is* Islam — total obedience to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and total avoidance of disobedience to them is exactly what taqwa means, and exactly what Islam is.

## Ayah 103: the rope, and why it must be this rope

**What is the "rope"?** Ibn Kathir reports the view that *ḥabl Allāh* means Allah's covenant, comparing 3:112, where "a rope from Allah and a rope from men" refers to pledges and treaties. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes it as the Holy Qur'an, citing a report from Ibn Masʿūd in which the Prophet ﷺ said that the Book of Allah is the rope of Allah extended from the heavens to the earth, and another from Zayd ibn Arqam with the words: the rope of Allah is the Qur'an (citing Ibn Kathir). The two readings converge, because in Arabic *ḥabl* means covenant too, and in the widest sense covers anything used as a connecting link. That is why the metaphor is so exact: this cord runs vertically — binding believers to their Lord — and horizontally, drawing everyone gripping it into one body.

**Why "all of you together."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this the heart of the passage, and it is worth following the argument. Everyone praises unity; nobody defends strife. Yet humanity keeps splitting into sects within sects and parties within parties, until even two people uniting in any real sense has become a myth. Why? Because every group wants unity *on its own programme*, and so does every other group — so every call to unity ends in another break-up. Expecting all humanity to accept a system devised by some human beings is, in Maʿārif's blunt phrase, self-deception.

So the Qur'an does not merely preach unity; it names the one centre no rational person has a ground to deny on principle — the system given by the Creator and Sustainer of all the worlds. It bypasses race, tribe, colour, geography and language as bases of belonging, because those are things no one chooses and no one can change: a black man cannot become white, an Indian cannot become an Arab, so such unities can never gather the whole of humanity. Faith can be chosen freely by anyone, anywhere, from any family or tribe. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the tragedy plainly: Muslims have themselves accepted race, language and nationality as dividing lines, and the link of unity stands severed.

**A rope you climb.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out a further subtlety in the image: those holding fast to the Book of Allah resemble climbers gripping a strong rope, protected from falling. If Muslims grip it with full strength, all together, no shayṭān will succeed in dividing them, and the collective strength of the community becomes stable and impregnable. Break away from it, and collective life is ruined — and individual life is not likely to fare any better.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here that Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said Allah is pleased with three things for you and displeased with three: that you worship Him alone and associate nothing with Him; that you hold to the rope of Allah all together and do not divide; and that you give sincere counsel to whomever Allah appoints over your affairs. The three that displease Him: "it was said" and "so-and-so said," asking many unnecessary questions, and wasting wealth.

**"You were enemies, and He joined your hearts."** Ibn Kathir says this was revealed about the Aws and Khazraj, who in the days of *Jāhiliyyah* were locked in war, hatred and long blood-feuds. When Islam came, those who accepted it became brothers who loved one another for Allah's sake, keeping good ties for His sake and helping each other in righteousness. He links it to 8:62–63 — had you spent everything on earth you could not have united their hearts, but Allah united them. Their disbelief had left them standing at the very edge of a pit of Fire; Allah saved them and delivered them to faith.

Ibn Kathir then recalls the moment the Prophet ﷺ reminded the Anṣār of exactly this, at the division of the spoils of Ḥunayn, when some of them were unhappy with their share — though the division was what Allah had directed His Prophet ﷺ to do. He addressed them: O Anṣār, did I not find you misguided and Allah guided you through me? Were you not divided and Allah united you through me? Were you not poor and Allah enriched you through me? To every question they answered, "Indeed, Allah and His Messenger have granted us bounty."

**The theological point buried in that.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: Allah is the Master of hearts, and activating mutual love and consideration in a people is purely a divine blessing. And one becomes deserving of Allah's blessings only through obedience to Him — not through disobedience and sin. So for Muslims wanting a stable organisation and unity among themselves, there is no alternative route: obedience to Allah must become the way of life. That is the hint in the ayah's close — "thus Allah makes His signs clear to you, that you may be guided."

**Which differences are meant here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question already under this ayah: is every difference despicable? No. A blameworthy difference is one in which individuals and groups stay away from the Qur'an and think in terms of their own whims. But where people stay united around the Qur'an, accept the explanation coming from the Prophet ﷺ, and then differ in opinion about subsidiary matters on the basis of God-given ability — that difference is natural and Islam does not forbid it. It is exactly this kind that was called a mercy for the community. What *does* become blameworthy is investing those subsidiary debates with the status of the mainstream of religion, so that they turn into controversy, confrontation, insult and vilification.

## Ayah 104: a community with a mission

Ibn Kathir explains the objective of this ayah as being that there be a *segment* of this Ummah devoted to this task — calling to righteousness, enjoining good and forbidding evil in the manner Allah commanded — even though it is also an obligation on every member of the Ummah, each according to his ability. Ad-Daḥḥāk said these are a special group of the Companions and a special group of those after them: those who perform jihad, and the scholars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that if a government does not shoulder this responsibility, it becomes obligatory on Muslims to establish and run such a group, because the Ummah's vital role depends on it — and reports (from Ibn Jarīr) that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said this group is the group of the noble Companions, since each of them considered himself personally charged with calling people to good.

**Why the mission is what keeps the rope in your hands.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the logic of these two verses: for the bond of unity to hold across the ages, Muslims must treat it as an obligation to enjoin on one another what the Qur'an and Sunnah call good and to hold one another back from what is not — so that "the cord of Allah" does not slip out of their hands. Here Maʿārif quotes the memorable line of his teacher, Shaykh al-Islām Mawlānā Shabbīr Aḥmad ʿUthmānī: *there is no way this cord of Allah can break — that one loses his hand-hold on it is, of course, possible.* It is to offset precisely that danger, Maʿārif says, that the Qur'an tells Muslims to keep educating one another, urging good deeds and restraining bad ones.

**What "khayr" means.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Prophet ﷺ himself explained *khayr* as *following the Qur'an and my Sunnah* (citing Ibn Kathir). Note also that the verse begins with *calling to good*, not merely forbidding evil — so this work is not reactive. It continues even when no evil practice is in sight, or when the time for an obligation has not yet arrived: reminding people of prayer for when it falls due, of Ramadan while it is still far off.

**Ma'rūf and munkar.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on the word choice. *Maʿrūf* literally means "recognised" — the good enjoined by Islam and promoted by all the prophets; *munkar*, "unrecognised" or "alien" — the evils it is well known the Prophet ﷺ declared impermissible. The Qur'an could have said *wājib* (obligatory) and *maʿāṣī* (sins) and did not. The implication is that this public work should concern what the whole Ummah recognises as good or evil without any difference of interpretation — not rulings derived through *ijtihād*, which have always been open to differing interpretations among capable jurists. Maʿārif calls it a pity that this principle is neglected: Muslims are made to fight over secondary issues as though it were some feat of piety, while sins the whole Ummah agrees upon go unchecked.

**The hadith of the three levels.** Ibn Kathir cites that Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart — and that is the weakest faith. In another narration he ﷺ added that beyond that there is not a mustard seed's weight of faith. Ibn Kathir also records from Imām Aḥmad that Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān reported the Prophet ﷺ swearing by Him in Whose Hand is his soul: you will enjoin righteousness and forbid evil, or Allah will send down a punishment from Him upon you, and then you will supplicate and He will not answer. At-Tirmidhī collected it and said "Ḥasan." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites both of these teachings as well, noting the first as narrated in Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah.

**Its conditions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful and practical here. Duty is proportionate to ability — that is the very structure of the hadith. It requires knowledge: one who cannot distinguish *maʿrūf* from *munkar* is not fit to instruct others, and may forbid the good and command the wrong; such a person is obliged first to learn what the Sharīʿah has determined, and until he has, this service is not open to him. Untrained enthusiasts delivering sermons without knowing Qur'an or Hadith, or ordinary people using hearsay to pick arguments, produce disorder and destruction, not reform. It also presupposes no formidable danger or unbearable harm: "unable with the tongue" does not mean the tongue will not move, but that he strongly fears his life will be taken or he will suffer serious injury or loss — such a person is not "able" and is not sinful for holding back. Should he choose to stake life and property anyway and go ahead, as many Companions and their Successors are reported to have done, that is determination at its highest and a feat of great merit — but it was not obligatory on them. And the level of the duty follows the level of the act: counselling someone who abandons the five obligatory prayers is itself necessary; counsel about the optional prayers is merely commendable. In every case begin with softness; firmness comes only if a soft call to an obligation is rejected outright. Maʿārif notes the common inversion — people object strongly over what is merely commendable and stay silent when obligations are dropped. It adds that the duty becomes operative for an individual when he actually sees the forbidden act before his eyes; where it is not before him, pursuing and punishing crime is the work of the Islamic government.

## Ayah 105: do not repeat their history

Ibn Kathir: in this ayah Allah forbids this Ummah from imitating the division and discord of the nations before it — nations that also abandoned enjoining righteousness and forbidding evil, though they had proof of its necessity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies: Muslims should not be like the Jews and Christians who, after clear injunctions had reached them, became divided over the basic code of faith because they preferred to follow their own desires, and so brought divine punishment on themselves. Maʿārif reads this verse as the complement of "hold fast to the rope of Allah" in 103: unity is sought there, the perpetual mission of daʿwah nurtures and strengthens it, and here Muslims are told to learn from communities destroyed by their own dissension.

Ibn Kathir records from Imām Aḥmad, through Abū ʿĀmir ʿAbdullāh ibn Luḥayy, that Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān stood at Makkah after Ẓuhr and reported the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying that the People of the Two Scriptures split into seventy-two sects, and this Ummah will split into seventy-three — all in the Fire except one, the *Jamāʿah* — and that some of his Ummah would be guided by desire, like one infected by rabies, no vein or joint left untouched. Abū Dāwūd recorded similarly.

**Which differences are blameworthy?** This is where the passage most needs the scholars, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it at length. The censured division is that which shows up through arrogant, egotistic self-assertion, whether in the fundamentals of religion or its subsidiaries — the phrase "after clear proofs had come to them" points to it, and the truth is that the fundamentals are clear, as are some subsidiaries. But subsidiary issues that have no clear support in the texts, or rest on texts open to more than one interpretation, are not what this ayah is about. Maʿārif cites the well-known authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ: one who performs *ijtihād* and reaches the correct ruling has a twofold reward, and if he errs he has one reward. A rewarded effort cannot be a blameworthy one. Maʿārif also reports from Qāsim ibn Muḥammad and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz that the difference of opinion among the Companions is a source of mercy and ease for people (as in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* from al-Bayhaqī and *al-Mudkhal*).

Maʿārif then states the principle precisely: in a legitimate *ijtihād*, only one view is true in Allah's sight, but which one is His to judge on the Day of Resurrection — when the one who reached the correct ruling receives a twofold reward and the one who did not is rewarded too. So a person may say his own choice seems closest to the Qur'an and Sunnah while admitting it may be wrong, and that the other view seems incorrect while admitting it may be right in Allah's sight. All the leading Imams of *fiqh* agree on this. It follows that no side in such a dispute is *munkar* — and raising an objection against what is not *munkar* is itself wrong.

The example given is striking. Imām al-Shāfiʿī and others held that one praying behind an imam must recite Sūrah al-Fātiḥah; Imām Abū Ḥanīfah held that he must not, and Ḥanafīs therefore do not. Yet nowhere in the entire history of the community is there a report of Shāfiʿīs treating Ḥanafīs as having deserted the obligation of prayer, or attacking them the way one criticises acts the Sharīʿah forbids. Maʿārif quotes Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd: those entitled to give fatwa have always given fatwa, one ruling a thing lawful and another unlawful, yet neither regarded the other as doomed to perdition by his ruling (*Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm*, p. 80).

Maʿārif adds a firm caveat: this concerns *ijtihād* under its standard conditions — on questions with no categorical decision in the Qur'an and Sunnah, or where the decision is unclear or admits more than one interpretation, undertaken by those with genuine mastery of the Qur'anic and hadith sciences, of Arabic, and of the sayings of the Companions and their Successors. Someone unqualified who dabbles in questions already settled by authoritative texts is not doing *ijtihād* at all; what he says does not affect the question. And Maʿārif is equally firm that the *manner* of disagreement common today — quarrelsome debate over tertiary matters nursed as if they were the basis of the faith, ending in mutual abuse — is itself an open violation of "and be not divided," and has no precedent among the Companions and their Successors.

## Living it

Read as a whole, the passage asks four connected things. **Guard yourself** — obey and do not defy, remember and do not forget, thank and do not be ungrateful, doing all you can (102). **Grip the rope with everyone else gripping it** — make Allah's revelation, not tribe, race, language or nation, the thing you belong to (103). **Do not treat unity as a mood**; it is a blessing Allah places in hearts, and one becomes deserving of His blessings only through obedience to Him. **Take responsibility for others' good**, within your knowledge and ability, gently first, on what the Ummah agrees is right and wrong (104) — that is the work that keeps the cord from slipping out of your hands, since the cord itself cannot break. And **refuse the fight** over matters where qualified scholars have honestly differed, because that quarrel is precisely the fracture ayah 105 forbids.

passages.title: Bright and darkened faces on the Day
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These four ayat show the moment when the human race is finally sorted — and what shows the verdict is the face. Ayah 106 names the Day "when some faces will become white and some faces will become black" (Ibn Kathir's rendering), then addresses the darkened ones with a question; ayah 107 turns to the bright faces and settles them in Allah's mercy forever; ayah 108 declares that these verses are recited in truth and that Allah wills no injustice; ayah 109 closes by reminding us who owns everything and where every matter finally returns.

What holds the four together is a single movement: **a scene of judgement (106–107), followed by Allah's own words about that scene (108–109)** — that it is recited in truth, that it involves no injustice, and that the One who decides it owns the heavens and the earth.

## Where these ayat sit

Our passage does not arrive out of nowhere. Just before it, in ayah 104, Allah commands, "Let there arise out of you a group of people" inviting to all that is good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong; and in ayah 105, "And be not as those who divided and differed among themselves after the clear proofs had come to them."

On ayah 105 Ibn Kathir comments that Allah forbids this Ummah — the worldwide community of Muslims — from imitating the division and discord of the nations that came before them, nations that had also abandoned enjoining righteousness and forbidding evil although they had proof of its necessity.

Ibn Kathir then opens our passage under a heading of his own: *The Benefits of Brotherly Ties and Unity and the Consequence of Division on the Day of the Gathering.* The heading tells you how he hears ayah 106 in its setting — as the Day on which unity and division are finally shown for what they were.

## The face as the register of the soul

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the Qurʼan returns to this image of bright and dark faces in several places, using a whole family of words for the same reality:
