- "On the day of Doom, you shall see those who lied against Allah (with) their faces blackened" (39:60);
- "Some faces on that day shall shine, laughing, joyous. Some faces on that day shall be dusty, overspread with darkness" (80:38–41) — where the words *ghabarah* (dust) and *qatarah* (an overspreading gloom) carry the sense;
- "Faces on that day shall be radiant, looking towards their Lord" (75:22) — *nāḍirah*, radiance.

The words *bayāḍ* (whiteness) and *sawād* (blackness) in our ayah, it notes, belong to that same family of expressions.

According to the majority of commentators, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the brightness is **the brightness of the light of faith**: the faces of the believers will be resplendent with that light, fresh and smiling from the happiness of the rewards Allah has bestowed on them. The darkness is **the darkness of disbelief**: the faces of the disbelievers covered with the gloomy anguish of disbelief, with "the added soot of sin and transgression" turning them still darker.

## Who are these people?

The early commentators identified the two groups in several ways, and the sources preserve the difference of view rather than flattening it.

**Ibn 'Abbas** (radiy Allahu 'anhu), as cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the faces of the followers of the Sunnah — the Prophet's ﷺ way — will be bright, and the faces of the followers of *bid'ah* — innovation in the revealed faith, something neither Allah nor His Messenger ﷺ intended — will be dark. Ibn Kathir reports the same view from Ibn 'Abbas, phrasing it as the faces of the followers of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah (the united main body of the Muslims) radiating with whiteness, and the faces of the followers of innovation and division being darkened.

**'Ata'** (rahimahullah), as cited from Qurtubi: the bright faces are those of the Muhajirin and the Ansar; the dark faces those of Banu Qurayzah and Banu Nadir.

**'Ikrimah** (radiy Allahu 'anhu), also from Qurtubi: the dark faces belong to those of the People of the Book who had confirmed the coming of the Prophet ﷺ before he was ordained, but who — once he had been given prophethood — did not accept or support him, and instead set about falsifying him.

**Al-Hasan Al-Basri**, quoted by Ibn Kathir on the words "Did you reject faith after accepting it?": "They are the hypocrites."

**From the Sunnah:** Abu 'Isa At-Tirmidhi recorded that Abu Ghalib said that Abu Umamah saw heads of the Khawarij hanging on the streets of Damascus and commented, "The Dogs of the Fire and the worst dead people under the cover of the sky. The best dead men are those whom these have killed" — then recited "On the Day when some faces will become white and some faces will become black" to the end of the ayah. Asked whether he had heard this from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he replied, "If I only heard it from the Messenger of Allah once, twice, thrice, four times, or seven times, I would not have narrated it to you." At-Tirmidhi said, "This Hadith is Hasan." Ibn Majah and Ahmad recorded similarly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same report from Tirmidhi, applying the dark faces to the Khawarij and the bright faces to those whom they killed.

**How to hold these together.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that there are further explanations besides these, but that they all lead to the same conclusion and are not contradictory — each names a striking instance of one underlying reality. Imam al-Qurtubi's own summary gathers them: the faces of sincere Muslims will be bright, while the faces of all those who altered their religion, or became apostates and disbelievers, or concealed hypocrisy in their hearts, will be dark. Ibn Kathir reaches the same breadth from the other end: after "Then taste the torment for rejecting faith," he comments simply that "this description befits every disbeliever."

## "Did you reject faith after accepting it?"

The words spoken to the darkened faces in ayah 106 come as a question: *akafartum ba'da imanikum*, "Did you reject faith after accepting it?" It is worth noticing that all three of the identifications the commentators give sit naturally under a question of that shape — Al-Hasan Al-Basri's hypocrites, 'Ikrimah's People of the Book who had confirmed the Prophet ﷺ and then turned against him, and Qurtubi's summary naming those who altered their religion or became apostates.

Then: "So taste the torment for rejecting faith."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this closing phrase — "now taste the punishment because you have been sinning" — indicates: the punishment of that Day is not an arbitrary imposition, but the consequence of what a person earned while living his mortal life. In its striking phrase, the blessings of Paradise and the hardships of Hell "are simply a changed form of our very deeds."

## Mercy is what the passage is built around

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a fine observation about the ordering of the two groups. In the opening statement of ayah 106, brightness is mentioned first and darkness after it. But when the detail begins — "As for those whose faces turn dark" — darkness is placed before brightness, although the sequence of the original statement would have required brightness first here as well.

This reversal, it suggests, points to Allah's main purpose in creating: **to bless His creation with His mercy; punishment is not the objective.** Those with bright faces come first, as the ones who deserve mercy and merit from their Lord. Then, at the close of the passage in ayah 107, "they will be in Allah's mercy, therein they shall dwell forever" — and named there, it says, very affectionately. So those deserving of mercy are identified at the very beginning and again at the end, and the mention of those whose faces turn dark remains *in between*. All of this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, points to Allah's limitless, endless mercy: human beings were certainly not created to serve as an exhibit of divine punishment, but to flourish under the sunshine of Allah's mercy.

**Why "Allah's mercy" rather than "Paradise"?** Ayah 107 does not say "they will be in the Garden"; it says "they will be in Allah's mercy." Ibn 'Abbas explained that *rahmah*, mercy, means Jannah — Paradise — here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Tafsir al-Kabir, draws out the wisdom in the choice of word: no one, however worshipful and pious, enters Paradise except through the sole mercy of Allah. Being devoted in acts of worship is not a feat of human excellence as such — the very ability to worship is itself a gift of Allah. Worship does not in itself create an inherent right to enter Paradise; it is Allah's mercy alone through which one enjoys its bliss.

**And it does not run out.** "They will be in Allah's mercy" is immediately qualified by *hum fīhā khālidūn*, "therein they shall dwell forever." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this means the mercy the believers rest in will not be temporary: it will be forever and eternal, never taken away and never reduced in their case. By contrast, it observes, in the case of those whose faces turn dark, it is not expressly mentioned here whether they will remain in that state forever. Ibn Kathir adds the same note of settled permanence about the believers: they will reside in Paradise for eternity, and shall never desire to be removed.

## Ayah 108: recited in truth, and no injustice

"These are the Ayat of Allah. We recite them to you" — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, these are the verses of Allah, His proofs and signs that He reveals to you, O Muhammad ﷺ. And *bil-ḥaqq*, "in truth": making known the true reality of this world and the Hereafter.

"And Allah wills no injustice to the 'Alamin" — the '*Alamin* meaning all the worlds, everyone in them. Ibn Kathir: He never treats them with injustice; rather, He is the Just Ruler who is able to do everything and has knowledge of everything, and therefore He has no need to treat any of His creatures with injustice. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties the same words back to the earning of punishment in ayah 106: whatever reward or punishment there is, is nothing but justice, and very much the perfect expression of divine wisdom and mercy.

## Ayah 109: everything belongs to Him, everything returns to Him

"And to Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth" — they are all, Ibn Kathir says, His servants and His property. "And all matters go back to Allah" — for His is the decision concerning the affairs of this life and the Hereafter, and His is the supreme authority in both.

Notice how this closes the passage. Ibn Kathir presents ayah 109 as following directly from the statement before it: it is *because* He is the Just Ruler with power and knowledge over everything, "and this is why He said next" that everything in the heavens and the earth is His and every matter returns to Him. The final ayah is not a change of subject; it is bound to the assurance that the judgement of ayat 106–107 carries no injustice at all.

## Living it

**Hold to the Sunnah and to the united body of the Muslims.** Ibn 'Abbas's reading of the two colours — brightness for the followers of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah, darkness for the followers of innovation and division — and Ibn Kathir's own heading over this passage, on unity and the consequence of division, both put the matter in the same place: how you stood towards the community of the Prophet's ﷺ way is not a question of temperament. It is something the sources say will one day show on the face.

**Let the fear be of turning back, not merely of falling short.** The question in ayah 106 is put to people who had faith, or who had confirmed the truth and then refused it. Ask Allah to keep you from being among them.

**And let hope have the last word.** The shape of this passage — mercy named at its opening, mercy named again at its close, and the warning held in between — is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it, deliberate. You were not created to be an exhibit of divine punishment. You were created to flourish under the sunshine of Allah's mercy — and even then, not by the weight of your worship, but by that mercy alone.

passages.title: The best community and the disgrace of its opponents
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat set two communities side by side. In ayah 110 Allah names the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ "the best community ever raised for humanity" — and immediately attaches the reasons: they enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah. Then, in the very same ayah, He turns to the People of the Scripture: had they believed, it would have been better for them, but most are rebellious. Ayat 111 and 112 spell out what that rebellion has cost them — they cannot really harm the believers, they will turn their backs in battle, and indignity is put over them wherever they may be.

What holds the passage together is a single logic: **honour is not an identity, it is an assignment.** One community was raised up to carry good to mankind and is praised for carrying it; another was given scripture, disbelieved in the signs of Allah, and killed the Prophets — and lost its standing. Read as one unit, these ayat are a portrait and a warning in the same breath.

---

## "Best" means best *for* people, not best *than* people

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the flow: the preceding verses had urged Muslims to hold firm to their faith and to bid the fair and forbid the unfair. Ayah 110 now tells them *why* those duties matter so much — they are the very grounds on which Allah has given this Ummah the rank of *Khayr al-Umam*, the best of communities, "when it does what it has been charged to do."

Ibn Kathir preserves a striking early gloss. Al-Bukhari recorded that Abu Hurayrah commented on this ayah: "(You, Muslims, are) the best nation of people for the people, you bring them tied in chains on their necks and they later embrace Islam." The image is arresting — even a captive ends up receiving the greatest good. The same reading, "the best of peoples *for* the people," is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Atiyah Al-'Awfi, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas. Ibn Kathir sums it up: "the Ummah of Muhammad is the most righteous and beneficial nation for mankind."

So the preposition carries the meaning. This is not a boast of superiority for its own sake. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way: this community "has been raised for the sole purpose of dispensing good to all beings created by Allah," charged with people's spiritual and moral reformation.

**Why this Ummah in particular?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two answers. The first, drawn from Sūrah al-Baqarah, is moderation: "And in the same way We made you a moderate Ummah" (2:143) — a balance visible across every department of its collective life. The second is the one this ayah itself supplies: no community contributed more to the mission of bidding the fair and forbidding the unfair. Earlier communities were also charged with it, but — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains — many of them did not have jihad as a religious obligation, so the duty could only be discharged by heart and tongue. The followers of Muhammad ﷺ were given a third instrument, the hand, which includes struggle in its various forms and also the enforcement of Islamic law through government. In other communities, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, the distinguishing features of religion were gradually worn away by inertia until the duty of *amr bi'l-maʿrūf* — the ordained mission of bidding the fair — was abandoned altogether. Of this Ummah, by contrast, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prophesied that there would remain, right up to the Day of Doom, a group of people who stay firm on bidding the fair and forbidding the unfair.

**And "you believe in Allah"?** Every prophet's community believed in Allah — so why list it as a distinguishing mark? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers plainly: belief as such is common to all, "but the degrees of perfection in belief differ." The preference given to this community is of a class of its own.

---

## Why the honour was given

Ibn Kathir attributes this standing first of all to the Prophet ﷺ himself — "the most regarded of Allah's creation and the most honoured Messenger with Allah" — sent with a complete and perfect Law never given to anyone before him, a Law in which few deeds take the place of the many that earlier nations performed. He then gathers a series of narrations:

- **Ahmad, At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Al-Hakim** recorded from Hakim bin Mu'awiyah bin Haydah, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "You are the final of seventy nations, you are the best and most honoured among them to Allah." At-Tirmidhi graded it *Hasan*; it is also narrated from Mu'adh bin Jabal and Abu Sa'id.
- **Imam Ahmad** recorded from 'Ali bin Abi Talib that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "I was given what no other Prophet before me was given" — and when asked what, he said: "I was given victory by fear, I was given the keys of the earth, I was called Ahmad, the earth was made a clean place for me, and my Ummah was made the best Ummah." Ibn Kathir says the chain is *Hasan*.
- **The Two Sahihs** record from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said a group of seventy thousand from his Ummah will enter Paradise with faces radiating "just like the moon when it is full." When Ukkashah bin Mihsan Al-Asadi rose and asked the Prophet ﷺ to supplicate that he be among them, he said, "O Allah! Make him one of them." When a man of the Ansar rose with the same request, he said, "Ukkashah has beaten you to it."
- **Imam Ahmad** records from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said he hoped those who follow him would be one-fourth of the residents of Paradise — the Companions said *Allahu Akbar* — then one-third, then one-half. **The Two Sahihs** record the same exchange from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud.
- **Imam Ahmad** records from Buraydah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, this Ummah takes up eighty of them." At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also collected it; At-Tirmidhi said *Hasan*.
- **'Abdur-Razzaq** records from Abu Hurayrah — and **Al-Bukhari and Muslim** also collected it — that the Prophet ﷺ said: "We are the last to come, but the foremost on the Day of Resurrection, and the first people to enter Paradise, although the former nations were given the Scriptures before us... Allah gave us the guidance of truth that they have been disputing about" — including Friday, over which they differed, with the Jews taking Saturday and the Christians Sunday.

---

## The condition inside the praise

Here is the hinge of the whole passage, and Ibn Kathir does not let the reader miss it: "**whoever among this Ummah acquires these qualities, will have a share in this praise.**"

Qatadah reported — Ibn Jarir recorded it — that 'Umar bin Al-Khattab recited this ayah during a Hajj, when he saw the people rushing about, and said: "Whoever likes to be among this [praised] Ummah, let him fulfil the condition that Allah set in this ayah."

And the reverse follows. Those of this Ummah who do not acquire these qualities, says Ibn Kathir, "will be just like the People of the Scriptures whom Allah criticized" — the very people condemned in the words, "They did not forbid one another from the Munkar which they committed" (5:79). The line between the two communities in this passage is not ancestry or a name on a form. It is enjoining good, forbidding evil, and true faith. Drop them, and you have crossed over to the side being criticised.

---

## The mirror: the People of the Scripture (end of ayah 110)

It is precisely because Allah has praised this Ummah for these qualities, Ibn Kathir explains, that He immediately turns to those who had scripture and did not live by it. "And had the People of the Scripture believed" — that is, in what was sent down to Muhammad ﷺ — "it would have been better for them."

The ayah is careful and fair: **"among them are some who have faith."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies these as those who confirmed the prophethood of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, such as Sayyidunā 'Abdullah ibn Salām. Ibn Kathir notes it is only a few who believe; the majority, he says, "follow deviation, disbelief, sin and rebellion" — *Fāsiqūn*, those who break out of obedience.

---

## Ayah 111: harm that is capped, not denied

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the argument back a few verses: in 98–101 the hostility of the People of the Book and their attempts to harm Muslims *religiously* had been exposed. Ayah 111 turns to their plans to harm Muslims *materially* — and its last sentence carries the prophecy that they shall not succeed. Notice the shape of the promise: harm is not denied outright, it is capped. Ibn Kathir's rendering is "They will do you no harm, barring a trifling annoyance"; whatever they manage will amount to *adhā* — irritation, nuisance — not real injury. And if it comes to fighting, "they will show you their backs, and they will not be helped."

Ibn Kathir reads this as good news of victory and dominance, and points to how it unfolded: at the battle of Khaybar Allah brought humiliation and disgrace on the Jews, and before that the Madinan tribes of Qaynuqa', Nadir and Qurayzah were humiliated; later the Companions defeated the Christians of Ash-Sham in many battles and took over its leadership. He adds that a group of Muslims will remain in the area of Ash-Sham upon the truth, apparent and victorious, until 'Isa son of Maryam descends — and that 'Isa will then rule according to the Law of Muhammad ﷺ, break the cross, kill the swine, banish the jizyah, and accept only Islam from the people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point historically: throughout the period of prophethood the People of the Book were never able to overcome the noble Companions, who are the primary addressees here. This applies particularly to the Jewish tribes who tried to sow seeds of discord among them, and the outcome was disgrace — "some paid jizya, some were killed while others were exiled."

---

## Ayah 112: indignity, and its two exceptions

"Indignity is put over them wherever they may be." Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is blunt: Allah has placed humiliation and disgrace on them wherever they may be, "and they will never be safe."

But the ayah itself carves out an exception, and it is important: *illā bi-ḥablin mina'Llāhi wa ḥablin mina'n-nās* — except when under a covenant from Allah, and a covenant from men.

- **A covenant from Allah** — Ibn Kathir explains this as the *Dhimmah*, the covenant of protection from Allah that requires them to pay the jizyah and makes them subservient to Islamic Law.
- **A covenant from men** — pledges of protection and safety offered to them by Muslims. Ibn Kathir notes that such a pledge may validly be given by Muslim men and women, "and even a slave, according to one of the sayings of the scholars." Ibn 'Abbas explained the phrase as a covenant of protection from Allah and a pledge of safety from people, and the same is reported from Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, As-Suddi and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the parallel passage in Sūrah al-Baqarah (2:61) mentions no exception at all, so this ayah completes the description, and lists the two situations under which the disgrace and misery do not become manifest: first, through a covenant of Allah — for example, that a minor child or a woman is not to be killed; second, through a treaty obligation. It then makes a lexical observation worth pausing on: the Qur'an says a covenant from *men*, and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, that word covers all men, believers and disbelievers alike. So the possibility that they live in freedom after making a peace treaty with Muslims is included — and so is the possibility that they come under the protection of non-Muslim powers through a treaty or an informal arrangement. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then applies this second possibility to a specific political situation of the commentator's own day, closing, as scholars do with such applications, with "Allah knows best." That application is his reading of contemporary events rather than part of the exegesis of the words themselves, and it is left aside here.)

The rest of the ayah names the settlement: "they have drawn on themselves the wrath of Allah" — they earned that anger, says Ibn Kathir, and deserved it — "and destitution is put over them," which he says they deserve both by decree and legislatively.

---

## Why it came to this

The ayah does not leave the verdict unexplained. It gives two reasons, and Ibn Kathir unpacks both.

**"Because they disbelieved in the Ayat of Allah and killed the Prophets without right."** What drove them to this, he says, was "their arrogance, transgression and envy" — and that is what earned them humiliation, degradation and disgrace throughout this life and the Hereafter.

**"Because they disobeyed and used to transgress the limits."** This second clause explains the first. What lured them into disbelieving in Allah's signs and killing His Messengers, Ibn Kathir writes, is that they often disobeyed Allah's commands, committed His prohibitions and transgressed His set limits. Small, repeated disobedience wore a road that eventually ran all the way to killing prophets. Ibn Kathir ends with a prayer: "We seek refuge from this behaviour, and Allah Alone is sought for each and every type of help."

---

## Living it

**Take the praise as a job description.** Ayah 110 does not say you are best and then list your privileges; it says you are best *for people* and then lists your work. If a Muslim is not, in some concrete way, of benefit to those around him, the ayah's description has not yet landed on him.

**Fulfil 'Umar's condition.** He recited this ayah in the middle of Hajj, looking at a crowd, and told them the honour has terms. Enjoin what is good, forbid what is wrong, believe in Allah — that is the entry fee for the praise, not a bonus on top of it.

**Do not become the mirror image.** Ibn Kathir's warning is the sharpest practical note in the passage: a community that stops forbidding evil among itself becomes exactly what 5:79 condemns, whatever name it carries.

**Read the promise of ayah 111 as calm, not complacency.** Opposition is real but capped at a trifling annoyance for those who are actually doing the work of ayah 110. The two ayat are joined; the security described belongs to the community described.

**And keep the diagnosis of ayah 112 in view for yourself.** Arrogance, envy and casual transgression are named as the road to ruin — not exotic sins, but ordinary ones left unattended.

passages.title: Not all alike: the upright among the People of the Book
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the Qur'an's correction to a lazy way of thinking. After a long stretch of Surah Al 'Imran spent rebuking those among the People of the Book who rejected the truth, Allah pauses to say: do not paint them all with one brush. Some of them stood for the right, believed, and did what believers do — and their good will not be lost. Ayah 113 announces the distinction and begins the portrait, ayah 114 completes the portrait, and ayah 115 gives Allah's verdict on it. That is what holds the three together: **a group is named, described, and then guaranteed.**

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the thread. In ayah 110, it had already been said that among the People of the Book there are those who believe, though most of them are disbelievers. Ayat 113–115 are the detail behind that brief statement. Maʿārif calls them "a complementary profile" of those from the People of the Book who did believe: by becoming Muslims, they adopted "the distinguishing hallmarks of the Faith that go to make believers the best of communities."

That last phrase is the key. What is described in these ayat is not a lesser, guest-grade faith granted to newcomers. It is the same set of marks that make believers what they are.

## Who these ayat came down about

Ibn Kathir gives this under the heading *Virtues of the People of the Scriptures Who Embrace Islam*.

Muhammad bin Ishaq and others, including Al-ʿAwfi reporting from Ibn ʿAbbas, said that these ayat were revealed "about the clergy of the People of the Scriptures who embraced the faith" — the religious figures of those communities. They are named: **ʿAbdullah bin Salam, Asad bin ʿUbayd, Thaʿlabah bin Saʿyah, Usayd bin Saʿyah**, and others like them.

Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion plainly: the ayah means that those among the People of the Book whom Allah rebuked earlier "are not at all the same as those among them who embraced Islam." Hence Allah's words in ayah 113, **لَيْسُوا سَوَاءً — "Not all of them are alike."** These two types of people are not equal; there are believers among the People of the Book, and there are criminals among them.

Notice the shape of the sentence. It does not begin by praising the good ones. It begins by refusing an equation: *not alike*. Before Allah tells you what these people did, He tells you what you must not do — flatten a community into a single verdict. The rebuke earlier in the surah was real, and it was aimed at the people it was aimed at. It was never a licence to stop looking at individuals.

## "A party that stands for the right" — ayah 113

**مِّنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ أُمَّةٌ قَائِمَةٌ**
*"a party of the People of the Scripture stand for the right."*

Ibn Kathir explains what that standing consists of: **they implement the Book of Allah, they adhere to His Law, and they follow His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.** He adds: "therefore, this type is on the straight path."

That gloss is worth pausing on, because it sets the bar. Standing for the right is not warm feeling or private sympathy for the truth. It is three concrete things: acting on the Book, holding to the Sacred Law — the law Allah has revealed and legislated — and following the Messenger ﷺ. A person who does those three is on the straight path, whatever community he came from.

Then the ayah tells us what such people do with their nights:

**يَتْلُونَ آيَاتِ اللَّهِ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ**
*"they recite the verses of Allah during the hours of the night, prostrating themselves in prayer."*

Ibn Kathir: **they often stand in prayer at night for Tahajjud** — the night prayer — **and recite the Qur'an in their prayer.** So the first thing Allah chooses to mention about them is not a public act at all. It is what they do in the hours of the night.

There is something else in the pairing of *reciting* with *prostrating*. The words of Allah go in through the tongue and the ear, and the body answers by going down to the ground. Recitation that produces prostration is recitation that has landed.

## The portrait completed — ayah 114

**يُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَيَأْمُرُونَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ الْمُنكَرِ وَيُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ وَأُولَٰئِكَ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ**
*"They believe in Allah and the Last Day; they enjoin Al-Maʿruf and forbid Al-Munkar; and they hasten in (all) good works; and they are among the righteous."*

Four things, moving outward in widening circles.

**They believe in Allah and the Last Day.** The foundation: the One they answer to, and the Day they answer on. Everything after this is downstream of these two convictions.

**They enjoin Al-Maʿrūf and forbid Al-Munkar.** Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps the two Arabic terms; the translation of the ayah renders the clause as *encouraging good and forbidding* its opposite. Whatever the shade of the words, the movement is unmistakable: faith here does not stay indoors. It concerns itself with the conduct of the people around it rather than treating one's own righteousness as a private arrangement.

**They hasten in all good works.** Not merely doing good, but hurrying toward it. A man who hurries toward something is a man who wants it.

**And they are among the righteous.** This is the seal. Allah does not say they are *near* the righteous or resemble them. He counts them **among** them — full membership.

Ibn Kathir notes that this is the same type of people Allah mentions again at the end of this very surah:

> "And there are, certainly, among the People of the Scripture, those who believe in Allah and in that which has been revealed to you, and in that which has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah." (3:199)

So the surah says it twice — here, and again near its close. It is not a passing concession. It is a settled truth Allah wanted stated more than once.

## "Nothing will be rejected of them" — ayah 115

**وَمَا يَفْعَلُوا مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَلَن يُكْفَرُوهُ**
*"And whatever good they do, nothing will be rejected of them."*

Ibn Kathir's explanation is short and enormous: **their good deeds will not be lost with Allah. Rather, He will award them the best rewards.**

Read the promise exactly as it is worded. Not *some* of what they do, and not *rejected sometimes*: whatever good they do, nothing of it is rejected. Nothing goes missing. Not one act is written off, refused at the door, or quietly dropped.

Then the ayah closes on a divine name:

**وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِالْمُتَّقِينَ** — *"for Allah knows well the Muttaqīn"* — the pious. Ibn Kathir explains: **no deed performed by any person ever escapes His knowledge, nor is any reward for those who do good deeds ever lost with Him.**

This is why the ayah does not end with "Allah will reward them." It ends with *He knows them.* Allah's knowledge is His own — we affirm it as He affirmed it for Himself, and we do not imagine it as anything like ours. Nothing escapes it. And it is precisely that which makes the guarantee unbreakable: a reward can only be lost if a deed can first be overlooked, and with Allah no deed is ever overlooked.

## The contrast that follows

The passage does not end in mid-air. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces what comes immediately after: having praised those from the People of the Book who embraced Islam, the text censures those who refused and insisted on their disbelief, not realising that their wealth and their children will be unable to save them from the punishment of Allah (3:116). Ibn Kathir's comment on that ayah is that nothing can avert Allah's punishment from striking them.

The two halves are meant to be read against each other. On one side: people whose every good deed is guaranteed against loss. On the other: people whose wealth and children will avail them nothing at all.

Maʿārif adds a further note from ayah 117: what disbelievers spend in this worldly life is simply wasted, because belief is a precondition for such spending to be acceptable with Allah. Had they believed, Maʿārif says, they would have been like other Muslims, who on suffering a worldly loss are compensated by Allah through reward and the forgiveness of sins.

## Living it

**Judge people, not categories.** The opening words of ayah 113 forbid the mental shortcut of assuming that because a group has been criticised, every person in it stands condemned. Allah criticised, and then Allah drew the line Himself. If the Qur'an refuses to lump people together, we have no right to.

**Let the night be part of your religion.** Of everything that could have been said about these believers, Allah led with what they did in the hours of the night with the Qur'an on their tongues and their foreheads on the ground. Ibn Kathir names it: Tahajjud, with recitation in the prayer. A religion with no night in it is thinner than theirs was.

**Do not keep goodness to yourself.** Belief in ayah 114 immediately produces enjoining and forbidding. Faith that never travels outward from the self is missing something the ayah treats as standard equipment.

**Hurry.** *Yusāriʿūna fil-khayrāt* — they hasten. The opposite of hastening toward good is not doing evil; it is intending to get around to it. The ayah quietly rules that out.

**Trust the ledger.** Whatever good you do will never be denied you. Ibn Kathir puts both halves of the guarantee together: no deed escapes Allah's knowledge, and no reward for a good deed is ever lost with Him. Nothing done for Him is mislaid.

passages.title: Charity of the disbelievers like a frost-blasted harvest
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These two ayat are the closing half of a comparison. Ayat 113–115 had just praised those from among the People of the Book who accepted faith — people who recite the verses of Allah during the hours of the night, prostrating themselves in prayer, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and of whose good deeds Allah says that nothing will be rejected of them. Ayat 116 and 117 turn to the other side of that contrast: those who refused, and what becomes of everything they had and everything they gave. Ayah 116 addresses the two things they relied on — wealth and children. Ayah 117 then takes what they spent, and shows it destroyed by a single image: a crop struck down just when it was ready to harvest.

The unit holds together as a single movement: **wealth cannot save them, children cannot save them, and even what they spend cannot save them — because the foundation is missing.**

## The setting: a comparison, not a blanket condemnation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points back to ayah 110, where it was said that among the People of the Book there are those who believe, though most of them are disbelievers. Ayat 113–115 fill in the first half of that statement, giving what Maʿārif calls a complementary profile of those who believed from among the People of the Book — who, by becoming Muslims, adopted the distinguishing hallmarks of faith that make believers the best of communities.

Ibn Kathir preserves who those ayat were about. Muhammad bin Ishaq and others, including Al-ʿAwfi reporting from Ibn ʿAbbas, said these ayat were revealed about the clergy of the People of the Scriptures who embraced the faith — naming ʿAbdullah bin Salam, Asad bin ʿUbayd, Thaʿlabah bin Saʿyah, Usayd bin Saʿyah, and others. The meaning of "Not all of them are alike" (3:113), Ibn Kathir explains, is precisely that those among the People of the Book whom Allah rebuked earlier are not at all the same as those among them who embraced Islam. These two types of people are not equal: among the People of the Book there are believers and there are also criminals. He connects the first group to the same type of people mentioned at the end of this surah: "And there are, certainly, among the People of the Scripture, those who believe in Allah and in that which has been revealed to you, and in that which has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah" (3:199).

So when ayah 116 begins "Surely, those who disbelieve…", it is completing a distinction that the Qur'an itself has just insisted on. Maʿārif puts it plainly: soon after praising those who had embraced Islam from among the People of the Book, the text censures those of them who did not embrace Islam and insisted on retaining their stance of disbelief.

## Ayah 116: what will not avail them

"Surely, those who disbelieve, neither their properties nor their offspring will avail them against Allah. They are the dwellers of the Fire, therein they will abide."

Ibn Kathir's comment on the phrase is brief and total: it means **nothing can avert Allah's torment and punishment from striking them.** Maʿārif says the same of those censured here — they did not realise that their wealth and their children will be unable to save them from the punishment of Allah, and that Hell shall be their eternal abode.

Notice what stands immediately before this in Ibn Kathir's own text. On ayah 115, "And whatever good they do, nothing will be rejected of them," he writes: their good deeds will not be lost with Allah; rather, He will award them the best rewards. And on "for Allah knows well the Muttaqin (the pious)" — *muttaqin* being those who are mindful of Allah and guard themselves against His displeasure — he writes that **no deed performed by any person ever escapes His knowledge, nor is any reward for those who do good deeds ever lost with Him.**

Those two comments sit side by side in the tafsir. For the pious, no good deed goes unnoticed by Allah and no reward is lost. For those who disbelieve, no property and no offspring avail anything.

## Ayah 117: the parable of the ruined harvest

"The parable of what they spend in this world is that of a wind of *Sir*; it struck the harvest of a people who did wrong against themselves and destroyed it. Allah wronged them not, but they wronged themselves."

**What is being compared.** Ibn Kathir records that Mujahid, Al-Hasan and As-Suddi said this is a parable **for what the disbelievers spend in this life.** The comparison is not with the miser. It is with money actually spent.

**The word *Sir*.** The Arabic describes a wind "in which there is *Sir*" (*rīḥin fīhā ṣirr*). Ibn Kathir gathers the explanations of the early authorities for what that word means:

- **A frigid wind** — as Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas and others have said.
- **Cold and snow** — ʿAtaʾ said this.
- **Fire** — also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

Ibn Kathir does not set these against one another. He says that this last meaning does not contradict the meanings mentioned before it, **because extreme cold weather, especially when accompanied by snow, burns plants and produce, and has the same effect fire has on such growth.** The "fire" reading, on his explanation, is not a rival opinion so much as the same destruction named by its effect.

**The timing is part of the image.** Ibn Kathir draws attention to what kind of disaster this is. The ayah mentions a calamity that strikes produce *that is ready to harvest*, destroying it by burning and **depriving its owner of it when he needs it the most.** Not a failed sowing — a crop that had come all the way to the point of being gathered in.

**Why the owners are called wrongdoers.** The ayah says the wind struck "the harvest of a people who did wrong against themselves." Ibn Kathir reads the parable as double-sided: such is the case with the disbelievers, for Allah destroys the rewards for their good deeds in this life, just as He destroyed the produce of the sinner because of his sins. And he adds the line that ties the two halves together: **"Both types did not build their work on firm foundations."**

## The condition Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states what the similitude is teaching: disbelievers simply waste what they spend in this worldly life, because **belief in Islam is a pre-condition in order that such spendings be acceptable with Allah, of whatever sort they may be.** No amount and no cause substitutes for that foundation.

And Maʿārif is careful about where the injustice lies. The closing words of ayah 117 — "Allah wronged them not, but they wronged themselves" — mean, as Maʿārif puts it, that the disbelievers inflict this injustice upon themselves: their spending goes to waste in this world and remains rewardless in the Hereafter. **Nobody is being cheated of a reward they had earned.**

Maʿārif then adds the merciful counter-image. If they were not to wrong themselves — if they were to embrace Islam — they would have been like other Muslims who, on suffering a worldly loss, are compensated by Allah through reward and forgiveness of sins, as is reported in ahadith. That is the difference the foundation makes. For the believer, a worldly loss is met with reward and with sins forgiven. For the one who refuses faith, what was spent goes to waste in this world and remains rewardless in the Hereafter.

## Living it

**Do not measure your standing by your assets.** Ayah 116 names the two things people counted on — wealth and children — and Maʿārif says flatly that neither will save them from the punishment of Allah. That is not a reason to despise wealth or children; it is a reason to stop reading them as a verdict on your standing with Allah.

**Check the foundation, not just the deed.** The parable's warning is not against giving; it is against giving without the belief that Maʿārif says is the precondition for spending to be acceptable with Allah. Ibn Kathir's phrase is the lesson in a line: the work was not built on firm foundations. It is worth asking honestly of your own good deeds whether they are built on that foundation.

**Take the words of ayah 115 seriously.** The same passage that says the disbelievers' spending is destroyed says of those who believe that whatever good they do will not be rejected of them, and that Allah knows well the pious. Ibn Kathir insists that **no deed performed by any person ever escapes His knowledge, nor is any reward for those who do good deeds ever lost with Him.** The small, unwitnessed good is not lost with Allah.

**Remember who the passage opens with.** It begins with people who did cross over — ʿAbdullah bin Salam and those Ibn Kathir names alongside him, clergy of the People of the Scriptures who embraced the faith. And it closes on a loss that Maʿārif says would not have been theirs had they embraced Islam: they would have been among those whom Allah compensates with reward and with forgiveness of sins.

passages.title: Do not take intimates who wish you ruin
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat give the believing community a rule about *closeness*: there are people you may deal with, trade with and live beside, and there are people you must not let inside — into your confidences, your plans, your decision-making. Ayah 118 issues the command and gives the reason; ayah 119 exposes the one-sidedness of a friendship the believers had drifted into; ayah 120 supplies the emotional proof of hostility, then tells the believers how to be safe from it.

What holds the three together is one movement of thought: **a prohibition, then the evidence for it, then the remedy.** And the remedy is the surprise. After all the warning about plotting, the passage does not tell the believers to plot back. It tells them to be patient, to fear Allah, and to know that "Allah surrounds all that they do."

---

## The setting: old friendships in a new Madinah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that these verses came down against a specific background. There were Jewish settlements around Madinah with long-standing friendly ties to the tribes of Aws and Khazraj — as neighbours, as allies, and as individual friends. When Aws and Khazraj accepted Islam, they naturally carried those old friendships forward. Individuals from these tribes, Maʿārif says, saw no problem in meeting their old friends with the same love and sincerity as before.

But something had changed on the other side that had not changed on theirs. Maʿārif states that hostility toward the Prophet ﷺ and the religion he brought ran so deep that sincerity toward anyone who had answered the prophetic call was no longer possible. So the outward relationship continued — while inwardly it had turned to enmity. And the surviving friendship became **cover**: it was used to stir trouble among the Muslims so their unity would break, and even to learn the community's organisational secrets and pass them on to its enemies.

That is the situation these ayat address. The people being warned — Maʿārif calls them the Anṣār of Madinah, meaning the Aws and Khazraj now that they had embraced Islam — were not being warned about strangers. They were being warned about friends.

Ibn Kathir frames the same command around the hypocrites: Allah forbids His believing servants from taking them as allies, so they do not get the opportunity to expose the secrets of the believers and their plans against their enemies. Maʿārif draws the circle wider — the warning covers anyone outside the believing community, "Jews, Christians, hypocrites or other disbelievers," insofar as they are hostile to the faith. The occasion was concrete; the principle is general.

---

## The word the whole passage turns on: *biṭānah*

Everything hangs on one word in ayah 118: *lā tattakhidhū biṭānatan min dūnikum* — "do not take as *biṭānah* those other than yourselves."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word beautifully. *Biṭānah* derives from *baṭn*, "inside," and stands opposite *ẓahr*, "outside." In a garment, the outer face is the *ẓihārah*, and **the lining — the layer that touches the body — is the *biṭānah***. From that image Arabic took the word for a friend, a confidant, one with whom secrets are shared; Maʿārif notes that the English phrase *hand in glove* comes close. It then cites the classical lexicon *Lisān al-ʿArab*: a man's *biṭānah* is the one who knows his secrets and has access to his affairs, in which he seeks his advice. Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in his *Mufradāt* and al-Qurṭubī in his *Tafsīr* give the same meaning.

Feel what that does to the verse. Allah did not say "do not be kind to them," or "do not live among them." He chose the word for *the lining of your own clothing* — the layer nobody sees, the layer that touches the body. The prohibition concerns a particular depth of access, not ordinary human decency. Ibn Kathir puts it in exactly those terms: the verse is about taking followers of other religions as consultants and allies, **"for advisors of a certain person have access to his most secret affairs."**

Maʿārif states the rule in the same spirit: Muslims should not take as confidants and advisers, in a way that leads to spilling sensitive secrets of one's own government, community or state, those outside their own community.

---

## Why: the reason given in ayah 118

**"They will not fail to do their best to corrupt you"** (*lā yaʾlūnakum khabālā*). Maʿārif renders it: they would spare no effort to do you mischief. Ibn Kathir writes that they try their very best to confuse, oppose and harm the believers by any wicked means at their disposal — and Maʿārif adds that the aim is not only material but spiritual, to pull believers away from the enjoined pursuits of their faith.

**"They desire to harm you severely"** (*waddū mā ʿanittum*). Maʿārif calls this sentence "a perfect mirror of the mentality" being described: they *want* you to be in trouble. Ibn Kathir says they wish the very worst and most difficult conditions for the believers.

**"Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, but what their breasts conceal is far worse."** Ibn Kathir explains that enmity shows on their faces and in what they sometimes let slip, while the enmity against Islam and its people sits deeper, in the heart. Maʿārif puts it vividly: the venom hidden in the hearts is far more fatal — though there are moments when the deceptive cool front is thrown off and the fangs become clearly visible.

**"Indeed We have made plain to you the Ayat, if you understand."** Ibn Kathir notes that the matter is apparent to every person of sound comprehension — hence the appeal to the intellect. Maʿārif ends with a question you cannot argue with: why would an intelligent person take such people as his confidant?

---

## From the Sunnah: everyone has two *biṭānah*s

Ibn Kathir records that **Al-Bukhari and An-Nasa'i** reported from Abu Saʿīd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah has not sent any Prophet nor appointed any Khalīfah but that he had two kinds of *biṭānah* — one that commands him with righteousness and urges him toward it, and one that commands him with evil and urges him toward it; and **"only those whom Allah gives immunity are immune."**

Both kinds of counsel, then, are the normal condition of even prophets and rightly-guided rulers. No one is structurally safe; protection is finally something Allah grants — which is why the passage ends at patience and taqwa rather than at strategy.

---

## ʿUmar and the scribe from Ḥīrah

Both commentaries preserve one incident showing how the first generation applied ayah 118. **Ibn Abi Hatim reported that Ibn Abi Ad-Dahqanah said** that ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab was told, "There is a young man here from the people of Ḥīrah" — in Iraq, who were Christians — "who is a proficient scribe. Why do you not appoint him as a scribe?" ʿUmar answered: **"I would then be taking advisors from among the disbelievers."**

The proposal was made precisely on the strength of the man's skill; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing the same report from Ibn Abi Hatim, describes the post as chief manager and scribe in ʿUmar's own office, and gives his reply as: if I were to take him in, I would be taking an insider from among non-Muslims. Ibn Kathir draws the ruling directly from this: the ayah and the story about ʿUmar testify that Muslims are not to use people of *ahl adh-dhimmah* as scribes in matters that affect the affairs of the Muslims and expose their secrets, for they might convey those secrets to combatant disbelievers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds al-Qurṭubī's sorrowful comment — al-Qurṭubī, it notes, being the famous scholar and commentator of the fifth century — that in his own day the teaching had been reversed: Jews and Christians were trusted with secrets and considered trustworthy, and through this came to prevail over the ignorant rich, the rulers and the chiefs. Maʿārif names the same policy as an active factor in the decline of the Ottoman Caliphate.

---

## The limit of the ruling — and it matters

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes care to fence ayah 118 off from any general licence toward hostility. Islam, it says, under the shade of its universal mercy, has given Muslims unusual instructions to treat non-Muslims with compassion, goodwill, beneficence, kindliness and tolerance — and the Prophet ﷺ put these into actual practice in all his dealings with them. Regarding non-Muslims resident in Islamic states or bound to Muslims by treaty, Maʿārif says the Prophet's ﷺ emphatic instructions for their protection are themselves part of Islamic law. It cites three warnings from the Prophet ﷺ (the first reported from Ibn Masʿūd, the second narrated by Sayyidunā ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them):

- Whoever harms a *dhimmī* — a protected non-Muslim — I shall be his opponent on the Day of Judgment, and I always defeat the one whom I oppose.
- My Lord has prohibited me to wrong the one protected by a treaty, or anyone other than him.
- Beware — whoever wrongs one protected by treaty, usurps his right, obligates him to do what is beyond his power, or takes from him something without his genuine consent, then I shall be the advocate *for him* on the Day of Judgment.

Side by side with these considerations, Maʿārif says, instructions were given to Muslims to protect their distinct group cohesion by not trusting the enemies of Islam and Muslims with their secrets. The verse restricts *confidence*, not *kindness*. A community can be generous, just and protective toward outsiders — and still not hand them the keys.

---

## Ayah 119: the love that runs one way

Then comes the most personal verse of the three: **"Lo! You are the ones who love them but they love you not."** Ibn Kathir explains: you like them because you think they are believers, since they pretend to be — but they do not like you, publicly or secretly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this strange and inverted: you go about loving them as friends, yet they are no friends of yours, and the position ought to have been exactly the reverse.

Why "ought"? Because of the next clause: **"and you believe in all the Scriptures."** Ibn Kathir explains that the believers have no doubt about any part of Allah's Book, while those described carry deep doubts, confusion and reservations about it. Maʿārif adds that the believers accept all the Scriptures without reservation as to whom they addressed, when they came down, or which prophet received them — while those on the other side do not accept the Muslims' Book or their Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir then cites Muhammad bin Isḥāq reporting from Ibn ʿAbbās — a statement Ibn Jarīr also collected — that this means you believe in *your* Book, in *their* Book, and in the earlier Books, while they disbelieve in your Book; and this is why **they** deserve to be the ones disliked, rather than you.

**"When they meet you, they say, 'We believe.' But when they are alone, they bite their *anāmil* at you in rage."** Ibn Kathir records from Qatādah that *anāmil* means the tips of the fingers, and explains that rage here is extreme anger and fury. The image is unforgettable — the smiling greeting in public, and in private a man biting his own fingertips because he cannot contain what is inside him. Ibn Kathir: they pretend faith and kindness before the believers while concealing the opposite in their hearts in every respect.

**"Say: Perish in your rage."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a declaration of outcome, not merely a rebuke: however much you envy the believers and rage at them, know that Allah shall perfect His favour upon His believing servants, complete His religion, raise high His Word and give dominance to His religion — therefore, die in your rage.

**"Certainly, Allah knows what is in the breasts."** This is the answer to a verse built entirely on concealment. They hide rage behind greetings; Allah has perfect knowledge of what is concealed in the hearts and chests. Ibn Kathir affirms that Allah will punish them for it in this life, that the good they dislike for the believers will come to the believers anyway, and that in the Hereafter awaits severe torment in the Fire, remaining there for eternity. The believer's comfort is not that he can detect hypocrisy, but that **he does not need to.** What is hidden from him is not hidden from Allah.

---

## Ayah 120: the emotional test, and the remedy

**"If a good befalls you, it grieves them; but if some evil overtakes you, they rejoice at it."** Ibn Kathir says this only emphasises the severity of the enmity, and makes it concrete: when the believers enjoy fertile years, victories, support and growing numbers and following, these people become displeased; when the Muslims suffer a drought, or their enemies gain the upper hand by Allah's decree — **"just as occurred during the battle of Uhud"** — they become pleased. Maʿārif renders the same verse as a further clarification of that mentality: if something good happens to you it annoys them, and if something evil befalls you they are delighted with it.

That mention of Uḥud is not incidental. Ibn Kathir notes that immediately after these ayat Allah mentions the story of Uḥud: the defeat with which He tested the believers, His distinguishing the believers from the hypocrites, and their patience. These verses are the doorway into that account — the reader is being told *who was smiling* on the day the Muslims were bleeding.

And then, instead of a counter-strategy, the remedy: **"But if you remain patient and have Taqwa, not the least harm will their cunning do to you. Surely, Allah surrounds all that they do."**

*Ṣabr* is patience and endurance; *taqwa* is the fear of Allah. Ibn Kathir says Allah is directing the believers to safety from the wickedness of evil people and the plots of sinners by recommending that they revert to patience, fear Allah, and trust Him. Then he gives the reason it works: Allah encompasses the enemies of the believers, while the believers have no power or strength except from Him. Whatever Allah wills occurs; whatever He does not will does not occur; nothing happens in His Kingdom except with His decision and according to His decrees. Ibn Kathir closes the passage with one sentence of his own summing all of it up — that whoever relies on Allah, Allah shall suffice for him.

That is why the ayah closes with *Allah surrounds all that they do* rather than with any instruction about them. Their scheming is not outside His encompassing; it is already inside it.

**Ṣabr and taqwa as a standing prescription.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this pair an effective measure against all hardships, and shows it is a recurring teaching in the Qurʼān: in **3:125**, in the section that follows immediately, divine help itself is made conditional on it ("if you stay patient and fear Allah and they come upon you in this heat of theirs, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand of the angels having distinct marks"); in **12:90**, "whoever fears Allah and keeps patience…"; and in **3:200**, toward the end of this sūrah, "be patient, be more patient than others, and guard your frontiers, and fear Allah so that you may be successful." Short as the two words look, Maʿārif observes, they are very comprehensive — containing a successful rule for individual and collective life, and for public, government and military affairs alike. It ends with a narration from Sayyidunā Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, cited as narrated by Aḥmad: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said he knew a verse which, if people were to take to it, would suffice them — **"And whoever fears Allah, for him He shall make a way out"** (65:2).

---

## Living it

- **Distinguish good treatment from deep access.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stacks up the Prophet's ﷺ warnings against wronging protected non-Muslims precisely so this verse is not misread. What is restricted is who becomes your *biṭānah*.
- **Ask which of your two *biṭānah*s has your ear.** The hadith recorded by Al-Bukhari and An-Nasa'i says both voices are always present, even around prophets and caliphs — and that safety from the second is something Allah grants.
- **When you are the target, the instruction is ṣabr and taqwa** — not counter-intrigue. The guarantee rests on Allah's encompassing knowledge and power, not on your ability to outmanoeuvre anyone.

passages.title: Setting out for Uhud and the wavering two clans
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat take the believers back to a single morning — the morning the Prophet ﷺ left his household in Madinah and posted his men at their stations for the battle at Uhud. Allah recalls that scene, names the moment when two groups among the Muslims were about to lose heart, and then reminds the whole community of Badr, where a small, poorly supplied force was given victory. What holds the three ayat together is one argument: *Allah hears and knows, Allah was their Protector, and Allah is the One who gave you victory when you had almost nothing* — so trust Him, and fear Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the link with what came just before. The preceding verses had said that no power could harm the Muslims if they observed patience (*ṣabr*) and fear of Allah (*taqwā*). The temporary setback at Uhud, it explains, came from a failure to observe those two fully. So these ayat open the file on Uhud — and they open it by reminding the community of what Allah did for them.

One thing to keep clear from the start: the ayat themselves cover only the setting out and the wavering of the two groups. They do not narrate the fighting or its outcome. Everything below about the march, the deployment and the battle comes from the historical background that Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān place before the verses in order to make them intelligible.

---

## The road to Uhud

**The motive was revenge for Badr.** Ibn Kathir reports that the idolaters had suffered many casualties among their noble men at Badr. The caravan Abu Sufyan had led returned safely to Makkah, and the remaining Makkan leaders and the children of those killed at Badr demanded of him: "Spend this money on fighting Muhammad!" The money from that caravan was spent on the expenses of war. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the relatives of the Qurayshī chiefs killed at Badr, appealing to traditional Arab pride, resolved that they would not rest until Badr was avenged.

**They came with three thousand men**, Ibn Kathir says, including the Aḥābīsh — tribes living around the city — and camped near Uhud facing Madinah. Maʿārif notes that the mountain was some three or four miles outside Madinah, and that the invading force included women, so that they could appeal to the men's sense of honour and implore them not to retreat.

**The consultation.** According to Ibn Kathir, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ led the Friday prayer, and when he had finished it he performed the funeral prayer for a man from Banū al-Najjār called Mālik bin ʿAmr. Then he asked the Muslims for advice: should they march out to meet the disbelievers, or fortify themselves in Madinah? ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy — the chief hypocrite — advised staying: a siege would be greatly disadvantageous to the enemy; if they attacked the city its men would face them while women and children threw rocks from above; and if they went home to Makkah they would return with failure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that in the Prophet's ﷺ own blessed opinion, warding off the enemy by staying in Madinah was easier and more likely to succeed — and that this was the first time Ibn Ubayy, who outwardly went along with the Muslims, was asked for his opinion.

But some Companions who had not been at Badr — zealous men, says Maʿārif, intensely eager to lay down their lives in the cause of Islam — advised going out to meet the enemy in the open, so that the enemy would not take them for cowards. The majority turned to that view.

**The armour.** The Prophet ﷺ went to his home, put on his shield and came out. The Companions were uneasy and said to one another, "Did we compel the Messenger of Allah to go out?" They said, "O Messenger of Allah! If you wish, we will remain in Madinah." He ﷺ answered that it is not for a Prophet to wear his shield for war and then lay down his arms before Allah decides in his favour. (Ibn Kathir transmits these words without naming a collection, so they are given here as he reports them.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments that this one sentence is sufficient to clarify the difference between a prophet and a non-prophet: a prophet cannot show weakness in that capacity — and in that there is a lesson for the community as well.

**The defection.** He ﷺ marched with a thousand of his Companions. When they reached the Shawṭ area, ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy went back to Madinah with a third of the army — Maʿārif puts it at about three hundred men — claiming he was angry that the Prophet ﷺ had not listened to his advice. He and his supporters said: "If we knew that you would fight today, we would have accompanied you. However, we do not think that you will fight today." Maʿārif reports his words to the same effect: *when my advice was rejected and action was taken on the advice of others, why should we fight and why should we endanger our lives?* Most of his comrades were hypocrites, though, Maʿārif notes, some Muslims too swallowed the bait and tugged along with them.

**The deployment.** With seven hundred men the Prophet ﷺ reached the hillside at Uhud and camped in the valley with the mountain behind them. He ﷺ said that no one was to start fighting until he issued the command. He appointed ʿAbdullāh bin Jubayr, of Banū ʿAmr bin ʿAwf, to lead the archers, who were fifty men, and said to them:

> Keep the horsemen away from us, and be aware that we might be attacked from your direction. If victory was for or against us, remain in your positions. And even if you see us being picked up by birds, do not abandon your positions.

Maʿārif describes the same posting: fifty archers on a hillock at the rear, told to stand guard against any attack from that side, specifically instructed not to concern themselves with the fighting down the hill whether the Muslims won or lost, and told simply not to move from their appointed place.

He ﷺ wore two protective shields and gave the flag to Muṣʿab bin ʿUmayr of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār; he allowed some young men to fight and not others, whom he allowed to take part at al-Khandaq two years later. Maʿārif adds that al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām was made commander of the mounted troops and Ḥamzah was given command of the unarmoured. Facing them, the Quraysh mobilised three thousand men with two hundred horsemen on each flank, Khālid bin al-Walīd leading the right and ʿIkrimah bin Abī Jahl the left, their grand flag given to Banū ʿAbd al-Dār.

Ibn Kathir dates Uhud to a Saturday in the month of Shawwāl in the third year of the Hijrah; ʿIkrimah said it occurred in the middle of Shawwāl, "and Allah knows best." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the ḥadīth narrations prove that this morning was that of the seventh of Shawwāl, Hijrah year 3.

---

## Ayah 121: the language of that morning

**"When you left your household in the morning…"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this as an example of the Qur'an's style in reporting events: as a general principle it does not describe an event in total detail. Events and their details are taken up when they carry implied points of guidance. Here a secondary detail — the time of leaving the house — is identified through the single word *ghadawta*, the morning departure. So is the point of departure: *min ahlika*, "from your household." The Prophet ﷺ was with his family at that moment, and when the time came he left, leaving them behind him, even though this attack was aimed at Madinah itself. The guidance built into that small phrase, says Maʿārif, is that when the command of Allah comes, love of family and home should not stop a person from obeying it.

Notice also what is left out. Details of what happened between leaving the house and reaching the war front go undescribed. The first thing reported is the first thing done on arrival: *tubawwiʼu al-muʼminīna maqāʿida li-l-qitāl* — posting the believers at their stations for the fighting. Ibn Kathir glosses it as designating them to various positions, dividing the army to the left and right sides, and placing them wherever he ﷺ commanded them.

**"And Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower."** Ibn Kathir: He hears what you say and knows what you conceal in your hearts. Maʿārif draws it out: by reminding the Muslims of these attributes, it is pointed out that everything said by the two groups at that time was in the knowledge of Allah, and absolutely nothing of what passed with them remained hidden from Him — and so it was with the end of the war; that too was not hidden from Him. The consolation and the warning arrive in the same breath: a heart that trembled unseen was seen.

---

## Ayah 122: the two groups, and the mercy hidden in the rebuke

**Who were they?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names them: Banū Ḥārithah of the tribe of Aws and Banū Salamah of the tribe of Khazraj. They lost the courage to fight when they saw the hypocrite ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy and his men breaking away — the column had just lost a third of its strength on the road to a battle it was already outnumbered in. But, Maʿārif says, Allah in His grace helped them come out of that state of apprehensiveness.

**Why it is not a verdict against their faith.** Maʿārif is careful here: their weakness was caused by that thought, and certainly not by any weakness in faith — a point it says Ibn Hishām, the famous historian of the Muslim battles, made very clear. And the Qur'an's own statement, *wa Allāhu waliyyuhumā*, "while Allah was their guardian," is, in Maʿārif's words, a testimony to their perfect faith. This is why some elders from these two tribes used to say: the verse contains a complaint against us, but at the same time it bears good news for us in the words *wa Allāhu waliyyuhumā*.

**Al-Bukhārī recorded** that Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh said that this ayah "was revealed about us, Banū Ḥārithah and Banū Salamah. I (or we) would not be pleased if it was not revealed, because Allah said in it, *but Allah was their Wali*." Ibn Kathir adds that Muslim recorded this ḥadīth from Sufyān bin ʿUyaynah. Sit with that for a moment: a Companion is glad that his people's worst moment was written into the Book forever — because the same sentence that records the wavering records that Allah did not let go of them.

**Notice the wording.** The ayah says they *were about to* lose heart — *hammat … an tafshalā*. The inclination came; Allah met it with His guardianship, and it passed.

**"And in Allah let the believers put their trust."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān builds its main teaching here. Muslims should not rely on superiority in men and materials — not that material needs of combat are to be ignored; they should gather whatever they can within their means, but the crucial thing is that total trust be placed in Allah alone. *Tawakkul* is one of the superior human qualities, and it does not mean cutting off all connection with the effort to collect material support. On the contrary: collect what is obviously needed to the best of your ability, use it, and then let Allah take care of the outcome — without becoming proud of what has been collected.

The good example is before us, Maʿārif says: the Prophet ﷺ himself organised the fighting strength of the Muslims, assembled weapons and war materials to the best of his ability, prepared battle plans appropriate to the time and place, and once on the war front set up entrenchments with combat-ready Companions placed in them. By handling these material arrangements with his own blessed hands he demonstrated that material facilities are also a blessing of Allah; ignoring them or turning away from them cannot be called *tawakkul*. The difference, Maʿārif says, is where the reliance is placed: the Muslim gathers the means yet trusts none but Allah, while the one without faith is left relying on brute material strength.

And note why *tawakkul* is prescribed exactly here. The apprehension of weakness that overtook Banū Ḥārithah and Banū Salamah, Maʿārif observes, was caused by that material lack of strength — so trust in Allah was suggested as the treatment for all sorts of apprehensions.

---

## Ayah 123: remember Badr

Having named the fear, Allah answers it with a memory.

**"And Allah has already made you victorious at Badr, when you were a weak little force."** Ibn Kathir places Badr on a Friday, the seventeenth of Ramadan, in the second year of the Hijrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān locates the site about eighty miles south-west of Madinah — a halting-place on the road between Makkah and Madinah, known for its abundance of water, something very important in the desert zones of Arabia — and dates the first armed encounter between believers and disbelievers to Friday in Ramadan of Hijrah year 2, corresponding to 11 March 624 CE. Ibn Kathir notes that Badr is known by the well that bears its name, which was named after Badr bin al-Narayn, the man who dug it.

**The numbers are the argument.** Ibn Kathir: the Muslims numbered three hundred and thirteen men, with two horses and seventy camels; the rest were foot soldiers without enough supplies for the battle. Maʿārif adds that they took turns riding those camels. The enemy army consisted of nine hundred to a thousand men, with enough shields and supplies, battle-ready horses and even various adornments. The expression *adhillah*, "when you were weak," means — as Maʿārif puts it — that you were at that time few in numbers and materials.

**Yawm al-Furqān.** Ibn Kathir calls Badr the Day of the Clarification, by which Allah gave victory and dominance to Islam and its people and disgraced and destroyed shirk, even though the Muslims were few; Allah gave victory to His Messenger ﷺ, supported His revelation, illuminated success on the faces of the Prophet ﷺ and his following, and brought disgrace to Shayṭān and his army. On a superficial view, Maʿārif observes, the battle looks like a local tribal war, but in truth it charted a revolutionary course in the history of the world — which is why the Qur'an calls it *Yawm al-Furqān*, a day of distinction. Maʿārif also cites Professor Philip Hitti's remark that this was Islam's first clear victory.

**The point of the reminder.** Victory is only from Allah, Ibn Kathir says — not because of a large army and adequate supplies. He brings the counter-example the Qur'an itself supplies: *and on the day of Ḥunayn, when you rejoiced at your great number, but it availed you naught* (9:25). Maʿārif turns the same lesson the other way round: the Muslims were few at Badr and won; they were more in number at Uhud, yet they lost. Muslims should not rely on numerical or material strength, military hardware or logistics, but should take victory as something that comes by the grace of Allah — and therefore keep watch that their relationship with Allah remains strong.

Maʿārif illustrates this with the letter of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) to his officer-in-command at Yarmūk, who had written requesting reinforcements. ʿUmar replied — in words Maʿārif cites from Ibn Kathir with reference to the *Musnad* of Aḥmad — that he was directing him to One who is most powerful in support and most protecting army-wise, Allah, the Mighty, the Exalted: "seek help from Him — because Muhammad, may Allah bless him, was helped on the day of Badr despite their being fewer in numbers as compared to yours. So, when this letter of mine reaches you — fight. And do not turn back to me." The narrator says that when they received the letter they mounted a sudden attack in the name of Allah, and the formidable forces of the disbelievers were defeated. ʿUmar knew, Maʿārif comments, that victory or defeat does not depend upon numbers but upon trust in Allah and His help.

**"So fear Allah, that you may be grateful."** Ibn Kathir explains *fa-ttaqū Allāh* as: fulfil the obligations of His obedience. Maʿārif notes that in many places the Qur'an prescribes *taqwā* together with *ṣabr* as a security shield against the machinations of the hypocrites and the harm of enemies — but here *taqwā* is mentioned alone and considered sufficient, because *taqwā* is so comprehensive a human attribute that *ṣabr* is already included within it. And note the direction of the sentence: fear of Allah leads to gratitude. You do not thank Allah for Badr merely by feeling warm about it; you thank Him by obeying Him.

---

## What the day looked like from inside

The material in this section comes from the lessons Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from the events of Uhud as a whole. It reaches beyond what these three ayat narrate, but it shows what the reliance commanded in ayah 122 looked like on the ground.

**Two voices on one field.** The Qurayshī disbelievers had brought their women so that they could excite the men to fight and shame them back into the battle if they retreated. The Prophet ﷺ saw Hindah, the wife of Abu Sufyan, leading a group of women chanting verses to arouse their men's fighting passions: *if you fight right on and win, we shall embrace you and make a soft bed for you; but if you turn back, we shall make you miss our love.* In contrast, the Prophet ﷺ was saying in his prayer: *O Allah, from You I draw my strength, and for You and in Your name I attack and fight. Sufficient for me is Allah, the only One good to trust.* Every word of that prayer, says Maʿārif, shows how Muslims should strengthen their connection with Allah not only in peace but in war — a pattern of behaviour that draws a clear line between the Muslims and other nations.

**Victory comes from Allah, not from piles of hardware.** Under that heading Maʿārif recalls what the Companions did that day. Abū Dujānah turned his body into a shield for the Prophet ﷺ, taking the incoming arrows on his back. Ṭalḥah's body was perforated with arrowheads, and still he did not leave his blessed master unprotected. Anas ibn al-Naḍir — the uncle of Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with them — had been absent from Badr and regretted it deeply, longing for the first chance to fight alongside the Prophet ﷺ. At Uhud, when the Muslims had scattered and the Quraysh were coming on in overwhelming strength, he began his charge sword in hand and met Saʿd, who was going with those who had scattered from the field. He called out: "O Saʿd, where are you going? I smell the scent of Paradise in this valley of Uhud" — and charged ahead, and after a hard fight laid down his life in the way of Allah. (Maʿārif attributes this to Ibn Kathir.)

Jābir said that when the Muslims became scattered, only eleven Companions were left with the Prophet ﷺ, Ṭalḥah among them, with the forces of Quraysh surging forward. Seven times the Prophet ﷺ asked who would take care of them; seven times Ṭalḥah offered himself at once; and each time the Prophet ﷺ sent another of the Anṣār forward instead, who fought and fell a martyr, and Ṭalḥah's wish went unfulfilled.

---

## Living it

**Take the means, then let go.** Post the archers. Put on the armour. Draw the plan. Then leave the outcome to Allah and refuse to become proud of what you have gathered. That is *tawakkul* as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it — not a substitute for effort, but the correct object of reliance once the effort is made.

**Do not measure your safety by the headcount.** The two groups faltered when the numbers moved against them. Allah's answer was not more men; it was *Allah was their Wali*, followed by the reminder of three hundred and thirteen at Badr.

**Stay at your post.** The instruction to the archers, as both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif report it, was absolute: hold your position whether victory is for us or against us, even if you see birds carrying us off. The lesson is not hidden — an assigned station is not to be abandoned because the situation appears to have changed.

**A moment of weakness is not the end of you.** Two groups were about to lose heart, and the Qur'an preserved the record — with *wa Allāhu waliyyuhumā* attached to it. Jābir was glad it was revealed. If Allah is your Guardian, He holds you through the wavering, and the honest record of your weakness can become good news you are grateful for.

**Gratitude is spelled taqwā.** Ayah 123 does not ask for a feeling in return for Badr. It asks for obedience — which, as Ibn Kathir puts it, is fulfilling the obligations of His obedience.
