passages.title: Angels sent down and the matter left to Allah
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These six ayat are Allah's own commentary on unseen help. He reminds the believers of a moment when the Prophet ﷺ steadied them with the promise of angels sent down in their thousands — and then, having raised their eyes to that astonishing support, He tells them plainly what the angels were *for*, what the fighting was *for*, and finally that the outcome of it all was never in the Prophet's ﷺ hands at all. The unit moves in one arc: **from reinforcement, to its purpose, to its results, to the One who decides.**

## Where we are

Ayah 123 has just recalled Badr — "And Allah certainly supported you at Badr when you were weak." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the surah is in the middle of discussing Uhud, and Badr is cited *in relation to* Uhud: there Allah's unseen support was mentioned briefly; here some of its details are given, along with the wisdom behind sending angels.

**Badr itself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places it about eighty miles south-west of Madinah, a halting-place on the Makkah–Madinah road, known for its abundance of water — no small thing in the Arabian desert. The first armed encounter between believers and disbelievers happened there on a Friday in Ramadan of the second year after the Hijrah, 11 March 624 CE. On the surface a local tribal skirmish; in truth, Maʿārif says, it charted a revolutionary course in world history — which is why the Qur'an calls it *Yawm al-Furqān*, the Day of Distinction. Maʿārif adds that by strong and authentic narrations the Muslims numbered 313, with two horses and seventy camels between them, riding in turns.

## Badr or Uhud? A genuine difference among the scholars

Ibn Kathir opens by stating that the commentators **differ** over whether the promise of angels in these ayat refers to Badr or to Uhud.

**The first view: Badr.** "When you said to the believers" (ayah 124) connects back to "And Allah has already made you victorious at Badr" (ayah 123). Ibn Kathir reports this from al-Hasan al-Basri, ʿAmr ash-Shaʿbi, ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas and several others, and notes that Ibn Jarir agreed with it.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from ʿAmr ash-Shaʿbi a detail that brings the scene alive: on the day of Badr word reached the Muslims that Kurz bin Jabir, a prominent tribal chief, was aiding the idolaters. The news weighed on them — and it was then that this promise of three thousand angels was revealed. As it happened, news of the idolaters' defeat reached Kurz and he did not reinforce them; and so, ash-Shaʿbi says, Allah did not reinforce the Muslims with the five thousand either.

**The second view: Uhud.** Others tied the promise to "And when you left your household in the morning to post the believers at their stations for the battle" — that is, Uhud. Ibn Kathir observes that on this reading the angels did not in fact come, because Allah made the help conditional: "But if you hold on to patience and have Taqwa" (ayah 125). The Muslims were not patient at Uhud; they ran. And so, in Ibn Kathir's stark phrase, they did not receive the support of even one angel.

Ibn Kathir's own leaning is toward Badr — because, he says, the angels *did* fight at Badr, as the evidence indicates — and he closes the discussion, as the scholars do, with *Allah knows best*.

## The arithmetic of the promise

A reader will notice the numbers do not sit still: one thousand in Sūrah al-Anfāl (8:9), three thousand in ayah 124, five thousand in ayah 125.

Ibn Kathir answers that there is no contradiction. The word in 8:9 rendered "in succession" means the angels follow one after another — which itself implies that thousands more are behind them. Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas put it as a rising sequence: Allah supported them with one thousand, then the number reached three thousand, then five thousand.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads real psychological wisdom into the escalation. The Muslims saw the enemy's thousand-strong force and measured it against their own 313, and called on Allah for help against such heavy odds. The answer came: one thousand angels — *your enemy's number, matched exactly*. Then came the present ayah's promise of three thousand, made — Maʿārif suggests — on account of the reports that reached the Muslims that Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muhāribi was marching toward Badr with his tribal forces in support of the disbelievers of Makkah, a detail it takes from Rūh al-Maʿānī. The enemy already outnumbered the believers three to one, and the news unsettled them; the promise of three thousand reversed the ratio, so that the Muslims would now be three times the enemy. The comfort is calibrated to the fear.

**The conditions.** Maʿārif identifies two attached to the five thousand: (A) that the Muslims hold firmly to *ṣabr* (patience) and *taqwā* (fear of Allah), and (B) that the enemy come upon them suddenly. The second, it says, did not materialise, so the promise of five thousand did not remain effective — though it adds honestly that major commentators and historians differ over what was actually sent, five thousand or three thousand, all the positions being recorded in Rūh al-Maʿānī.

Ibn Kathir explains the first condition simply: "if you observe patience while fighting the enemy, all the while fearing Me and obeying My command." Note the shape of it — the heavenly reinforcement is not a substitute for the believer's effort; it is *keyed* to it.

## The words themselves

**Musawwimīn — "having marks."** The angels of ayah 125 are described as bearing marks of distinction. Ibn Kathir reports through Abu Ishaq as-Subayʿi, from Harithah bin Mudarrib, that ʿAli bin Abi Talib said the angels were distinguished at Badr by wearing white wool; their horses too carried special markings. An army with an insignia — recognisable, and therefore reassuring to the eye that catches sight of it.

**Min fawrihim hādhā — "rushing."** Ibn Kathir records that al-Hasan, Qatadah, ar-Rabiʿ and as-Suddi understood this of the *angels*: they will rush to you instantaneously. Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means "all at once." A third reading is also mentioned: before their anger subsides — that is, while the fury of battle is still hot. Maʿārif, reading the sudden coming of the *enemy*, makes it the second condition of the promise. The Arabic carries a sense of immediacy either way: no delay between the need and the answer.

## Why send angels at all? — the heart of the passage (ayah 126)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question the whole passage exists to answer. Allah has given a single angel power enough to overturn an entire habitation — the land of the people of Lūt (peace be upon him) was overturned single-handedly by Jibrīl (peace be upon him). So why an *army*? And once angels are on the field, why was every last disbeliever not annihilated?

Ayah 126 answers it in Allah's own words: **"Allah made it not but as a message of good news for you and as an assurance to your hearts."** Maʿārif points to the two phrases — *illā bushrā* (only that it be good news) and *li-tatma'inna qulūbukum* (that your hearts may be at rest) — and to the even plainer instruction in Sūrah al-Anfāl, "So make those who believe firm" (8:12), which is addressed to the angels themselves. Their assignment was the *believers' hearts*, not the enemy's necks.

How does one steady a heart? Maʿārif suggests several forms — a spiritual strengthening, or simply letting the believers know the angels were standing ready to help them: by appearing to them, by voice signs, or by some other method. At Badr all these methods were seen. Some of the noble Companions heard the voice of Jibrīl (peace be upon him) calling "Charge, Haizum!" — Haizum being his steed. Some of them saw angels; Maʿārif cites Muslim for this. And according to some narrations, Maʿārif notes on the authority of al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, when an angel resolved to strike a disbeliever the man's head came away of itself. All of it, Maʿārif says, belongs to one chain of divine support whose purpose was to impress on the Muslims that the angels were with them.

Then Maʿārif draws the conclusion that reaches past Badr entirely: **the obligation of jihād was placed on human beings in this mortal world precisely so that they might deserve merits and ranks in the Hereafter.** Had Allah willed that countries be conquered by armies of angels, the very name of disbelief and disbelievers would have been effaced from the face of the earth. But in this system of the material world He has not willed it so: faith and disbelief, obedience and sin, continue side by side. The great divide comes on the Day of Resurrection, when the true and the false become all distinct.

Ibn Kathir says the same from another angle: Allah told you of the angels' descent to encourage and reassure you — but know that **victory comes only from Allah**, and had He willed He would have defeated your enemy without your having to fight them at all. He cites Sūrah Muhammad: "But if it had been Allah's will, He Himself could certainly have punished them. But He lets you fight in order to test some of you with others" — and then the promise that those killed in His way will never have their deeds lost, will be guided, and admitted to a Paradise already made known to them (47:4–6).

The ayah closes on two of Allah's names. Ibn Kathir glosses them: **al-ʿAzīz**, the Almighty whose power can never be undermined, and **al-Hakīm**, perfect in wisdom in every decree and every decision.

## What the fighting actually accomplishes (ayah 127)

Having said that victory belongs to Allah alone, ayah 127 sets out why He nonetheless commands the believers to fight — out of His wisdom, as Ibn Kathir puts it. Ibn Kathir then treats the ayah as a list of *consequences*:

- **"That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieve"** — that a part of a nation should perish.
- **"or expose them to infamy"** — by disgracing them and forcing them to return with only their rage, having failed in their aim to harm you.
- **"so that they retire frustrated"** — going back to their land without achieving their aims.

Not necessarily annihilation. Sometimes attrition; sometimes only humiliation and a wasted journey. Allah names the modest outcomes alongside the dramatic one, which is itself a mercy to a believer who measures success too narrowly.

## "Not for you is the decision" (ayah 128)

This is the pivot of the passage, and Ibn Kathir calls it a statement testifying that the decision — in this life and the Hereafter — belongs to Allah alone, with no partner. Its meaning, he says: **"The matter is all in My Hand."** He gathers the parallels: "your duty is only to convey the Message, and on Us is the reckoning" (13:40); "Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills" (2:272); "Verily, you guide not whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills" (28:56). Muhammad bin Ishaq's gloss is precise: *"No part of the decision regarding My servants is yours, except what I command you."*

**When it came down.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that with this ayah the text returns to the main event of Uhud after the brief mention of Badr in between. The sources give more than one occasion, and they are worth hearing together.

Al-Bukhari recorded, from Salim bin ʿAbdullah on the authority of his father, that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — as he raised his head from bowing in the second unit of Fajr, after saying *Samiʿ Allāhu liman hamidah, Rabbanā wa lakal-hamd* — say, "O Allah! Curse so-and-so." Then Allah revealed this ayah. An-Nasa'i also recorded it. Imam Ahmad records the same narration with the names given: al-Harith bin Hisham, Suhayl bin ʿAmr, Safwan bin Umayyah. Ibn Kathir adds the ending that transforms the whole episode: **all of these men were pardoned — they embraced Islam later on.**

Al-Bukhari also recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ would make such supplications after rising from bowing — praying, "O Allah! Save al-Walid bin al-Walid, Salamah bin Hisham, ʿAyyash bin Abi Rabiʿah, and the weak and the helpless among the believers. O Allah! Be hard on the tribe of Mudar and let them suffer years of famine like that of the time of Yusuf" — saying it aloud; and sometimes at the Dawn prayer he would say, "O Allah! Curse so-and-so," mentioning some Arab tribes. Then this ayah was revealed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records this second kind of occasion as well — a further account, which it attributes to Sahih al-Bukhari, that the Prophet ﷺ invoked evil fate on some disbelievers, whereupon this ayah came down; and Maʿārif comments, on the authority of Bayān al-Qurʼān, that in it the Prophet ﷺ was counselled to remain patient and forbearing.

And al-Bukhari recorded, from Hamid and Thabit, that Anas bin Malik said the Prophet ﷺ was injured at Uhud and said, **"How can a people achieve success after having injured their Prophet?"** Then "Not for you is the decision" was revealed. Imam Ahmad's narration from Anas gives the wound: his front tooth was broken and he sustained injuries on his forehead until blood dripped on his face, and he said, "How can a people achieve success after having done this to their Prophet who is calling them to their Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored?" Muslim also collected this. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, relating the same occasion, specifies the tooth as the lower right premolar.

Sit with that for a moment. The most beloved of Allah's creation, bleeding from a wound inflicted by the very people he was calling to their Lord — and the revelation that comes is not vengeance but a redrawing of the boundary: *the verdict is not yours*. Ibn Kathir explains the two possibilities the ayah names: **"whether He turns in mercy to pardon them"** — pardoning the acts of disbelief they commit, delivering them from misguidance to guidance — **"or punishes them"** in this life and the Hereafter because of their disbelief and their errors, **"verily, they are the wrongdoers,"** and so they deserve such a fate. And history recorded which of the two it was: the men named in that dawn supplication became Muslims.

## The closing seal (ayah 129)

"And to Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth." Ibn Kathir: everything is indeed the property of Allah and all are servants in His Hand. "He forgives whom He wills, and punishes whom He wills" — for His is the decision, and none can resist it. Then the line that ends any argument: **Allah is never asked about what He does, while they will be asked.**

And yet the passage does not close on power. It closes on **"and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** After all the angels and the armies and the sovereign right to punish, the final word given to us is mercy.

## Living it

- **Take help as a gift, not a substitute.** The angels came as *bushrā* and heart's-rest; the fighting still fell to the believers. Whatever unseen help Allah sends you, your own effort is not thereby cancelled.
- **The support was conditioned on ṣabr and taqwā** (ayah 125). Maʿārif observes on ayah 123 that these two — patience and fear of Allah — are prescribed again and again in the Qur'an as a shield against the machinations of the hypocrites and the harm of hostile enemies, and that taqwā is so comprehensive a human quality that ṣabr is contained within it. Right there, in these two behaviour models, lies the secret of an entire organised struggle and the clear victory that comes in its wake.
- **Hold the line between your work and Allah's.** Ayah 128 draws it for the Prophet ﷺ himself. You convey, you strive, you pray — the verdict on hearts is not yours to issue.
- **Be slow to write anyone off.** The men cursed by name at Fajr died Muslims. If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was told the outcome was not his to declare, no one else is in a position to declare it either.

passages.title: The prohibition of compounded interest
passages.tafsir:
# The prohibition of compounded interest (3:130–132)

These three ayat move from one prohibition to the whole shape of a believing life. **Ayah 130** forbids *riba* — interest — in the very form the Arabs of that time knew best. **Ayah 131** sets that prohibition against the Fire. **Ayah 132** then lifts the reader out of a single ruling into the principle behind every ruling: obey Allah and obey the Messenger ﷺ, and you may be shown mercy.

What binds them is *taqwa* — the fear of Allah, the sense of responsibility before Him. Ayah 130 closes by commanding it ("but fear Allah that you may be successful"), and ayah 131 opens by commanding it again in a sharper key ("guard yourselves against the Fire"). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the link explicit: dealing in interest is a sin that *deprives a person of taqwa*, and the verses that follow stress the positive side of taqwa, along with the promise of reward for those who observe it.

---

## What riba looked like when this ayah came down

Ibn Kathir opens with the practice itself. Allah, he says, prohibits His believing servants from dealing in riba and from requiring interest on their capital "just as they used to do during the time of Jahiliyyah" — the age of ignorance before Islam.

The mechanics were simple and merciless. When a loan fell due, the creditor would say to the debtor: **either pay now, or the loan will incur interest.** If the debtor could not pay and asked for deferment, he did not get mercy — he got a bill for the delay. And then the same thing happened the next year, and the next. Ibn Kathir's summary is the whole tragedy in one line: this "would occur year after year until the little capital becomes multiplied many times."

That is what the Qur'an is pointing at with the phrase *aḍʿāfan muḍāʿafah* — "doubled and multiplied," rendered in our translation as *multiplying it many times*. It is not an abstract economic category. It is a picture of a man's small debt swelling past any hope of repayment, precisely *because* he was too poor to pay it on time. The one thing that should have drawn compassion — inability — became the trigger for the charge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says of these words that they indicate riba's "unjust and evil nature."

---

## Does "multiplying it many times" limit the prohibition?

This is the question a careful reader will ask immediately, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes it head-on. If Allah forbids riba *"doubled and multiplied,"* does that mean only extortionate, compounding interest is forbidden, and a modest rate is allowed?

No. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that these words **"are not used in a restrictive sense."** It refers the reader to the detailed rules of riba and the philosophy underlying its prohibition, discussed thoroughly at Sūrah al-Baqarah, verses 275–278, and states that it is evident from there that riba is prohibited in any case, "even though its rate is not so high as to make it doubled or multiplied."

So why the phrase at all? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons:

**1. It describes the reality of the time — and exposes it.** The words are used "only to explain the factual position prevalent at that time," and in doing so they "indicate its unjust and evil nature." The Qur'an does not merely legislate against riba; it holds up a mirror to what riba had actually done to people, so that the prohibition is felt and not just filed.

**2. It describes where riba always ends up.** This is the subtler point, and worth sitting with. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that even where the interest charged is *simple* and not compound, "once a person is engaged in the business of interest he does not stop at charging interest in one transaction only." He reinvests the income of that interest in another loan, and keeps investing the interest proceeds in similar transactions "again and again, and thus the ultimate result is that the original interest charged through the first transaction is doubled and multiplied."

In other words, "doubled and multiplied" is not a threshold you have to cross before the ruling bites. It is the destination of the road, named at the road's entrance. The Qur'an forbids the first step by showing you where the last one leads.

---

## Ayah 131: the warning of the Fire

Having commanded taqwa in ayah 130, Allah — in Ibn Kathir's words — "threatens them with the Fire and warns them against it": **"Guard yourselves against the Fire prepared for the disbelievers."**

Notice how little distance the passage puts between a matter of money and a matter of eternity. A man's ledger and a man's destination are set down in consecutive breaths. And notice the word *prepared*: the Fire is not spoken of as something that might one day be built, but as something already made ready.

Ibn Kathir does not, here, take the ayah into any discussion of who among the sinful enters the Fire or for how long. He presents it for what it plainly is: a warning delivered to believers, who are told to *guard themselves* against a place prepared for those who reject Allah. The reader is left with the warning itself, undiluted, and with the command of taqwa on either side of it.

---

## Ayah 132: "Obey Allah and the Messenger" — the heart of the passage

Then comes what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls "a cardinal command of Faith," stated in a handful of words: **"Obey Allah and the Messenger, so you may be shown mercy."**

Notice first what mercy is tied to. Not to sentiment, not to affiliation — to *obedience*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that in this whole passage, Allah "has made it clear in these verses that the obedience to Allah and His Messenger does not become genuine and effective through lip-service alone. Instead, the obedient ones are known by what they are and what they do, by their traits of character and their deeds."

**Why are two obediences named?** This is the question Maʿārif ul Qurʼān builds its commentary around, because the pairing is not unique to this ayah — the pattern of commanding obedience to Allah and immediately following it with the command to obey the Messenger ﷺ appears in the Qur'an "again and again." That repetition, it says, is there to remind us that these are the basic principles of Islam and *īmān*: first, affirming Allah, His Oneness, and that man is there to worship and obey Him; second, the confirmation of His Messenger ﷺ and of obedience to him.

And obedience to the Messenger ﷺ is not a second, parallel authority alongside Allah's. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds this in the Qur'an itself: *"And he does not speak out of his own desire. It is not but a revelation revealed"* (53:3–4), and *"And whoever obeys the Messenger, he surely obeys Allah"* (4:80). The conclusion it draws is direct: **"the obedience to the Messenger is the very same as the obedience to Allah. It is nothing separate from it."**

So the question returns with more force: if they are one, why state them separately?

### The answer: the Messenger's ﷺ mission was never only to hand over the text

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds it this way. Allah sent a Book to guide man in this world, *and* a Messenger — and the Messenger ﷺ was charged with four duties, all gathered in the Qur'an's recurring description, *"who recites to them His verses and makes them pure and teaches them the Book and the wisdom"*:

1. To convey the verses of the Qur'an precisely and exactly in the form they were spoken when revealed.
2. To cleanse people of outward and inward impurities.
3. To teach the community not only the contents of the Book but also its purpose.
4. To teach people *wisdom* along with the Book.

Then comes the observation that makes the whole argument land. The people the Prophet ﷺ was addressing were "the eloquent people of Arabia who had command over the finer points of the Arabic language." Teaching *them* the Qur'an could never have meant teaching them the literal meaning of the Qur'anic words — they understood all that perfectly well. So the purpose of the teaching and clarification must have been something else: that an injunction stated **briefly or in summary form** in the Qur'an was clarified and elaborated by the Prophet ﷺ and communicated to people through a revelation that does not form part of the Qur'an — what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls *waḥy ghayr al-matluww*, **the un-recited revelation**, inspired into his blessed heart.

The examples are decisive:

- The Qur'an says in many places no more than *"Establish the salah and pay the zakah."* Even where units of prayer are named — *qiyām*, *rukūʿ*, *sajdah* — they remain undefined; the modality is simply not there. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the angel Jibrāʼīl (peace be upon him) came as commanded by Allah and taught all the details by demonstration before the Prophet ﷺ, who then conveyed word and deed to the people of his Ummah.
- The Qur'an commands zakah, but the thresholds, how much is due at each, which possessions are zakatable and which are not — all of this was given by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who even had these committed to writing as executive orders and passed on to several Companions.
- And — the example that brings us straight back to ayah 130 — the Qur'an says, *"And do not eat up each other's property by false means"* (2:188). But there are deals and transactions of all sorts: buying and selling, rentals, tenancy, wages. Which forms are unjust, inequitable, or harmful to the public interest, and therefore *bāṭil*, false? **"All these details were given to the community by the Holy Prophet ﷺ by the leave of Allah."** And, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, the same is true of all the legal rulings of Islamic Law.

That is the loop this passage quietly closes. Ayah 130 forbids riba in a few words. Knowing what actually counts as wrongfully devoured wealth in a real transaction — the thing every believer needs in order to obey — comes through the Messenger ﷺ. A person who accepted the Qur'anic prohibition but rejected the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of it would be left holding a command he could not carry out.

### Why the danger was real

Since these details were conveyed by the Prophet ﷺ under the guidance of divine revelation yet **do not appear in the Qur'an**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, there was a real likelihood that "the uninitiated may be deceived into believing that these detailed rulings were not given by Allah Almighty," and so need not be carried out as part of one's obedience to Allah. It further notes that this was no small matter: there were chances that the enemies of Islam would find an excuse here to inject chaos into a basic Islamic principle and lead Muslims away from the right path.

This is why, it says, the Qur'an deals with the subject in a variety of ways: by naming *wisdom* alongside the Book among what the Prophet ﷺ teaches — pointing to elements beyond the words of the Book that are still binding; by stating that he was sent *"to explain for people"* the meanings and objectives of what was revealed to them (16:44); and by the oft-quoted verse, **"Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it"** (59:7).

And the Prophet ﷺ himself foresaw the objection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith — reported, as it names them, by **al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Baihaqi and Imam Ahmad** — in which he ﷺ warned against the man reclining on his couch who, when an order of the Prophet's ﷺ reaches him, bidding something or forbidding something, says: *"This we do not know. We only follow what we find in the Book of Allah."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's conclusion is that the repeated pairing of the two obediences is there to counter exactly this ignorance — the attempt to separate the Prophet's ﷺ detailed explanations of Qur'anic injunctions, preserved in his ahadith, from obedience to Allah, and then to discard them. The reality, it says, is that the two cannot be separated. It closes with a Persian couplet whose sense is:

> What he said was said by Allah,
> Voiced, though, it was by a slave of Allah.

---

## Living it

**Do not treat "multiplied many times" as your licence.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has closed that door: the prohibition is not confined to extortionate or compounding rates. The phrase names what riba does to people, not the point at which it becomes forbidden.

**Watch the moment the ayah is really about.** The Jahili sin Ibn Kathir describes was not lending — it was answering a man's request for more time with a charge for the delay, again and again, until a small debt had multiplied beyond reach. That is the transaction the ayah calls out, and it is worth asking honestly whether anything in our own dealings works the same way.

**Let obedience be visible.** Mercy in ayah 132 is attached to obeying, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists that obedience does not become genuine through lip-service — the obedient are known "by what they are and what they do."

**And take the Sunnah as part of that obedience, not as an optional supplement.** A believer who wants to keep his wealth clean cannot do it from the Qur'an's summary alone; the details of what is *bāṭil* in trade came to the Ummah through the Prophet ﷺ by the leave of Allah. Ayah 132 places both obediences in one sentence for exactly this reason — and ends not with a threat but with an open hand: *so you may be shown mercy.*

passages.title: Racing to forgiveness and the traits of the righteous
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a single invitation with a portrait attached. Ayah 133 issues a command — hasten toward forgiveness and toward a Garden vast beyond imagining — and ayat 134–135 answer the obvious question: *hasten how, and as what kind of person?* Ayah 136 then closes the circle by handing back to these people exactly the two things they were told to race toward: forgiveness from their Lord, and Gardens.

## Where this falls in the surah

Ibn Kathir reads these verses as the continuation of what precedes them. In ayah 130 Allah forbids the believers to consume riba "doubled and multiplied" — the practice of Jahiliyyah in which, when a loan came due, the creditor would say to the debtor, *either pay now, or the loan will incur interest*, year after year, until a little capital had multiplied many times over. Then ayah 131 warns of the Fire "prepared for the disbelievers," and ayah 132 commands obedience to Allah and the Messenger ﷺ.

Ayah 133 is the answering movement. Where the Fire was *prepared for the disbelievers*, the Garden is *prepared for the Muttaqin*, the God-fearing — Ibn Kathir draws that parallel explicitly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the sequence of commands: first "obey the Messenger" (132), then "race one another toward forgiveness from your Lord and toward Paradise" (133). Having been pulled back from a way of taking that devours other people, the believer is now pushed forward toward a way of giving — which is precisely what ayah 134 opens with.

## "Race" — and race toward *what*?

Ayah 133 is a command of urgency. Ibn Kathir glosses the whole ayah as Allah "encouraging His servants to perform righteous deeds and to rush to accomplish the acts of obedience," and pairs it with its sister verse in Sūrat al-Ḥadīd: "Race with one another in hastening towards forgiveness from your Lord, and Paradise the width whereof is as the width of the heaven and the earth" (57:21).

But forgiveness is not a place one can run to. So Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that here "Forgiveness stands for the means of obtaining forgiveness — that is, good deeds which bring forth forgiveness." What is striking is how the early authorities each named a different door into that one house. Sayyidunā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) explained it as **the fulfilment of obligations**; Ibn ʿAbbās as **Islam** itself; Abū al-ʿĀliyah as **hijrah**; Anas ibn Mālik as **al-takbīr al-ūlā**, the first call of "Allāhu Akbar" in the prayer; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr as **perfection of obedience**; Ḍaḥḥāk as **jihād**; and ʿIkrimah as **tawbah**, repentance. Maʿārif comments that though expressed differently these convey one theme: forgiveness covers all good deeds that become the means of obtaining Divine forgiveness. The practical effect is generous — whatever good is in front of you right now is a legitimate lane in this race.

**An apparent problem, and its resolution.** Maʿārif raises a question a careful reader should feel: here we are commanded to compete, yet elsewhere Allah says, "And do not covet something by which Allah has made some of you excel some others" (4:32). The answer given is that excellences (*faḍāʼil* — merits, ranks, virtues) are of two kinds. The first relates to what cannot be achieved by a person, being beyond his power and control — we may call these **non-electable**: colour, or beauty, or birth into a morally high family cannot be chosen and acquired. These Allah Himself gave to His creation in His infinite wisdom; chasing them leads to nothing but envy and malice. Let a man keep wishing his skin were a different colour — what is he going to get out of that desire? Nothing. The other kind is **electable**: the vast range of merit-worthy deeds a person can actually achieve by effort. *That* is where we have been asked to accelerate, and not in one verse only: "Try to get ahead of one another in good deeds" (2:148, 5:48), and "in this, then, aspire the aspirers" (83:26). Maʿārif adds the counsel of a sage: one who has a natural or physical handicap beyond his power to correct should remain contented and unaffected by the achievements of others, and simply go on doing what he does — for if he pines over the handicap and envies others, he will be unable to perform to his own capability and will end up doing little or nothing at all.

## Why forgiveness is named before the Garden

Maʿārif draws attention to the order in ayah 133: forgiveness first, Paradise after. This may be, it suggests, to indicate that entry into Paradise is impossible without Divine forgiveness. The reason is obvious: a person may spend a lifetime doing good and abstaining from evil, and still the aggregate of his good deeds cannot pay the price of Paradise. What takes him there is only the forgiveness of his Lord, and His grace. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Strive to be straight and true, take the middle course and seek glad tidings — for one's deeds shall not take anyone into Paradise." People said, "Not even yours, O Messenger of Allah?" He said, "Not even mine, unless it is that Allah covers me up with His mercy." (Maʿārif cites this from *al-Targhīb wa al-Tarhīb*, with reference to al-Bukhārī and Muslim.)

This does not make deeds pointless — Maʿārif is careful here. As is the customary practice of Allah, He bestows His grace upon a servant who does what is good; in fact, one who is given the very ability to do good is really given the signal that Allah is pleased with him. So let none of us be tardy in the performance of what is good. Deeds are not the price of Paradise; they are the sign that mercy is already at work.

And because divine forgiveness is the primary factor in entering Paradise, Maʿārif notes, the text does not present forgiveness in the absolute sense but says **"forgiveness from your Lord"** — *min Rabbikum*. By doing so, the text highlights Allah's attribute as the Lord, showing thereby His added grace and mercy for His servants.

## A Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth

Ibn Kathir reports that "as wide as the heavens and the earth" draws attention to the spaciousness of Paradise. He offers a way of feeling it: Allah describes the couches of Paradise as "lined with silk brocade" (55:54) — so what about their outer covering? It was also said that Paradise is as wide as it is long, because it is a dome under the Throne, and the width and length of a dome or a circle are the same in distance. This is supported by what is found in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "When you ask Allah for Paradise, ask Him for al-Firdaws, which is the highest and best part of Paradise. From it originate the rivers of Paradise, and above it is the Throne of the Most Beneficent."

Maʿārif adds a note on why this comparison is used at all: since the human mind cannot conceive, within the confines of its experience, any vastness greater than that of the heavens and the earth, Paradise has been likened to them — a way of saying that it is very vast indeed. And if the *width* is so great, who can imagine the length, which should be greater still?

Al-Bazzār recorded from Abū Hurayrah that a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked about this very ayah: if Paradise is as wide as the heavens and the earth, *where is the Fire then?* The Prophet ﷺ replied, "When the night comes, it overtakes everything — so where is the day?" The man said, "Where Allah wants it to be." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Similarly, the Fire is where Allah wants it to be." Ibn Kathir gives two readings of this: first, that our not seeing the night during the day does not mean the day is not somewhere else; and second, that when day overcomes this part of the world, night overtakes the other. Paradise is in the utmost heights, above the heavens and under the Throne; the Fire is in the lowest of lows. So Paradise being as wide as the heavens and the earth does not contradict the fact that the Fire exists wherever Allah wills it to be.

**A second reading of the word.** Maʿārif notes that all of the above assumes the Arabic word *ʿarḍ* means "width." But some commentators adopted another possible interpretation: *ʿarḍ* is also used in the sense of **price** — what is offered against an object of sale. On that reading, Paradise is no ordinary commodity: the entire heavens and the earth are its price. Maʿārif cites *al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr*, transmitting from Abū Muslim, that if a price were to be put on Paradise, the heavens and the earth together with whatever is in them would be its price — the purpose being to demonstrate the most exalted status of Paradise, unmatched by anything in its greatness. Either way the point is the same: an object of unimaginable worth and magnitude — and with such a thing in view, what else should one do but hasten toward it?

Finally, "**prepared** for the God-fearing" tells us, as Maʿārif reads it, that Paradise has already been created; and clear indicators in the Qur'an and Hadith seem to suggest the existence of Paradise on the seventh heaven, which is its surface.

## The portrait: why people-facing traits come first

Maʿārif makes a structural observation worth pausing on. Allah has made God-fearing Muslims live as models for others — the Qur'an sends us to "the path of those whom You have blessed" (1:6) and exhorts us to "be with the truthful" (9:119). But there are all sorts of people in the world, including clever ones who would pose as good and impersonate the genuine. For this reason a fine line of distinction had to be drawn, showing how the favoured servants of Allah can be identified by their special traits of character — so that people abstain from wrong guides and follow the true ones. That is what ayat 134–135 do; and this is what is hinted at a few verses later in "This is a declaration for mankind, and a guidance, and a lesson for the God-fearing" (3:138).

And notice the order: the qualities relating to *human rights and social behaviour* come first, and those relating to *the rights of Allah* after. Maʿārif explains that the rights of Allah, despite their supreme status above all rights, are not meant to benefit Allah in any way — He needs none of them, nor does He suffer in any way if they are not fulfilled; His Being is absolutely free of all such concerns, and the one who worships Him is the one who gains. Moreover He is Very-Merciful, so whoever falls short in His rights may regret it at any time, turn to Him and repent sincerely, and have his sins instantly forgiven from that eternal fountain of mercy. But when one person fails another's rights, that other runs into a real loss — and loss suffered by one human being at the hands of another is not so easily forgiven and forgotten. Moreover, the correct balance of the universal order and the reform of human society hinge on the fulfilment of mutual rights: a slight shortfall can trigger disorders, fights and wars, while high morals turn even enemies into friends and let feuds raging through centuries subside into peace.

## Ayah 134: giving in ease and in hardship

"Those who spend in prosperity and in adversity." Ibn Kathir unpacks the pair: in hard times and easy times, while active or enthusiastic and otherwise, healthy or ill, and in all conditions — just as Allah said, "those who spend their wealth by night and day, in secret and in public" (2:274). Such believers, he says, are never distracted from obeying Allah, spending on what pleases Him, being kind to His servants and their relatives, and other acts of righteousness.

Maʿārif reads the phrase as meaning they are so used to spending for the good pleasure of Allah that they spend whatever they can under all conditions — more from more and less from less — and draws out three lessons. **First**, the poor must not consider themselves free from the obligation of spending, lest they deprive themselves of the opportunity; before Allah, spending one penny out of a thousand pennies has the same status as spending one dollar out of a thousand dollars. **Second**, whoever keeps giving within the limits of his capacity — especially when circumstances are straitened — discovers that the habit of giving and sharing has come to stay and will not go extinct; and that very quality may draw down the mercy of Allah, who in His grace bestows new openings and increases in one's means of sustenance. **Third**, a person in the habit of spending on others, helping the poor, the needy and the deprived, would never even think of usurping what belongs to them against their wishes.

The examples are humbling. Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) once gave away a single piece of grape in charity, because she had absolutely nothing else with her at that time; according to another early report, there was a time when she gave one onion. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Guard yourself against the Fire even if it be by giving a piece of date in charity, and do not turn back one who begs empty-handed, even if it be by giving a cloven hoof from a goat." Maʿārif also relates a hadith reported by Imam al-Rāzī in his *al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr*: the Prophet ﷺ one day exhorted people to spend in charity, and those with gold and silver lost no time in giving; somebody brought date-flakes because he had nothing else, and they were accepted and given in charity; then another person came and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have nothing to spend in charity — however, I am known as a man of honour among my people, so I give my sense of honour in charity, after which I shall never be angry with a person in future, no matter how much he insults me."

That story sets up something important. The Qur'an uses the word *yunfiqūn*, "they spend," without determining **what** is spent. Maʿārif reads that generality as suggesting it includes not only money but everything else that can be spent — one who spends his time and labour in the way of Allah is likewise credited with *infāq fī sabīlillāh*, spending in the way of Allah; and the hadith just quoted supports this view.

**Why name prosperity and adversity specifically?** Because, Maʿārif suggests, these may be the two conditions of life in which a person habitually tends to forget Allah: when very rich and up to the neck in luxury, and, fairly often, when worrying about his adversity. The verse settles that the favoured servants of Allah are unique in character: they forget Him neither in luxury nor in distress. Bahādur Shāh Ẓafar, the last Mughal emperor of Delhi, made this Qur'anic idea the subject of his poetry: not much of a man is he, no matter how wise he be, who does not remember Allah when wealthy and does not fear Allah when angry.

## Swallowing rage

*Al-kāẓimīn al-ghayẓ* describes those who repress anger — who, when angry, control it rather than acting on it, and even forgive those who hurt them. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as meaning that they do not satisfy their rage upon people; rather, they refrain from harming them and await their reward with Allah. The narrations he gathers here are among the most quoted in the Sunnah:

- **Imam Aḥmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said** that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The strong person is not he who is able to physically overcome people. The strong person is he who overcomes his rage when he is angry." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith is also recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.
- **Imam Aḥmad recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "He who gives time to a debtor or forgives him, then Allah will save him from the heat of Jahannam. Behold! The deeds of Paradise are difficult to reach, for they are on top of a hill, while the deeds of the Fire are easy to find in the lowlands. The happy person is he who is saved from the tests. Verily, there is no dose of anything better to Allah than a dose of rage that the servant controls; and whenever the servant of Allah controls it, he will be internally filled with faith." Ibn Kathir says its chain of narration is good, it does not contain any disparaged narrators, and the meaning is good.
- **Imam Aḥmad recorded that Sahl ibn Muʿādh ibn Anas said, from his father**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever controlled rage while able to act upon it, then Allah will call him while all creation is a witness, until He gives him the choice of any of the Ḥūr he wishes." Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah collected this hadith, which at-Tirmidhī said was *ḥasan gharīb*.
- **Ibn Marduwyah recorded that Ibn ʿUmar said** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "There is not a dose of anything that the servant takes which is better than a dose of control of rage that he feels, when he does it seeking Allah's Face." Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mājah also collected this hadith.

Notice the recurring image: rage as a *draught* to be swallowed. It goes down hard; what it fills you with is faith.

## Pardon — and then the rung above it

Ibn Kathir explains "and who pardon men" as meaning they forgive those who treat them with injustice, so that they hold no ill feelings about anyone in their hearts — "and this is the most excellent conduct in this regard." Which is why the ayah closes, "verily, Allah loves the Muhsinin, the good-doers": this good conduct, he says, is a type of *iḥsān*, excellence in the religion. He then cites, without naming a collection, a hadith that reads: "I swear regarding three matters: no charity shall ever decrease the wealth; whenever one forgives people, then Allah will magnify his honour; and he who is humble for Allah, then Allah will raise his rank."

Maʿārif reads ayah 134 as a combination of three qualities, a ladder of three rungs. **One**: when hurt, do not flare up in anger or lose self-control. **Two**: surrender the option of taking revenge and forgive the wrongdoer from the depths of the heart. **Three**: rise higher still and actually *do good* to the one who caused you pain — which is why the ayah ends with *muḥsinīn*, those who do good. The Qur'an states the principle more clearly elsewhere: "Repel evil with what is best, then the one between whom and you there is enmity shall become as if he was a fast friend" (41:34). This was the supreme measure of the moral training Allah gave to His noble Messenger ﷺ, whose guideline was: join with him who severs relations with you, forgive him who does injustice to you, and do good to him who is bad to you. Maʿārif also relates, without naming a collection, that on the Day of Resurrection a proclamation will go forth from Allah asking whether anyone has any rights due to Him — if so, let him stand — and those who rise on that occasion will be the ones who forgave the injustices done to them by people in their life on earth; and, in another hadith, that whoever likes to have lofty palaces and elevated ranks should forgive the one who did him injustice, give to the one who never gave him anything, and join up with the one who severed relations with him.

Two illustrations from Maʿārif make it concrete. Maʿārif relates — citing *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, which in turn cites Imam al-Bayhaqī — that the maid of ʿAlī Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn ibn Sayyidunā Ḥusayn (may Allah be pleased with him) was helping him with his wuḍūʼ when the water-pitcher slipped from her hands and soaked his clothes. Sensing the impending danger, she recited: *"and those who suppress anger and forgive people."* Hearing this, he became totally silent. She then recited the second sentence: *"and Allah loves those who do good."* He said, "All right, go. I give you your freedom." And Imam Abū Ḥanīfah, accosted in a busy marketplace by a man who heaped insults on him, controlled his anger and said nothing; he went home, put a considerable quantity of gold and silver coins in a gift-wrapped tray, went to the man's house and presented it, saying, "Today you did something very good to me. You gave me of your good deeds. It is in gratitude of this great favour that I am presenting this gift." The man was affected, repented, got rid of his bad habit for good, asked the Imam's forgiveness, entered his circle as a disciple, and finally became a great scholar.

## Ayah 135: what they do when they fall

Now the passage turns to the rights of Allah. Maʿārif summarises: true Muslims do not disobey Allah — and should they ever fall into sin under the compulsions of human weakness, they immediately turn to Allah, repent, seek His forgiveness, and resolve to abstain from that sin in future.

The ayah names two categories: *fāḥishah* — a shameful, immoral act — and "wronging themselves." Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and exact: if they commit an error, they follow it with repentance and ask forgiveness. And here he places one of the most astonishing narrations in the corpus. **Imam Aḥmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said** that the Prophet ﷺ said: a man once committed an error and said, "O Lord! I committed an error, so forgive me." Allah said, "My servant committed an error and knew that he has a Lord Who forgives or punishes for the error. I have forgiven My servant." The man committed another error and said the same, and Allah said the same. And a third time. And a fourth — and Allah said, "My servant knew that he has a Lord Who forgives or punishes for the error. Bear witness that I have forgiven My servant, so let him do whatever he likes." Ibn Kathir notes that a similar narration was collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ. Read alongside the ayah's own condition — *and they do not persist in what they have done, while they know* — the point is not licence but the inexhaustibility of the door: the sinner who keeps returning is dealing with a Lord who keeps opening.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded that Anas ibn Mālik said, "I was told that when this ayah was revealed, Iblīs cried." That single line tells you what the enemy of man loses when a believer learns to repent rather than despair.

"**And none can forgive sins but Allah**" — Ibn Kathir: this means that none except Allah forgives sins. The question is rhetorical and the door is single; there is no other office to apply to.

"**And do not persist in what they have done, while they know.**" Ibn Kathir: they repent from their error, return to Allah before death, do not insist on error, and if they err again, they repent from it. On "while they know," Mujāhid and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr commented: "Whoever repents, then Allah will forgive him." On that reading, the knowledge that stops persistence is the knowledge that pardon is genuinely available — as Allah says, "Know they not that Allah accepts repentance from His servants?" (9:104), and "whoever does evil or wrongs himself but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness, he will find Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110).

Maʿārif adds a diagnosis and a prescription. The **diagnosis**: involvement in sin is caused by one's negligence in remembering Allah — so if a sin has been committed, one should immediately turn to Allah, renew the zeal to obey Him, and start remembering Him as He should be remembered. The **prescription**: forgiveness of sins depends on two things — to regret past sins and pray for pardon, and to resolve fully not to go near them in future.

## Ayah 136: the race, completed

"For such, the reward is forgiveness from their Lord, and Gardens with rivers flowing underneath, wherein they shall abide forever. How excellent is this reward for the doers."

Ibn Kathir points out that this is the reward *for these qualities*; that the rivers carry all kinds of drinks; that "wherein they shall abide" means forever and ever; and that in the closing words Allah praises Paradise. Read against ayah 133, the structure is beautiful: they were commanded to hasten toward *forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden*, and ayah 136 hands them precisely that — *forgiveness from their Lord and Gardens*. The finish line is exactly what they were pointed at.

## Living it

The passage asks for four concrete things, and each of them is available today:

- **Give something, whatever your circumstances.** A single grape. An onion. A piece of a date. Your time, your labour. The point of "in prosperity and adversity" is that there is no season in which giving stops.
- **When rage comes, swallow it** — knowing there is no dose better to Allah than a dose of rage the servant controls, and that what fills the empty space is faith.
- **Then go further than restraint**: forgive the person from the depth of the heart, and if you can, do him an actual good. That is where the ayah's word *muḥsinīn* lives.
- **When you fall — and you will — do not let the fall become a residence.** Remember Allah, ask forgiveness, resolve not to return. The sin that ruins is not the one committed but the one persisted in knowingly.

And through it all, keep the order of ayah 133 in view: forgiveness first, then the Garden. We run, but we do not buy. May Allah Almighty bestow upon us the good fortune to become possessed of these supreme morals identified by the Holy Qur'an. Āmīn.

passages.title: Travel the earth and see how the deniers ended
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are Allah's answer to a community that has just taken a heavy loss: what happened to you is not unprecedented, and the story of those who denied the truth has an ending you can go out and see. Ayah 137 sends the wounded believers to look at history; ayah 138 tells them what that history is *for*. Together they turn a battlefield loss into a lesson in how Allah runs the world.

## After Uhud

Ibn Kathir places this passage precisely. Under the heading *"The Wisdom Behind the Losses Muslims Suffered During Uhud,"* he explains that "Allah states to His believing servants who suffered losses in the battle of Uhud, including seventy dead."

Hold that number for a moment. Seventy dead, out of one community. And behind such a loss there must have pressed on every heart the question: *if we are the people of truth, why did this happen to us?*

Ayah 137 does not begin by consoling. It begins by widening the lens.

## "Many similar ways were faced before you" (ayah 137)

> **قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ سُنَنٌ** — "Similar situations came to pass before you."

Ibn Kathir renders the opening as *"Many similar ways (and mishaps of life) were faced [by nations (believers and disbelievers) that have passed away] before you."* And he explains what it points to: "the previous nations who followed their Prophets before you, they too suffered losses."

Notice how much comfort is folded into that one sentence. The word rendered "ways" is *sunan*, and Ibn Kathir's rendering has it as *many* ways, faced by nations that have already passed away — believers among them. So the believers at Uhud were not being told they had fallen out of Allah's favour. They were being told they had joined a line. The communities that followed their Prophets before them also took losses. Uhud was their entry into that company, not their expulsion from it.

And it is essential to hear the rest of Ibn Kathir's sentence, because the consolation is not that everyone suffers. It is where the suffering leads: "However, the good end was theirs, and the ultimate defeat was for the disbelievers."

That is the claim. Now comes the evidence.

## "So travel through the earth, and see"

> **فَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَانظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الْمُكَذِّبِينَ** — "so travel through the earth, and see what was the end of those who denied."

Ibn Kathir supplies the link between the two halves of the ayah in three words. Having said that the good end belonged to the earlier believing nations and the ultimate defeat to the disbelievers, he continues: "**This is why** Allah said, *so travel through the earth, and see what was the end of those who denied*."

That "this is why" is the hinge of the whole passage. The command to travel is not a change of subject; it is the proof offered for the claim just made. You have suffered a loss. So did they. And here is how you can check for yourself that a loss is not the ending — go out into the earth and see how it actually finished for those who denied.

Two things are worth feeling in that command.

**It sends you out.** The instruction is to travel through the earth, not merely to sit and reason your way to reassurance. The evidence Allah offers is spread across the world, in the places where earlier peoples lived and ended.

**And it directs you to the *end*.** Not to the middle of the story — to *"what was the end of those who denied."* That is the precise correction a defeated believer needs. Ibn Kathir has just told us that the earlier nations "too suffered losses" and yet "the good end was theirs." A loss, then, is not a verdict. The verdict is the end, and the end is what you are being sent to look at.

The people you are told to look at are named by what they did: *"those who denied."* Not by tribe, not by era — by the act of calling the truth a lie. That is what makes the lesson carry across centuries. The category is old, and Ibn Kathir tells us how it has always closed: "the ultimate defeat was for the disbelievers."

## Ayah 138: three words, and who each is for

> **هَٰذَا بَيَانٌ لِّلنَّاسِ وَهُدًى وَمَوْعِظَةٌ لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ** — "This is an insight to humanity — a guide and a lesson to the God-fearing."

Having pointed to history, Allah now says what this whole disclosure *is*. Ibn Kathir takes the words in turn.

**بَيَانٌ — *bayān*, a plain statement, an exposition — for mankind.** Ibn Kathir explains: "the Qur'an explains the true reality of things and narrates how the previous nations suffered by the hands of their enemies." Two things are being made plain, then. The first is *the true reality of things* — how the world actually is, beneath appearances. The second is the concrete record: what earlier nations went through at the hands of their enemies. The Qur'an is not only stating the principle; it is laying out the cases. And this plain statement is addressed to *mankind* — it is public, offered to all people.

**هُدًى — *hudā*, guidance.** Ibn Kathir first notes why the Qur'an merits the description: "for the Qur'an contains the news of the past." Then comes the turn that matters. The guidance, he says, is "for your hearts." The news of the past is not merely archived information; it is meant to reach the heart and set its direction. The same historical fact that leaves one person merely informed reorients another.

**مَوْعِظَةٌ لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ — *mawʿiẓah*, admonition or instruction, for the *muttaqīn*.** *Muttaqīn* is rendered here as the God-fearing — those who keep a guard between themselves and Allah's displeasure. And Ibn Kathir gives the admonition a very concrete job: it is "to discourage committing the prohibited and forbidden matters." A *mawʿiẓah*, on this reading, is not a lecture that adds new data. It is a word that moves you — that makes you pull back from something Allah has forbidden.

**Do not miss the structure of the ayah.** The plain statement is for mankind at large; the guidance and the admonition are named for the God-fearing. The same passage, the same history — and it lands differently depending on who receives it. Nothing in the text changes. The receiver does.

There is a quiet warning inside that. If a believer reads about the end of those who denied and feels nothing — no reorientation of the heart, no pulling back from the forbidden — then the passage has reached them only as a plain statement, and the two better shares have gone past them.

## Where the passage is heading

Ibn Kathir reads these ayat as the opening of a longer consolation. Immediately after, he says, "Allah comforts the believers" in ayah 139 — telling them not to become weak "because of what you suffered," and assuring them that "the ultimate victory and triumph will be yours, O believers." Ayat 137 and 138 lay the ground for that comfort: losses came to the believing nations before you, the end belonged to them and defeat to those who denied, and this disclosure is given to guide your heart and move your conduct.

## Living it

**Judge by the end, not by the loss you are standing in.** The instruction of ayah 137 is to look at *"what was the end of those who denied."* Ibn Kathir's own framing sets the losses of the earlier believing nations beside the fact that "the good end was theirs." Any reading of events — in our own lives or in the state of the ummah — that takes a present setback as the final verdict is making the very mistake this ayah was revealed to correct.

**Let history be evidence, not entertainment.** Ibn Kathir's comment on *"a plain statement for mankind"* is that the Qur'an "explains the true reality of things and narrates how the previous nations suffered by the hands of their enemies." The stories are given to show you how things really are. Read them for that, not as tales.

**Measure yourself by which of the three words reaches you.** Ask honestly, after reading a passage like this: was that only a plain statement to me, or did it become guidance *for my heart* and an admonition that actually discouraged me from what Allah has prohibited? Ibn Kathir's gloss makes the test concrete — the mark of the *mawʿiẓah* landing is that it turns you away from the forbidden.

**And take your losses as membership, not rejection.** Seventy dead did not mean Allah had abandoned that community. It meant they stood where the nations who followed their Prophets had stood before them — those for whom, as Ibn Kathir says, "the good end was theirs."

passages.title: Do not falter: days alternate and Paradise is not won untested
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are Allah's answer to a defeated, wounded, grieving community. After the losses at Uhud, He forbids His believers two things — collapse of nerve about the future and corrosive sorrow over the past — and then gives them the reasons: their enemies bled too, days of dominance are rotated among people by turns, and Paradise was never going to be handed to anyone untested.

What holds the passage together is a single movement of thought: first the command (139), then the consolation (140), then the wisdom (140–141), then the challenge that turns consolation into responsibility (142–143). Comfort here is never sentimental. It ends by telling the survivors to get back up.

## The moment: the field of Uhud

Ibn Kathir gathers this whole stretch — from ayah 137 through 143 — under one heading, "The Wisdom Behind the Losses Muslims Suffered During Uhud," and notes that the losses included seventy dead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene: the initial success of the Muslim army turned into a defeat in this battle because of some of their own shortcomings; seventy noble Companions gave their lives; and the Prophet ﷺ himself was hurt.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies three causes of the setback, and it is worth noticing that all three are internal:

1. The Muslim archers could not abide by the standing orders the Prophet ﷺ had given them, because a difference of opinion broke out among them — some favoured holding the position they already held, others saw no need to stay there and opted for collecting the spoils with everybody else.
2. The news that the Prophet ﷺ had been martyred on the battlefield weakened their resolve to fight.
3. The disagreement had arisen over something very serious: an explicit command of the Prophet ﷺ, obedience to which was mandatory.

Yet, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, in spite of all this Allah let the balance of the battle tilt in favour of the Muslims and the enemy retreated.

Now picture the mood the verses land in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it plainly: the Muslim fighters were virtually torn apart with wounds; the bodies of their most valiant fighters lay strewn before their eyes; even the Prophet ﷺ had been wounded by a merciless enemy; and on top of the grief was the shock of their own mistakes. They were, it says, "on the horns of a dilemma" — pining over the past, with acute danger that they might become weak in the future, so that the duty of leading the people of the world entrusted to them would be hampered. Ayah 139 is aimed exactly at those two gaps.

## Ayah 139: two prohibitions, one promise, one condition

**"Do not falter and do not grieve."** The two commands are not repetition. Ibn Kathir glosses *wa lā tahinū* — "so do not become weak" — as weakness "because of what you suffered." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the split in time: *do not let weakness or inertia come near you in the future*, and *do not pine over what has gone by*. One prohibition guards the road ahead; the other cuts the rope tying them to the wreckage behind.

That is a striking way to treat people who have just been beaten. Allah does not ask them to feel nothing; He forbids the two responses that would have finished them — the sagging of resolve and the grief that ties a person to a past he cannot change.

**"And you are the uppermost."** Ibn Kathir's comment is short and absolute: "for surely, the ultimate victory and triumph will be yours, O believers." The verse does not say *you will feel better*. It states a settled outcome about the end of the matter, spoken over people who at that moment looked and felt like losers.

**"If you are believers."** The promise carries a condition, and both commentaries take the condition seriously. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as: it is you who shall prevail *if* you hold on to the path of faith and belief, with total confidence in the promises made by Allah, never turning your backs on obedience to the Prophet ﷺ and on jihad in the way of Allah. Supremacy and glory, it says, can be achieved through one and only one basic source — having faith and fulfilling its demands.

And it is careful to spell out that "the demands of Faith" are not only inward. They include the preparations that must be made in view of an impending war: consolidating military power, assembling and readying all relevant hardware, and harnessing all other means to that end — of course, it adds, in proportion to ability and capacity. Faith here is not offered as an alternative to competence; it is what makes competence obligatory.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then stands back and looks at what this verse did in real time: this call of the Qur'an "made broken hearts throb again," and sulking bodies were aglow with a fresh spirit. Just imagine, it says, how Allah groomed the men who carried His message — and how He gave Muslims for all times to come a principle and rule of procedure: never shed tears over dead issues; instead, do all you can to get together the means to strength and power.

## Ayah 140: the wound cuts both ways

**"If a wound touches you, a wound like it has touched the other people."** Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is blunt: if you suffered injuries and some of you were killed, then your enemies also suffered injuries and fatalities. The pain was not one-sided, though from inside it always feels that way.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the arithmetic further, and it is a remarkable piece of consolation. If seventy Muslim men were martyred with many wounded — is it not that these same believers had, a year before, condemned an identical number of their enemies to Hell and wounded many? And in this very battle, initially, many men from the enemy ranks were killed and wounded. The believers were being asked to see the whole ledger, not the page in front of them.

**"Such days We rotate among people."** Ibn Kathir explains that at times — *out of wisdom* — Allah allows the enemy to overcome the believers, although the final good end will be theirs. Note the two words he adds: the rotation is permitted deliberately, and it is wise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the customary practice of Allah in this mortal world: days of hardship and ease, pain and comfort, suffering and peace are caused to occur among people by turns. From that it derives a rule for any community of truth: if a falsely-motivated power succeeds in getting a short-lived upper hand, the group motivated by the truth should not lose heart and conclude that from this point onwards they are always doomed to nothing but defeat. Instead of that negative attitude, they should go about finding out the *causes* of that defeat, and once they have discovered those, take corrective measures and eliminate all possibilities of repeating those mistakes. In the end, the group motivated by the truth shall emerge as the ultimate victor.

Read that against the three causes of Uhud listed above and the point becomes concrete. The Qur'an forbids despair and, in the same breath, forbids the laziness that skips the post-mortem.

## Ayat 140–141: what a defeat was for

The verses then give the purposes behind the reversal, one after another.

**"So that Allah may know those who believe."** Ibn Kathir's rendering carries a gloss inside the wording itself — "and that Allah may know (test) those who believe" — and he reports the meaning from Ibn ʿAbbās: "So that We find out who would be patient while fighting the enemies." The same double rendering, "knows (tests)," returns in ayah 142.

**"And that He may take martyrs from among you."** Ibn Kathir: those who would be killed in Allah's cause and gladly offer their lives seeking His pleasure. The seventy are not presented as a mere cost of the defeat — they are named among its purposes. Allah *took* them; they were not simply lost.

The verse then adds, **"and Allah likes not the wrongdoers"** — a warning set down in the middle of the consolation, so that no one mistakes divine comfort for divine indifference to conduct.

**"And that Allah may test those who believe" (141).** Ibn Kathir gives two ways this works: by forgiving them their sins, if they have any; otherwise, Allah will raise their grades according to the losses they suffered. So the same hardship functions either as a washing or as a promotion. Either way the believer comes out of it ahead of where he went in.

**"And destroy the disbelievers" (141).** Ibn Kathir explains the mechanism rather than just asserting the outcome: it is the conduct of the disbelievers that if they gain the upper hand, they transgress and commit aggression — however, this conduct only leads to "ultimate destruction, extermination, perishing and dying out." Their turn in the rotation is precisely what undoes them. The victory they win becomes the licence for the transgression that finishes them.

Put the two verbs side by side and you have the shape of the passage: the same rotating days that *purify* one group *destroy* the other. The days are identical; what differs is what each people does with them.

## Ayah 142: Paradise was never going to be free

**"Do you think that you will enter Paradise before Allah knows (tests) those of you who will perform Jihad and knows (tests) those who are the patient?"** Ibn Kathir puts the question in the plainest terms: do you think that you will enter Paradise without being tested with warfare and hardships? You will not earn Paradise until you are tested, and thus Allah knows who among you are the ones who struggle and fight in His cause and are patient in the face of the enemy.

He then places the verse alongside others that say the same thing, showing this is a fixed principle and not a one-off rebuke. From Sūrat al-Baqarah: "Or think you that you will enter Paradise without such (trials) as came to those who passed away before you? They were afflicted with severe poverty and ailments and were so shaken…" (2:214). And from the opening of Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt: "Alif Lam Mim. Do people think that they will be left alone because they say: 'We believe,' and will not be tested?" (29:1–2).

Notice that the verse names two qualities, not one: those who perform jihad, and the patient. The first is what a person does; the second is what he endures while doing it — Ibn Kathir joins them in a single phrase, "the ones who struggle and fight in His cause and are patient in the face of the enemy." Uhud tested both, and the verse refuses to let anyone claim Paradise on the strength of an untested profession of faith.

## Ayah 143: "You used to wish for death"

**"You did indeed wish for death before you met it. Now you have seen it openly with your own eyes."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a direct address: O believers, before today you wished that you could meet the enemy and were eager to fight them. What you wished has occurred — so fight them and be patient.

Here the source cites a hadith. In the Two Sahihs it is recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not wish to encounter the enemy, and ask Allah for your well-being. However, if you do encounter them, then observe patience and know that Paradise is under the shade of swords."

The hadith holds two things together that we usually split apart. Never *court* the trial — ask Allah for well-being, because appetite for hardship is not a virtue. But if the trial arrives at your door, do not flinch from it, because the highest reward sits exactly where the danger is.

Ibn Kathir then makes a fine observation about the wording. The verse says "now you have seen it" — of death. But death is not a thing the eye can see. What they saw, he says, was the moment when the swords appeared, the blades were sharpened, the spears crisscrossed and men stood in lines for battle. He identifies this as a figure of speech that mentions imagining what can be felt but not seen. Death had been an idea they longed for from a distance; at Uhud it stood in front of them wearing a face.

## Living it

Read as a whole, the passage asks a believer for four things, and the sources support each one.

**Refuse both collapses.** Do not go weak about what is coming and do not pine over what has gone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this a permanent rule, not merely advice to one army on one day: Muslims should never shed tears over dead issues — instead they should do all they can to get together the means to strength and power.

**Diagnose, don't despair.** When the people of truth are beaten, the instruction is to go looking for the *causes* of that defeat, take corrective measures, and eliminate all possibilities of repeating those mistakes. At Uhud those causes were standing orders not kept, a report of the Prophet's ﷺ death that weakened resolve, and a disagreement over an explicit command of the Prophet ﷺ whose obedience was mandatory. The audit is part of the faith, not a substitute for it.

**Prepare in proportion to your capacity.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists that the demands of faith include real, material readiness — military power consolidated, hardware assembled and made ready, every other means harnessed, in proportion to ability and capacity. Trust in Allah's promise and preparation for His cause are two halves of one obedience.

**Expect the test, don't request it.** Ayah 142 removes the fantasy of an untested Paradise; the hadith in the Two Sahihs removes the opposite error of longing for the encounter. Ask Allah for well-being. And when the day comes anyway, be patient — the rotation of days is in His hand, the purification of the believers is His purpose, and "you are the upper-most, if you are believers."

passages.title: Muhammad is only a messenger; death is decreed
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat were revealed after the Muslims' setback at the battle of Uhud, and they do one thing above all: they pull the believers' faith off the person of the Prophet ﷺ and fasten it back onto Allah, who does not die. Ayah 144 corrects the panic — Muhammad ﷺ is a messenger, and messengers pass on. Ayah 145 removes the fear underneath the panic — no soul dies except by Allah's leave, at an appointed term. Together they say: the thing you dread cannot come early, and when it comes it does not end the religion.

## The rumour on the field of Uhud

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. When the Muslims suffered defeat at Uhud and some of them were killed, Shaytan shouted, "Muhammad has been killed." Ibn Qamiʾah went back to the idolaters and claimed, "I have killed Muhammad." Some of the Muslims believed the rumour. And here is the detail worth pausing on: Ibn Kathir says they claimed this could happen, because Allah had narrated that it had occurred to many Prophets before. So the Muslims' resolve was weakened and they did not actively participate in the battle. This, Ibn Kathir says, is why Allah sent down to His Messenger ﷺ the words of ayah 144.

That is the moment ayah 144 answers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks us to feel what that news did to them before we judge them for it. These were people who, out of unflinching devotion and love for their most dear mentor and the messenger of Allah, had staked everything they had — money, property, children and their very lives — for his sake, considering their sacrifices the most desirable achievement of this mortal life, and proving it by their deeds. Now, mid-battle, with defeat looming after the initial victory and the Muslims losing ground, they hear of the passing of the one who was the very pivot of their struggle and the symbol of all their hopes.

The natural outcome, Maʿārif says, was that a large group of the noble Companions started retreating from the battlefield in a state of confusion. And Maʿārif is careful about how to read that retreat: it was no doubt the result of fleeting confusion and, in the least, without any indication of turning away from Islam.

Not everyone broke. Ibn Kathir preserves a small, blazing exchange: Ibn Abi Najih said that his father said that a man from the Muhajirin passed by an Ansari man who was bleeding during Uhud and said to him, "O fellow! Did you know that Muhammad was killed?" The Ansari man said, "Even if Muhammad was killed, he has indeed conveyed the Message. Therefore, defend your religion." This story was collected by Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bayhaqi in *Dalaʼil An-Nubuwwah*. That wounded man had already understood, on his own, exactly what ayah 144 was about to teach the rest.

## "Muhammad is no more than a messenger"

The phrase is not a diminishment of the Prophet ﷺ. Read it in its own terms: a messenger is one sent with a message, and the message is what endures. Ibn Kathir's gloss is precisely this — he is to deliver Allah's Message and may be killed in the process, just as happened to many Prophets before. The clause "and indeed Messengers have passed away before him" is not new information; it is a reminder that the pattern the Companions half-remembered in their panic is in fact the norm.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the principle at stake, and calls it bipolar — two poles that must both be held at once.
