**The first pole:** it must be fully realized that Islam gives great importance to the unique respect and love given to the Holy Prophet ﷺ, so much so that it has been made an integral part of faith, and the slightest deviation or weakness in this delicate matter has been equated with straight kufr (disbelief).

**The second pole:** at the same time, Muslims must not fall prey to the same disease that afflicted the Nazarenes and Christians, who exaggerated the respect and love due to Sayyidna ʿIsa (peace be upon him) by taking it to the extremes, invested him with partnership in the divinity of Allah Almighty, and started to worship him.

Ayah 144 is the sentence that holds both. It does not ask you to love him less. It tells you what he *is* — Allah's messenger — so that your love has the right shape and does not slide into worship. That is why Maʿārif can say there was a secret behind the whole crisis: behind the temporary debacle, the wounding of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, the spreading of the news that he had passed away, and some Companions losing heart because of it — that secret was nothing but that Muslims should come to understand this basic principle and become practically firm when the challenge comes.

Maʿārif also states plainly what the ayah is warning the Muslims of: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is going to leave this mortal world one day or another, and that they must hold on to faith firmly after him as well, in the same measure as they did during his blessed times.

## "Will you then turn back on your heels?"

The question is put with a rebuke in it. Allah said this, Ibn Kathir notes, while chastising those who became weak. And Ibn Kathir does not soften what "turn back on your heels" means here: it means to become disbelievers.

This is severe language for what was, in fact, a moment of confused retreat. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the register is set so high. The truth of the matter, it says, was that Allah Almighty intended to mould into a group the Companions of His Messenger who were pious and angelic and who could become role models for the whole world. It was for this reason that an ordinary mistake by them was considered to be very serious. Therefore they were addressed over their retreat from the battlefield in a fashion similar to what it would have been had they deserted the fold of Islam — not because they had, but because that is the standard to which they were being raised. And with this expressing of wrath came the warning that all obligations of faith, worship and jihad are for Allah, who is Living and Eternal.

**"And whoever turns back on his heels can never harm Allah at all."** This dissolves the whole self-important logic of desertion. Allah is not diminished by your leaving. The loss is entirely yours.

**"And Allah shall soon reward the grateful."** Ibn Kathir identifies exactly who these grateful ones are: those who obeyed Allah, defended His religion, and followed His Messenger ﷺ — *whether he was alive or dead*. Notice too that the same refrain, "the grateful," closes ayah 145 as well, with the wording shifted from "Allah will reward" to "We shall reward."

## Ayah 145: the appointed term

"No soul can ever die without Allah's Will at the destined time." Ibn Kathir: no one dies except by Allah's decision, after he has finished the term that Allah has destined for him. That is what *kitāban muʼajjalan*, "at an appointed term," is pointing to. Ibn Kathir places two other ayat beside it: "And no aged man is granted a length of life nor is a part cut off from his life, but it is in a Book" (35:11), and "He it is Who has created you from clay, and then has decreed a stated term for you to die; and there is with Him another determined term for you to be resurrected" (6:2).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the practical upshot as plainly as it can be stated: in order to teach steadfastness under calamities and hardships, it has been said that the death of every human being lies written with Allah Almighty — fixed is its date, the day and the time. Death cannot come to take one away before that, nor could one continue to live after that. **If so, getting scared about a certain death means nothing.**

Ibn Kathir says the ayah "encourages cowards to participate in battle," because doing so, or avoiding battle, neither decreases nor increases the life term. And he gives an example of a man who took the ayah at its word. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that Habib bin Suhban said that a Muslim man, Hujr bin ʿAdi, said in a battle: "What prevents you from crossing this river to the enemy? *And no person can ever die except by Allah's leave and at an appointed term?*" He then crossed the Euphrates riding his horse, and when he did, the Muslims followed him. When the enemy saw them, they started shouting, "*Diwan*" — Persian for "crazy" — and they ran away.

Understand what this ayah is doing to a frightened heart. It does not promise you will survive. It tells you, in Ibn Kathir's terms, that going into battle or staying out of it changes nothing about the term — because the term belongs to Allah's decision, not to the enemy's.

## Two intentions, two returns

"And whoever seeks the return in this world, We shall give him out of it; and whoever seeks the return in the Hereafter, We shall give him out of it."

Ibn Kathir's reading turns on an asymmetry the English can hide. Whoever works for the sake of this life will only earn what Allah decides he will earn — **however, he will not have a share in the Hereafter.** Whoever works for the sake of the Hereafter, Allah will give him a share in the Hereafter, *along with* what He decides for him in this life. He supports this with 42:20 — "Whosoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We give him increase in his reward, and whosoever desires the reward of this world, We give him thereof, and he has no portion in the Hereafter" — and with 17:18–19, where the one who desires the quick-passing world is readily granted what Allah wills and then has Hell appointed for him, while the one who desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the necessary effort while a believer has his striving appreciated.

On this reading, the deciding factor is not the outward work but what the worker is after.

**Why is this here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties it to one of the apparent causes of the disaster. The Companions posted by the Holy Prophet ﷺ as guards on the hill at the rear saw that fellow Muslims were busy collecting spoils following the initial victory. Some of them started thinking that, with the victory won, there was no need for them to stay at their post — so why should they too not go in and take part in the collection? They moved away from where they were ordered to be. That movement is what the close of ayah 145 touches.

And Maʿārif immediately protects them from being misread — a point of real fairness. In its real sense, the collection of spoils is not the same as the unabashed pursuit of the material which the Sharīʿah of Islam condemns; on the contrary, collecting spoils, depositing them in safe custody and spending them where they must be spent is all a part of jihad, and for that matter an act of worship. Moreover, those Companions would have been entitled to receive their due share of the spoils under Islamic Law even if they had not actively participated in the collection. **Therefore, it cannot be said that these blessed Companions abandoned their post of duty under the temptation of worldly gains.** Rather, as with ayah 144, even minor mistakes made by major people draw more attention. Granted that their collecting of spoils could be related to the desire for worldly gain, at the most in some minor way — and equally granted the possibility that this small connection had not influenced their hearts — yet it was in order to take the morals of the noble Companions to the highest possible level that this act was identified as "the seeking of return in this world," so that not even the tiniest speck of worldly temptation could find its way into their hearts.

Then the refrain again: **"And We shall soon reward the grateful."** Ibn Kathir: We shall award them with Our favour and mercy in this life and the Hereafter, according to the degree of their appreciation of Allah and their good deeds.

## The day the ayah came true

Ibn Kathir notes that the Sahih, Musnad and Sunan collections gathered various chains of narration stating that Abu Bakr recited this ayah when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died.

Al-Bukhari recorded that ʿAʼishah said that Abu Bakr came riding his horse from his dwelling in As-Sunh. He dismounted, entered the Masjid and did not speak to anyone until he came to her in her room and went directly to the Prophet ﷺ, who was covered with a marked blanket. Abu Bakr uncovered his face, knelt down and kissed him, then started weeping and proclaimed: "My father and my mother be sacrificed for you! Allah will not combine two deaths on you. You have died the death which was written for you." Listen to that last phrase — *the death which was written for you.* That is ayah 145 in the mouth of a grieving friend.

Then, as Ibn Kathir relates from Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Bakr came out while ʿUmar was addressing the people. Abu Bakr told him to sit down, but ʿUmar refused; the people attended to Abu Bakr and left ʿUmar. And Abu Bakr said: "To proceed — whoever among you worshipped Muhammad, then Muhammad is dead, but whoever worshipped Allah, Allah is alive and will never die." And he recited ayah 144.

The narrator added: "By Allah, it was as if the people never knew that Allah had revealed this verse before until Abu Bakr recited it, and then whoever heard it started reciting it." Saʿid bin Al-Musayyib said that ʿUmar said: "By Allah! When I heard Abu Bakr recite this ayah, my feet could not hold me, and I fell to the ground."

Abu Bakr's sentence is the creed of these two ayat compressed to its core: **Allah is alive and will never die.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the whole Uhud episode in exactly this light. The injury caused to the Holy Prophet ﷺ during that temporary setback and the news of his passing away on the battlefield were a concealed divine arrangement, through which all that could happen to the noble Companions after him was revealed during his very lifetime, so that any slip in their conduct could be corrected in his very words — ensuring that these ardent lovers and devotees of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not lose their coolness under exacting conditions, especially when his passing actually took place. This is exactly what happened later, when the noble Companions, even the greatest among them, were overwhelmed with the severest emotional shock at the time of his passing. At that juncture it was Sayyidna Abu Bakr who used the authority of Qurʼanic ayat such as these to explain the situation to them, as a result of which all of them were able to accept the truth and control their emotions.

## Living it

**Attach yourself to Allah, not only to the people who bring the religion to you.** Teachers, scholars, parents — all of them pass on, as the messengers before him passed on. Maʿārif's two poles apply here: give the Prophet ﷺ the unique respect and love that faith requires, and keep the object of worship unmistakable.

**Measure your faith by what survives loss.** Ibn Kathir defines the grateful as those who obeyed Allah, defended His religion and followed His Messenger ﷺ whether he was alive or dead. Grief is allowed — Abu Bakr wept over that blessed face, and ʿUmar's legs gave way beneath him. Desertion is not.

**Let the fixed term free you, not paralyse you.** Hujr bin ʿAdi did not use the appointed term as an excuse to sit still; he used it to cross the river. As Ibn Kathir puts it, going into battle or avoiding it neither decreases nor increases the life term.

**Guard your post, and guard your intention while you stand there.** The guards on the hill left not through cowardice but through a reasonable-sounding conclusion that the job was finished — and Maʿārif insists they were not chasing worldly gain. Yet ayah 145 still puts the question underneath every action: which of the two returns am I actually working for?

passages.title: Prophets' devoted followers who never faltered
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** after the shock of Uhud, Allah turns the believers' eyes to earlier generations — the devoted followers who fought alongside their prophets, who did not collapse when disaster struck or when their prophet himself was taken, and whose only recorded speech was a prayer. Ayah 146 describes what they refused to do, ayah 147 records what they said, and ayah 148 records what Allah gave them. Three ayat, one arc: **steadfastness, supplication, reward.**

## The moment behind the words

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. When the Muslims suffered defeat at Uhud and some of them were killed, Shaytan shouted, "Muhammad has been killed." Ibn Qamiʼah went back to the idolaters and claimed, "I have killed Muhammad." Some of the Muslims believed the rumour and thought the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been killed — reasoning that this *could* happen, since Allah had narrated that it had occurred to many prophets before. Ibn Kathir says the result was exactly what you would expect: the Muslims' resolve was weakened and they did not actively participate in the battle.

Not everyone broke. Ibn Kathir relates that Ibn Abi Najih said that his father said that during Uhud a man from the Muhajirin passed by an Ansari man who was bleeding and said to him, "O fellow! Did you know that Muhammad was killed?" The Ansari man answered: "Even if Muhammad was killed, he has indeed conveyed the Message. Therefore, defend your religion." Ibn Kathir notes that this story was collected by Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bayhaqi in *Dalaʼil An-Nubuwwah*.

That man's answer is, in essence, the whole of our passage. And it is the answer Allah Himself gives in the ayat immediately before ours (3:144–145): the Messenger ﷺ is a Messenger, messengers have passed away before him, and no person can ever die except by Allah's leave and at an appointed term. Then — as Ibn Kathir puts it — "Allah then comforts the believers because of what they suffered in Uhud" with ayah 146.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the same link: the previous ayat admonished the Muslims for some of their shortcomings during the battle of Uhud; these ayat now "cite examples set by men of Allah from earlier communities showing how steadfast they were on the battlefield, something which should be emulated by the present addressees." So this is not history for its own sake. It is a mirror held up to a shaken community: *this is what the believers before you did.*

## What exactly is ayah 146 describing?

The Arabic — *wa ka-ayyin min nabiyyin qātala maʿahu ribbiyyūna kathīr* — is compact, and the classical scholars read it in more than one way. Ibn Kathir lays the views out rather than flattening them into one:

- **First view:** it means that many prophets *and* their companions were killed in earlier times. This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir.
- **Second view:** it means that many prophets witnessed their companions' death before their eyes.
- **Third view:** Ibn Ishaq, in his *Sirah*, explained it as: "Many a Prophet was killed, and he had many companions whose resolve did not weaken after their Prophet died, and they did not become feeble in the face of the enemy. What they suffered in Jihad in Allah's cause and for the sake of their religion did not make them lose heart. This is patience — *and Allah loves the patient*." Ibn Kathir reports that As-Suhayli agreed with this explanation and defended it vigorously, and that it is supported by Allah's words *maʿahu ribbiyyūna kathīr* ("and along with him many Ribbiyyun"). In his book about the battles, Al-Amawi mentioned only this explanation.

Notice why that third reading lands so hard on a Muslim who has just heard the rumour that the Prophet ﷺ is dead. It says: *this has happened before, and the believers of before did not fall apart.* The comfort and the correction arrive in the same sentence.

## Who are the *Ribbiyyūn*?

This is the word the passage turns on, and the sources give it real depth.

**Its root.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *Ribbiyyūn* as a derivation from *Rabb* (Lord) — formed like *Rabbānī* — meaning "of the Rabb," of the Lord; which is why the translation there renders it *men of Allah*. Citing *Ruh al-Maʿani*, it notes that the use of the vowel sound "i" in place of "a" here is irregular. Some commentators, it adds, take *Ribbiyyūn* to mean "many groups," deriving it from the word *Ribbah*, which means "the group."

**How the early authorities read it.** Ibn Kathir gathers them:

- Sufyan Ath-Thawri reported that **Ibn Masʿud** said *ribbiyyūna kathīr* means **thousands**.
- **Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, As-Suddi, Ar-Rabiʿ and ʿAtaʼ Al-Khurasani** said the word means **"large bands."**
- ʿAbdur-Razzaq narrated that Maʿmar said that **Al-Hasan** said it means **many scholars** — and he also said that it means **patient and pious scholars.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same from Ibn ʿAbbas and Hasan al-Basri, that the *Ribbiyyūn* here are the *ʿulamaʼ* (religious scholars) and *fuqahaʼ* (jurists), citing *Ruh al-Maʿani*.

Hold those together and the picture is striking. These were not a handful of heroes. They were **thousands**, in **large bands** — and on another reading, they were the people of knowledge: the scholars and jurists. Learning did not keep them off the field; it put them on it. And the name itself ties them back to *ar-Rabb*: they are named for their Lord.

## The three things they never did

The heart of ayah 146 is a triple denial: *fa-mā wahanū … wa mā ḍaʿufū … wa mā istakānū*. Each verb does distinct work.

**1. *Wahanū* — they did not lose heart.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it to *wahn* and glosses it as "to lose heart under suffering" or "wilt under pressure." This is the *inner* collapse — the morale that drains out of a person when the blow lands. And the ayah specifies what they endured: *for that which befell them **in Allah's way***. It is not that nothing hurt them. It is that the hurt did not hollow them out.

**2. *Ḍaʿufū* — they did not weaken.** Qatadah and Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas explained this to mean: they did not weaken **after their Prophet was killed.** That is precisely the scenario the rumour at Uhud had just placed in front of the Muslims.

**3. *Istakānū* — they did not degrade themselves.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Baydawi, derives it from *istakānah*: "to be subdued and rendered weak and immobile." Ibn Kathir gives the range of the Salaf: it means they did not revert from the true guidance and religion — "rather, they fought on the path that Allah's Prophet fought on until they met Allah." Ibn ʿAbbas said it means they did not become humiliated; As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said it means they did not give in to the enemy.

So the sequence runs from inside outwards: the heart did not sink, the strength did not fail, and they neither bent before the enemy nor bent their religion to survive.

Then the seal: **"And Allah loves the patient"** (*wa-Llāhu yuḥibbu ṣ-ṣābirīn*). Ibn Ishaq's comment is the key to it — after describing everything they bore, he says simply: **"This is patience."** *Sabr* here is not passive endurance in a corner; it is holding your ground under loss — and that is what the ayah says Allah loves.

## "And all they said was…"

Ayah 147 is one of the most humbling sentences in the Qurʼan. After all that endurance, Allah reports their speech — and it contains no boast, no complaint, no accounting of their own sacrifice. *Wa mā kāna qawlahum illā an qālū* — "and they said nothing but": **"Our Lord! Forgive us our sins and our transgressions, establish our feet firmly, and give us victory over the disbelieving folk."** Ibn Kathir adds a small, powerful detail: this was the statement that they *kept repeating*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān breaks the prayer into four requests. These are people who, "inspite of their own sacrificing conduct, kept praying to Allah Almighty to":

1. Forgive their **past sins**;
2. Condone any **shortcomings that may have crept in during their present efforts** in Allah's way;
3. **Enable them to remain steadfast** — "establish our feet firmly";
4. **Make them prevail** over enemies.

Look at the order. Victory is asked for **last**. Two requests for forgiveness come **first**, then steadfastness, and only then the outcome. These are people in the thick of striving in Allah's cause whose opening word is *ighfir lanā* — forgive us.

## What their prayer asks of us

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out three implications, and they are the practical heart of the passage.

**Never be proud of a good deed.** No matter how great the accomplishment or how exacting the struggle in the way of Allah, a believer simply does not have the right to pat himself on the back — because his very accomplishment of a good deed is, in all reality, the direct outcome of nothing but the grace and mercy of Allah Almighty, without which no good deed can even issue forth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith here — it does not name a collection at this point, so we can convey only its meaning: *had it not been for the grace and mercy of Allah, we would not have received guidance to the straight path, nor would we have been able to pay zakah and perform salah.*

**Seek forgiveness even in the middle of the good deed.** It is not within one's control to perform a deed exactly in accordance with the demands of the supreme magnificence of the One who holds the reins of Creation and Command in His hands. However hard one tries, falling short is inevitable, "especially when it comes to doing things as is the due and right of Allah." Therefore, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, seeking forgiveness is necessary *during the very course* of such a deed. That is exactly the second phrase of their prayer — forgiveness sought for shortcomings in the very struggle they were still in the middle of.

**Pray for steadfastness, because continuity is not yours to guarantee.** Who can say for sure that he will be given the ability to go on doing his good deed in the future just as he is doing it now? It is all a matter of *tawfīq* — the God-given ability to perform what is good. So we repent over any shortcomings in what we are doing in the present and pray that Allah makes us steadfast and persistent in the future. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that for a true Muslim this prayer "should become his second nature."

And one further observation from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties the prayer straight back to Uhud: the request for forgiveness of **past** sins, appearing first, is "a subtle hint to the fact that pain caused or defeat suffered in this mortal life is, more than often, a reflection of one's past sins which can be cured through repentance and seeking of forgiveness." A community that had just tasted defeat is being shown where the real repair begins — with *istighfār*.

## The two rewards (ayah 148)

*Fa-ātāhumu-Llāhu thawāba d-dunyā wa ḥusna thawābi l-ākhirah.*

Ibn Kathir explains **"the reward of this world"** as **victory, triumph and the good end** — and **"the excellent reward of the Hereafter"** as *added to* the gains in this life. Not one instead of the other: both.

That matches what Allah says in ayah 145, just before: whoever desires a reward in the world will be given of it, and whoever desires a reward in the Hereafter will be given thereof. Ibn Kathir's comment there is exact: whoever works for the sake of this life will only earn what Allah decides he will earn, and will have no share in the Hereafter; **whoever works for the sake of the Hereafter, Allah will give him a share in the Hereafter, along with what He decides for him in this life.** Ayah 148 shows that pattern fulfilled — both rewards together.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a single added word. Allah does not say merely "the reward of the Hereafter" but *ḥusn* — beauty, the better. Right here in this mortal world, Allah gave them ultimate supremacy over the enemies and granted them success in their mission; then comes the reward in the Hereafter, which "is certainly the real one, an ideal state of peace and happiness which will never fade out." That one word marks the difference between a reward that ends and a reward that does not.

The passage then closes as ayah 146 closed — with Allah's love: **"And Allah loves the good-doers"** (*al-muḥsinīn*). Ayah 146 sealed their endurance with His love for the patient; ayah 148 seals their reward with His love for the good-doers.

## Carrying it

For a believer reading this after a defeat — personal or communal — the passage offers a sequence rather than a slogan:

- **Expect the blow, and refuse the three collapses.** Do not lose heart inwardly, do not weaken in effort, do not degrade yourself by surrendering your religion. What befalls you "in Allah's way" is not evidence that you were wrong to be on that path.
- **Do not let the loss of a leader become the loss of the mission.** As the Ansari man said at Uhud while he was bleeding: the Message has been conveyed — so defend your religion.
- **Let your speech in hardship be a prayer, and let it open with forgiveness rather than grievance.** Ask, before victory, for what makes you fit for victory.
- **Keep repeating it.** Ibn Kathir's detail — that this prayer was the statement they *kept repeating* — is the model. Their steadfastness was not one heroic moment; it was a sentence they lived inside.

passages.title: Obeying disbelievers turns you back on your heels
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat are Allah's answer to a whisper that went around Madinah in the worst hour of the battle of Uhud. The Muslims had been thrown back, a rumour spread that the Prophet ﷺ had been killed, and voices began suggesting that the sensible thing now was to give up and go back. Ayah 149 names that advice for what it is — a road back to ruin. Ayah 150 replaces the false patron with the true One: *bal Allāhu mawlākum* — "Rather, Allah is your Guardian." Ayah 151 then turns the whole scene around and announces what Allah will do to the very enemy who looked, that afternoon, like the winner.

The three hold together as one movement: **a warning about whose word you take, a correction about whose help you rely on, and a promise about how the contest actually ends.**

---

## The moment behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene plainly. When the Muslims suffered their temporary setback at Uhud and rumours circulated that the Prophet ﷺ had been martyred, the hypocrites saw their opening. Under the cover of a battle that seemed nearly lost, they said to the Muslims: *now that the Prophet ﷺ is no longer with us, why not go back to our old faith and be rid of all this conflict?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments on how ugly this conduct was and how thoroughly it exposed them as enemies rather than well-wishers.

That is the "advice" ayah 149 is answering. It arrives dressed as pragmatism — *end the trouble, return to how things were* — and it is offered at the exact moment when a person is least able to think clearly.

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on this passage by saying that Allah is warning His believing servants against obeying the disbelievers and the hypocrites, because such obedience leads to utter destruction in this life and in the Hereafter. Note that he includes both groups: the open enemy and the one embedded in the community. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the contrast with what came just before — earlier ayat instructed the believers to follow the men of Allah; here the instruction is not to act on the advice of hypocrites and anti-Islam people, but to remain on guard against them. The believer is not left without counsel; he is told where to take it from.

**How the day had unfolded.** Ibn Kathir preserves the account of Al-Barāʾ, recorded by Al-Bukhari. The Prophet ﷺ placed ʿAbdullah bin Jubayr over the archers with a clear order: hold your position — if you see us defeating them do not leave it, and if you see them defeating us do not come to our aid. The idolaters broke and fled. The archers saw the fleeing and called out, "The booty, the booty!" ʿAbdullah bin Jubayr reminded them of the command; they would not listen. When they left their post, the Muslims were overrun and seventy of them were killed. Ibn Kathir also cites a narration of Muhammad bin Ishaq, reporting from ʿAbdullah bin Az-Zubayr, from Az-Zubayr bin Al-ʿAwwām, describing it from inside the moment: victory was within arm's reach, the archers came down off the mount for the spoils, the rear lines were left uncovered, the enemy horsemen took the chance and attacked from behind — and then a person shouted that Muhammad had been killed.

That shout is where our passage begins. A community that has just lost seventy of its men, that believes its Prophet ﷺ may be dead, is precisely the community to whom someone will say: *be reasonable, go back.*

---

## Ayah 149: "back on your heels"

The threat is not stated as *they will kill you* or *they will defeat you*. It is: **"they will send you back on your heels, and you will turn back as losers."**

The image is of a person who has been walking forward and is now reversed — retreating over ground already covered, undoing the journey step by step. Ibn Kathir's rendering makes explicit what the turning back is *from*: "you will turn back (from faith) as losers." The loss is not territory or a battle. It is the whole of what was gained.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is especially valuable here, because it explains the *mechanism*. The real objective of anti-Islam people, it says, is to disengage Muslims from their faith through engineered suspicion — sometimes overtly, but also covertly, the covert method being designed and implemented so as to gradually decrease the love and honour of Islam from their hearts, resulting in a reversal of their position. Two things follow from that:

**First, the harm is calibrated to be slow.** No one is asked to abandon faith in a single step. The heels move backwards one at a time. What is being eroded is not doctrine first but *love and honour* — the warmth a believer feels toward his religion. Once that has drained away, the formal abandonment is only paperwork.

**Second, this yields a test you can actually apply.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes: those aiming to push the Muslims into a state of loss cannot be their friends, even if they claim to be. The claim is not the evidence. The direction they are moving you is the evidence.

The ayah says "if you *obey*" — not *if you speak to them*, or *if you live among them*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies the three things the believers were told to withhold: do not listen to such enemies, do not make them a party to the community's own consultations, and do not follow any advice they give. It is a warning about the chain of command inside your own heart — whose voice gets to move your feet.

---

## Ayah 150: "Rather — Allah is your Guardian"

Ayah 150 opens with *bal* — "rather," "no indeed." It is a word of correction: it snatches away the sentence someone else was in the middle of and puts the truth in its place. *You have no patron now that the Prophet ﷺ is gone* — **rather, Allah is your mawlā.**

*Mawlā* is rendered in our translation as "Guardian," and by Ibn Kathir as "protector." It is a word for the one who has charge of you, who stands over your affair and to whom you belong. Ibn Kathir explains that in this ayah Allah is commanding the believers to obey Him, to take Him as their protector, to seek His aid and to trust in Him. The passage does not merely forbid a bad alliance; it names the alternative. A heart that has been told only *not* to lean somewhere will lean anyway.

Then: *wa huwa khayr an-nāṣirīn* — "and He is the best of helpers." A superlative among helpers. It concedes the existence of other helpers and settles the ranking. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the practical edge of this: the Muslims are to place their trust in Allah and rely on His help alone, and even if their antagonists come up with plans of help, the Muslims should not go by these against the injunctions of Allah and the Messenger ﷺ. Help that costs you your obedience is not help. It is the price of the retreat described in ayah 149, paid in instalments.

**The word on the battlefield itself.** In the hadith of Al-Barāʾ recorded by Al-Bukhari, after the rout Abu Sufyan called out over the field, "O Hubal, be high!" The Prophet ﷺ told the Companions to answer him back, and when they asked what to say, he taught them the words: "Allah is Higher and more Sublime." Abu Sufyan then boasted, "We have the (idol) Al-ʿUzza, and you have no ʿUzza." Again the Prophet ﷺ told them to answer him back, and again he gave them the words: **"Allah is our protector and you have no protector."**

So on the day itself, from the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ, the answer to the enemy's triumph was the very truth ayah 150 states. Abu Sufyan measured the day by the field — his boast, in the same narration, was that their victory that day was vengeance for the Muslims' victory in the battle of Badr. The believers were taught to measure it by *whose* they were.

---

## Ayah 151: "We shall cast terror into their hearts"

Ayah 150 said Allah is the best of helpers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that what follows is a recounting of some of that help in action. Ayah 151 is the first instalment.

**"We shall cast."** The verb is in the future. This was revealed to people who had just been beaten. Nothing on the ground yet corresponded to it. Ibn Kathir describes it as good news: Allah conveys that He will put fear of the Muslims, and feelings of subordination to the Muslims, in the hearts of their disbelieving enemies, because of their Kufr and Shirk.

Notice where the divine act lands: not on their armies, their numbers, or their supply lines, but **in their hearts** — in the one place no Muslim sword had reached. Whatever advantage the enemy held on the field that day is left untouched by this ayah. What is touched is the enemy's nerve.

**How it actually happened.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the background of the promise. On the authority of Baydawi, the disbelievers of Arabia marched back to Makkah after Uhud without any obvious reason, in spite of the defeat that had overtaken the Muslims. After covering a certain distance on the road, they awoke to their folly. But when they thought of marching back to Madinah, Allah filled their hearts with such awe and fear that they could not muster the courage to do so. The most they could manage was to hire a Madinah-bound villager to go and tell the Muslims that they were coming back. The whole affair came to the knowledge of the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah through revelation, and he marched out to Hamrāʾ al-Asad to apprehend them — but they had already fled from there. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that this was the background in which the present ayah was revealed.

Read the promise against that: an enemy that had won the field and could not make itself walk back onto it.

**Why: "because they joined others in worship with Allah, for which He sent no authority."** The word is *sulṭān*, rendered "authority." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it includes all revealed or rational bases of their position. So the indictment is total. Shirk — assigning to others a share in what belongs to Allah alone — has no scripture behind it and no argument behind it. It stands on nothing.

And this is why the terror is *just*, not merely tactical. A heart built on nothing is a heart with nothing under it. The fear Allah casts is, in a sense, the truth of their position finally reaching them. Abu Sufyan's own cry, "O Hubal, be high!", was a summons to exactly what this ayah says Allah sent down no authority for.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here what the Two Sahihs record from Jābir bin ʿAbdullah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was given five things that no other Prophet before me was given. I was aided with fear the distance of one month, the earth was made a Masjid and clean place for me, I was allowed war booty, I was given the Intercession, and Prophets used to be sent to their people, but I was sent to all mankind particularly." The first of the five is precisely the promise of ayah 151, established as a standing gift to the Prophet ﷺ, not a one-off relief after a single battle. ("Masjid" here means a place of prayer; "clean place" means a means of purification, as in tayammum.)

**The two abodes.** The ayah closes past this world: "their abode will be the Fire and how evil is the abode of the wrongdoers." Ibn Kathir notes that alongside the fear placed in their hearts, Allah has prepared torment and punishment for them in the Hereafter. So the passage answers the taunt on two levels. Abu Sufyan's claim in the same narration — that in war the victory is always undecided and is shared in turns by the belligerents — is a true statement about afternoons. It says nothing about destinations.

---

## Living it

**Consider the source, not the tone.** The counsel in ayah 149 came wrapped in concern — *end the conflict, spare yourselves*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's test is about outcome, not manner: someone aiming to push you into a state of loss is not your friend, whatever he claims.

**Watch for the slow reversal.** The danger the ayah names is not only a dramatic renunciation but heels moving backwards — love and honour for Islam gradually decreasing in the heart until the position has reversed. Ask of an influence not "is this haram?" but "which way is it walking me?"

**Guard the room where decisions are made.** The instruction was not only to refuse their advice but to keep them out of the community's consultations. Who you deliberate with shapes what you conclude.

**Replace, don't just refuse.** Ayah 150 does not leave a vacuum. It hands the believer a Guardian, and Ibn Kathir spells out the response it calls for: obey Him, take Him as your protector, seek His aid, and trust in Him.

**Judge by the promise, not by the afternoon.** Ayah 151 was given to people who had just been defeated, and it was fulfilled on a road out of Makkah where a victorious army lost its nerve. The believer's calculation of who is winning has to include what Allah has undertaken to do — including in places, like the enemy's heart, where no human effort reaches.

passages.title: The rout at Uhud and Allah's pardon after it
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take the believers back into the worst hours of the battle of Uhud — the moment victory turned into rout — and walk them through it slowly. What holds ayat 152–155 together is one movement: **promise fulfilled → order disobeyed → defeat and grief → mercy sent down → pardon announced.** The passage opens with "Allah did indeed fulfill His promise to you" (152) and closes with "Allah, indeed, has forgiven them" (155). Everything painful sits between those two statements.

## The day, as the sources tell it

Al-Bukhari recorded that Al-Bara' said: at Uhud the Prophet ﷺ appointed 'Abdullah bin Jubayr as commander of the archers and instructed them, "Retain your position, and if you see that we have defeated them, do not abandon your positions. If you see that they defeated us, do not rush to help us." The instruction was unconditional — hold this ground whichever way the battle goes.

At first the battle went beautifully. Al-Bara' continues: "The disbelievers gave flight when we met them, and we saw their women fleeing up the mountain." Then the archers said, "The booty, the booty!" 'Abdullah bin Jubayr told them, "Allah's Messenger ﷺ commanded me not to allow you to abandon your position." In Al-Bara's words: "They refused to listen, and when they left their position, Muslims were defeated and seventy of them were killed."

A separate report preserves how that hour looked from inside the ranks. Muhammad bin Ishaq said that 'Abdullah bin Az-Zubayr narrated that Az-Zubayr bin Al-'Awwam said that at the moment the enemy broke, "there was no big or small effort separating us from capturing them." Then, he says, the archers went down the mount seeking to collect the booty: "They uncovered our back lines to the horsemen of the disbelievers, who took the chance and attacked us from behind. Then a person shouted, 'Muhammad has been killed.' So we pulled back, and the disbelievers followed us."

Every phrase of ayah 152 maps onto a day like that.

## Ayah 152, phrase by phrase

**"Allah did indeed fulfill His promise to you"** — Ibn Kathir: this refers to *the beginning of the day of Uhud*. Note what is established before any rebuke: the failure was never on Allah's side.

**"when you were killing them (taḥussūnahum) with His permission"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this as slaying your enemies, and "with His permission" as "He allowed you to do that against them." Even their strength in that opening hour was borrowed, not owned.

**"until when you *fashiltum*"** — Ibn Jurayj said that Ibn 'Abbas said *fashiltum* means **"lost courage."** The turn begins not with the enemy's strength but inside the believers' own chests.

**"and fell to disputing about the order, and disobeyed"** — Ibn Kathir names it: "such as the mistake made by the archers," the argument on the hilltop over whether the order still bound them.

**"after He showed you what you love"** — that is, victory over the disbelievers. The disobedience came *after* the gift, which makes it heavier, not lighter.

**"Among you are some that desire this world and some that desire the Hereafter"** — Ibn Kathir identifies the first group as "those who sought to collect the booty when they saw the enemy being defeated." Then, **"He made you flee from them, that He might test you":** Allah "gave them the upper hand to try and test you, O believers."

**"But surely, He forgave you, and Allah is Most Gracious to the believers."** Ibn Kathir says He forgave the error they committed — adding "and Allah knows best" — because the idolaters were many and well supplied while the Muslims had few men and few supplies.

### "Some desire this world" — how Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it

What made these Companions "seekers of the mundane"? Only the intention to go and collect spoils — and their due share of it would have been *exactly the same* whether they collected it or held their post. So the act in itself "cannot be classed as the unqualified pursuit of the material." Yet, given how human nature works, the thought of spoils entering their hearts then "is not totally unimaginable." Maʿārif's conclusion is striking: Allah very much likes to see the hearts of His Messenger's Companions clean and untouched "even by the remotest idea of any tilt towards material possession" — and so this faint inclination is itself equated with *seeking of the mundane*. The severity of the wording measures how high their standard was, not how far they had fallen.

## Ayah 153: running, and the voice behind you

**"When you were going up (tuṣʿidūna)"** — Al-Hasan and Qatadah said this means "go up the mountain."

**"without even casting a side glance at anyone"** — Ibn Kathir: "you did not glance at anyone else due to shock, fear and fright." The tunnel vision of terror.

**"and the Messenger was in your rear calling you back"** — "for you left him behind you, while he was calling you to stop fleeing from the enemy and to return and fight." As-Suddi describes it: some Muslims ran away to Al-Madinah, some went up Mount Uhud to a rock and stood on it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept heralding, **"Come to me, O servants of Allah! Come to me, O servants of Allah!"** Ibn Kathir notes that similar was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the painful question: how could they not return when *he* was calling? It notes that according to hadith narrations, the Muslims heard the call of Sayyidna Ka'b ibn Malik and reassembled. The author of Ruh al-Ma'ani resolves this by saying the Messenger's ﷺ own call was simply not heard by them. Maulana Ashraf Thanavi in Bayan al-Qur'an adds that the real cause of the confusion was the news that the Prophet ﷺ had fallen a martyr; his call carried no refutation of that news, and even if his voice reached them, the possibility remains that it was not *recognised* — whereas Ka'b's call included the fact that he ﷺ was alive. Thanavi still concedes the rebuke: had they stayed unagitated and firm, they could have recognised the calling voice.

### Those who did not run

Al-Bukhari recorded that Qays bin Abi Hazim said he saw Talhah's hand paralysed, "because he shielded the Prophet ﷺ with it." In the Two Sahihs, Abu 'Uthman An-Nahdi said that on that day only Talhah bin 'Ubaydullah and Sa'd remained with the Prophet ﷺ.

Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib said, "I heard Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas saying, 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave me arrows from his quiver on the day of Uhud and said, **"Shoot, may I sacrifice my father and mother for you."**'" Al-Bukhari also collected this hadith. And the Two Sahihs recorded that Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas said he saw two men in white, one to the Prophet's ﷺ right and one to his left, defending him fiercely — "I have never seen these men before or after that day" — understood to mean the angels Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them.

Abu Al-Aswad reported that 'Urwah bin Az-Zubayr said that Ubayy bin Khalaf had sworn in Makkah to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that when he came at him on the day of Uhud, Mus'ab bin 'Umayr intercepted him and shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his body — and Mus'ab was killed.

Al-Bukhari recorded that Anas bin Malik said that when the Muslims turned their backs and fled, his uncle Anas bin An-Nadr said, "O Allah! I apologize to You for what these have done, and I denounce what these pagans have done," and said to Sa'd bin Mu'adh, "Paradise! I am smelling its aroma coming from before Uhud." He advanced, fought, and was killed; more than eighty stab wounds, sword blows or arrow holes were found on his body. When ayah 152 says "some of you desire the Hereafter," this is the face behind the phrase. And it is recorded in the Two Sahihs that Sahl bin Sa'd, asked about the injuries the Messenger ﷺ sustained, said that his face was injured, his front tooth broken and his helmet smashed on his head.

### "Distress upon distress" — where the scholars differ

Ibn Kathir renders *ghamman bi-ghamm* as "He gave you grief over your grief." The early authorities read the two griefs differently, and the sources report the disagreement rather than settle it:

- **Ibn 'Abbas:** the first grief was the defeat, especially when it was rumoured that Muhammad ﷺ was killed; the second was the idolaters going up the mount, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "O Allah! It is not for them to rise above us."
- **'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf:** the first was the defeat, the second the rumour of the Prophet's ﷺ death — "which to them, was worse than defeat." Ibn Marduwyah recorded both of these.
- **Mujahid and Qatadah:** the first was hearing he ﷺ was killed, the second the casualties and injury. It has also been reported that Qatadah and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas said it was the opposite order.
- **As-Suddi:** the first was the victory and booty they missed; the second, the enemy rising above them on the mount.

**Why "requital"?** *Athābakum* normally belongs to the vocabulary of *reward*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the tension: the outward form was, no doubt, that of punishment, but the real purpose was "a sort of affectionate correction, something similar to a well-meaning reprimand from a father to his son or a teacher to his student" — a form of training and correction, very different from a pure legal punishment.

**Its stated aim:** "to teach you not to grieve for that which had escaped you, nor for what struck you" — not over the booty and triumph missed, nor over the injury and fatalities, as Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf, Al-Hasan, Qatadah and As-Suddi stated. Grief was administered as a cure for grief: a heart schooled here would not be ruled again by what it loses. The ayah closes, "And Allah is Well-Aware of all that you do."

## Ayah 154: sleep sent down on a battlefield

Ibn Kathir calls this a reminder of Allah's favour: tranquillity and slumber came over them "while they were carrying their weapons and feeling distress and grief." Here slumber is a favour and carries meanings of calmness and safety, as Allah said of Badr, "when He covered you with a slumber as a security from Him" (8:11).

Al-Bukhari recorded that Anas said that Abu Talhah said, "I was among those who were overcome by slumber during the battle of Uhud. My sword fell from my hand several times and I would pick it up, then it would fall and I would pick it up again." At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Al-Hakim recorded from Anas that Abu Talhah said, "On the day of Uhud, I raised my head and looked around and found that everyone's head was nodding from slumber" — this is the wording of At-Tirmidhi, who said, "Hasan Sahih."

**Two parties, two inner states.** Ibn Kathir identifies the sleepers as "the people of faith, certainty, firmness and reliance on Allah," certain that Allah would give victory to His Messenger ﷺ and fulfil his objective. The second group he identifies as the hypocrites, who "only thought about themselves" and were not overcome by slumber because of their worry, fright and fear; they "thought wrongly of Allah — the thought of ignorance," concluding that the idolaters had achieved ultimate victory and that Islam and its people would perish. This, Ibn Kathir notes, is typical of people of doubt and hesitation when hardship arrives.

Ibn Ishaq recorded that 'Abdullah bin Az-Zubayr said that Az-Zubayr said — a report Ibn Abi Hatim collected — "I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when fear intensified and Allah sent sleep to us… By Allah! As if in a dream, I heard the words of Mu'attib bin Qushayr, 'If we had anything to do with the affair, none of us would have been killed here.'" The Qur'an quotes that sentence back at its speaker.

**The answer given is destiny.** "Say: Indeed the affair belongs wholly to Allah" — and "Even if you had remained in your homes, those for whom death was decreed would certainly have gone forth to the place of their death." Ibn Kathir: "this is Allah's appointed destiny and a decision that will certainly come to pass, and there is no escaping it." The complaint assumes staying home was a way out. There is no such way.

**And the purpose:** "that Allah might test what is in your breasts, and to purify that which was in your hearts" — so that He tests you with whatever befell you, distinguishing the deeds and statements of the believers from those of the hypocrites: **a test, not a punishment**, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses.

## Ayah 155: how a slip happens, and how it is erased

"Shaytan only caused them to err because of some of what they had earned" — that is, because of some of their previous errors, says Ibn Kathir, who adds a saying of some of the Salaf: **"The reward of the good deed includes being directed to another good deed that follows it, while the retribution of sin includes committing another sin that follows it."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops this into a law of the heart: all deeds, good and bad, have a sort of magnetic pull of their own. One good deed makes the next easier and the heart itself starts desiring good; one sin clears the way for others and the heart starts desiring what is sinful. And from Maulana Ashraf 'Ali Thanavi in Masa'il us-Suluk: "As explained in hadith, sin makes the heart dark and when the heart goes dark, Satan prevails."

Maʿārif also asks how ayah 155 (Shaytan made them slip through what they had earned) fits with 154 (so that Allah may test). Its answer: the particular past mistake was the obvious reason that gave Satan his incentive — but behind the slip and its outcome stood the wise arrangements of the Creator, covered by the expression "so that Allah may test you." It relays too, from Ruh al-Ma'ani, a report from Zajjaj that Satan made them recall some of their sins, in the presence of which they hesitated to appear before their Lord.

Then the verdict: **"But Allah, indeed, has forgiven them. Surely, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Forbearing."** Ibn Kathir explains that He has pardoned their giving flight; He forgives sins, pardons and exonerates His creatures. The ayah that recorded the failure ends on two names of mercy.

## What the pardon settles

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not minimise what happened: the majority of the fifty Companions commanded to guard the hill-top left a post they were explicitly told to hold no matter what, and the retreat took place while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was unmoved at the front line, calling them back from behind. Viewed without reference to personalities and circumstances, it says, that action would certainly be classed as a very serious breach of conduct in a military encounter. And yet, in these very ayat, their grief was physically changed into tranquillity through drowsiness, they were told the suffering was a test and not a punishment, and forgiveness was proclaimed in clear words — in 152 and again in 155. Maʿārif reads the repetition as deliberate: to comfort the noble Companions themselves, and — incidentally — to refute the hypocrites, who had chided the Muslims for not acting on their advice.

That pardon governs how believers speak afterwards. Imam Ahmad recorded that Shaqiq said that when 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf's words "I did not run away during Uhud" were conveyed to 'Uthman, he replied: **"How can he blame me for an error that Allah has already forgiven"** — and recited this very ayah. And Maʿārif relates that when someone satirised 'Uthman and other Companions for having run from the battlefield that day, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said, "Nobody has the right to criticize that which Allah has expressly proclaimed to have been forgiven" (Sahih al-Bukhari).

On this basis Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamaʿah: the Companions are not above sin — sins can be and have been committed by them — yet it is not permissible for the Muslim community to ascribe evil or defect to them in a derogatory manner. It cites al-'Aqa'id an-Nasfiyah ("It is necessary that one should not talk about the Companions except in a good manner") and Ibn Taymiyyah's al-'Aqidatul Wasitiyah, which adds that most of the narrations imputing drawbacks to them are lies planted by enemies or reports reversed by additions and alterations, and that whatever truth there may be in something is to be taken as their own independent judgment.

## Living it

**Obedience is not conditional on your reading of the situation.** The archers judged that the purpose of the order had been served — an erroneous independent judgment, as Maʿārif puts it, but one that stood in clear contravention of a definite instruction from the Prophet ﷺ.

**Watch the heart in the hour of success.** Nothing collapsed while the fighting was still hard; it collapsed at the moment of visible victory, when the spoils came into sight.

**Do not read every hardship as abandonment** — the same ayat that describe the rout call it a test (152, 154) and the grief a correction. And **guard the small sins**: ayah 155 traces the slip back to what was earned beforehand.

**Do not despair after failure.** The passage ends not with the seventy dead but with "Allah, indeed, has forgiven them."
